readings.title: Reading #9. Sylvia Earle, underwater hero
readings.qtype: Short answer + True / False / Not Given
text: She has spent her working life studying the world's oceans. Sylvia Earle is an underwater explorer and marine biologist who was born in the USA in 1935. She became interested in the world's oceans from an early age. As a child, she liked to stand on the beach for hours and look at the sea, wondering what it must be like under the surface.

When she was 16, she finally got a chance to make her first dive. It was this dive that inspired her to become an underwater explorer. Since then, she has spent more than 6,500 hours under water, and has led more than seventy expeditions worldwide. She has also made the deepest dive ever, reaching a record-breaking depth of 381 metres.

In 1970, she became famous around the world when she became the captain of the first all-female team to live under water. The team spent two weeks in an underwater 'house'. The research they carried out showed the damage that pollution was causing to marine life, and especially to coral reefs. Her team also studied the problem of over-fishing. Fishing methods meant that people were catching too many fish, Earle warned, and many species were in danger of becoming extinct.

Since then she has written several books and magazine articles in which she suggests ways of reducing the damage that is being done to the world's oceans. One way, she believes, is to rely on fish farms for seafood, and reduce the amount of fishing that is done out at sea. Although she no longer eats seafood herself, she realises the importance it plays in our diets. It would be wrong to tell people they should stop eating fish from the sea, she says. However, they need to reduce the impact they are having on the ocean's supplies.

tasks.title: Short answer questions (1–4)
tasks.type: NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER from the passage
items: What career did Sylvia decide to follow after her first dive?
How far under water did she go in order to break a world record?
What was causing harm to everything living in the sea?
Where does Sylvia think we should get our fish from?
why: "It was this dive that inspired her to become an underwater explorer". "Decide to follow a career" = "inspired her to become".
"The deepest dive ever, reaching a record-breaking depth of 381 metres". Kalitda "381 metre", matnda "metres" — matndagidek yozing.
"The damage that pollution was causing to marine life". "Harm" = "damage", "everything living in the sea" = "marine life".
"One way, she believes, is to rely on fish farms for seafood". "Think" = "believes".

tasks.title: TRUE, FALSE or NOT GIVEN (1–5)
tasks.instr: Har javob uchun matndagi gapni ko'rsating.
items: Sylvia Earle lives in the USA.
Until 1970, nobody had lived underwater before.
Sylvia Earle was worried about the amount of fish that were being caught.
Her books offer some solutions to marine problems.
She thinks people should avoid eating seafood.
why: Matnda u AQShda TUG'ILGANI aytilgan ("born in the USA"), hozir qayerda yashashi aytilmagan. Tug'ilgan joy ≠ yashash joyi.
Matnda "the first ALL-FEMALE team to live under water" deyilgan — birinchi ayollar jamoasi. Undan oldin erkaklar yashaganmi-yo'qmi, aytilmagan. Cheklovchi so'zga e'tibor bering.
"People were catching too many fish, Earle warned". "Worried" = "warned", "amount" = "too many".
"Books ... in which she suggests ways of reducing the damage". "Offer solutions" = "suggests ways".
"It would be wrong to tell people they should stop eating fish from the sea". O'zi dengiz mahsuloti yemaydi, lekin boshqalarga buni tavsiya qilmaydi — tuzoq.
tasks.note: 2 va 5-savollar eng yaxshi tuzoq misoli. 2-savolda "all-female" so'zi, 5-savolda uning o'zi va boshqalar farqi javobni belgilaydi.

readings.title: The accident that gave us the microwave
text: In 1945 an American engineer called Percy Spencer was testing a magnetron, a device used in radar equipment during the Second World War. While he stood in front of the machine, he noticed that a chocolate bar in his pocket had melted. Spencer had left school at twelve and had no university degree, but he had already registered dozens of patents.

Curious, he sent for a bag of popcorn kernels and held them near the magnetron. They popped. The next morning he tried an egg, which exploded in the face of a colleague who leaned over it. Spencer understood that the waves were heating the water inside the food, and that the heat came from the inside out.

The first commercial microwave oven went on sale in 1947. It was nearly two metres tall, weighed 340 kilograms and cost about 5,000 dollars — as much as a house in some parts of the country. Restaurants and ships bought a few, but ordinary families did not.

Everything changed in 1967, when a smaller model appeared for less than 500 dollars. By 1975 microwaves were selling faster than gas cookers in the United States, and today they are found in more than 90 per cent of American homes. Spencer himself received no extra payment for the invention beyond the company's standard bonus of two dollars.

The first microwave oven was sold to restaurants.
Microwaves outsold gas cookers in the US by 1975.
More than 90 per cent of homes worldwide have a microwave today.

"Had left school at twelve and had no university degree".

readings.title: The woman who mapped the ocean floor
text: When Marie Tharp finished her geology degree in 1944, American universities were short of male students because of the war, and for the first time women were accepted onto the course. After graduating she moved to New York and found work at Columbia University, where she was given a desk but not a place on the research ships: women were not allowed on board until 1965.

Her colleague Bruce Heezen collected measurements of ocean depth from the Atlantic; Tharp turned thousands of numbers into pictures. Working by hand, she drew the shape of the sea floor, line by line, on long sheets of paper. In 1952 she noticed something nobody expected: a deep valley running along the middle of the underwater mountain chain.

Heezen called her idea "girl talk", because it supported the theory of continental drift, which most scientists then rejected. For almost a year he refused to publish it. Only after the same valley appeared in recordings of underwater earthquakes did he agree that she was right. The discovery became one of the main pieces of evidence for plate tectonics, the idea that the Earth's surface is made of moving plates.

Tharp's name did not appear on the most famous map she helped create, published in 1977, although her drawings were the basis for it. Recognition came late: she received her first major award in 1996, at the age of seventy-six, and the Library of Congress later named her one of the great cartographers of the twentieth century.

"In 1996, at the age of seventy-six".

readings.title: The first photograph
text: The oldest surviving photograph was taken in 1826 or 1827 by a French inventor, Joseph Nicéphore Niépce, from an upstairs window of his house in Burgundy. The picture shows the roofs of farm buildings and a tree. To make it, Niépce covered a metal plate with a kind of natural tar which hardens in light, and left the plate inside a wooden box with a lens for at least eight hours — some experts believe several days.

Niépce called the process heliography, from the Greek words for "sun" and "writing". He was not trying to make art: his first aim had been to copy printed pictures cheaply. He worked alone for years, spending much of his small income on materials, and received no public attention during his life.

In 1829 he agreed to work with Louis Daguerre, a painter from Paris. Niépce died four years later, and in 1839 Daguerre announced a faster process, the daguerreotype, which needed only a few minutes. The French government bought the invention and gave it to the world; Daguerre became famous, while Niépce's name was almost forgotten for a century.

The original plate was lost for many years and rediscovered in a London storeroom in 1952. It is now kept in Texas in a sealed case filled with a gas that protects it from air. Visitors often say it is difficult to see anything at all: the image is pale, and the light in the photograph comes from both sides, because the sun moved across the sky while the picture was being made.

intro: Diagram labelling — matndagi tavsifni rasmga ko'chirish. Javob deyarli har doim OT (qism nomi) bo'ladi.
Avval chizmaga qarang: nima tasvirlangan, qaysi qismlar allaqachon nomlangan? Nomlangan qismlar — langar.
Keyin matndan o'sha nomlangan qismni toping. Javob shu jumlaning yonida turadi.
Joy predloglari eng muhim: above (ustida), below/beneath (ostida), inside (ichida), on either side (ikki yonida), at the base (tagida), through (orqali).
Yo'nalish so'zlari jarayon sxemasida keladi: enters, passes, flows into, is carried to, comes out of.
Javob so'z chegarasidan oshmasin: "ONE WORD ONLY" bo'lsa, "metal ring" emas, "ring".
Diagram labelling savollari odatda (USUALLY) matn tartibida joylashadi: topilgan javobdan keyin qidiring, topilmasa nomlangan qismlarga qayting.

readings.title: Reading #10. The electric revolution
text: Your next car may be electric. We look at the technologies that will bring the revolution.

The main reasons why electric cars are not more popular at present are their price and their relatively small range. Existing battery systems only allow electric cars to travel a distance of between 100 and 160 km. However, this distance may not be a problem for urban drivers. A recent Sydney study reported that 20 percent of journeys were 30 km or less, and recent data from the US suggests that ?? percent of trips taken there are 48 km or less.

An innovative company called Better Place is aiming to make electric cars an option for all drivers. It wants to see existing vehicles replaced by electric vehicles which, it says, offer a number of benefits. Firstly, they can be powered by renewable energy which produces zero emissions. What is more, electric motors are more efficient and can convert more than 90 percent of power into movement, whereas the efficiency of diesel or petrol engines is less than 20 percent. To achieve its aim, Better Place plans to use technology which is already available.

The plan is simple but revolutionary. It starts with the installation of a home charge point, and through this, the vehicle will be plugged into the electricity grid whenever it is in the garage, typically at night. In the morning, with a fully charged battery, the car is capable of as much as 160 km in urban motoring conditions. In addition to the home charge point, the battery can be topped up by charge points at work and at supermarkets.

The battery is linked to a control centre by smart technology inside the vehicle. Better Place can then ensure that the car is charged with electricity from renewable sources at the cheapest price. For longer trips, a navigation system directs the driver to the nearest switch station, where the depleted battery can be replaced with a charged one by a robot within a couple of minutes.

the depleted battery can be replaced

readings.title: Inside a wind turbine
text: A modern wind turbine looks simple from a distance, but it contains more than eight thousand parts. The structure stands on a concrete base, sometimes twenty metres across, which is buried under the ground. Above this rises the tower, a hollow steel tube with a ladder and, in larger machines, a small lift inside.

At the top of the tower sits a box about the size of a bus. This box is called the nacelle, and it holds the working parts of the machine. Attached to the front of the nacelle is the hub, and three blades are fixed to the hub. Each blade is made of glass fibre and can be longer than eighty metres — longer than the wing of a large aircraft.

Inside the nacelle, the slow turning of the blades, about fifteen times a minute, is passed to a gearbox, which increases the speed to around 1,500 turns a minute. The fast shaft then drives the generator, where movement becomes electricity. Behind the generator, at the back of the nacelle, a small weather station measures wind speed and direction; a motor called the yaw drive turns the whole nacelle so that the blades always face the wind.

The electricity travels down cables inside the tower to a transformer at the base, which raises the voltage so that the power can be carried along the grid. A single large turbine produces enough electricity for about two thousand homes, and modern machines start working in a wind of only three metres a second.

readings.title: How a vacuum flask keeps drinks hot
text: The vacuum flask was invented in 1892 by the Scottish scientist James Dewar, who needed to store extremely cold gases in his laboratory. He never patented it; a German company began selling flasks for tea and coffee eleven years later.

The flask works by stopping the three ways in which heat moves. Its heart is a glass or steel bottle with double walls. The air between the two walls is removed, leaving a vacuum. Because heat cannot travel through empty space by conduction, very little warmth escapes through the sides.

The inner surface of both walls is covered with a thin layer of silver, which acts like a mirror and reflects heat back into the liquid. This stops radiation. At the bottom of the inner bottle there is a small glass point, sealed after the air was taken out; this is the weakest part, so the bottle sits on a soft pad of rubber or foam inside the outer case.

The outer case, usually plastic or metal, protects the fragile bottle and stays cool to touch. At the top, a tight stopper made of plastic or cork closes the neck; this prevents convection, the movement of warm air upwards and out. Many modern flasks add a cup, which screws over the stopper and serves as a lid. Together these parts can keep a drink hot for up to twenty-four hours, though every time the flask is opened it loses several degrees.

readings.title: The parts of a traditional water mill
text: Water mills have ground grain into flour for more than two thousand years, and a few still work in Central Asia and Europe today. The building is usually placed beside a fast stream. Water is taken from the stream further upriver and carried along a narrow channel, called the leat, which runs almost level so that the water arrives above the height of the wheel.

At the end of the leat the water passes through a wooden gate, the sluice, which the miller opens and closes to control the flow. From there it falls onto the wheel. In an overshot mill the water lands in buckets at the top of the wheel and turns it by weight; in an undershot mill the water pushes the bottom of the wheel instead, and less power is produced.

The wheel turns a horizontal beam, the axle, which passes through the wall into the building. Inside, a large wooden gearwheel, the pit wheel, changes the direction of the movement from horizontal to vertical. A vertical shaft then carries the movement upwards to the millstones on the floor above.

There are always two millstones. The lower one, the bed stone, never moves. The upper one, the runner stone, turns just above it, leaving a gap thinner than a sheet of paper. Grain falls into the centre of the runner stone from a wooden box called the hopper, moves outwards between the stones, and leaves the edge as flour, which slides down a wooden chute into sacks on the floor below.

readings.title: Reading #11. The Boeing 787
text: The Boeing 787 'Dreamliner' has been described as the airliner of the future. We look at the technology that makes it different.

Until now, airliner fuselages have been made of aluminium sheets. Large aircraft can have 1,500 of these sheets with between 40,000 and 50,000 metal fasteners. The 787 is the first airliner to be built with a one-piece fuselage made from a special material called 'composite'. Not only does this make the airliner quicker and easier to build, but it also makes it a lot lighter.

The advantage of this weight reduction is that the 787 uses 20 percent less fuel than other airliners of a similar size, which makes it much more environmentally friendly. The reduced weight also means that the Boeing 787 can fly further than many other airliners of a similar size, carrying 210 passengers or more up to 15,200 kilometres before refuelling.

Sometimes an airliner needs to change from one type of engine to another. This is a difficult and time-consuming process. The 787 has a revolutionary engine attachment on the wing which means that the engines can be changed in a much shorter time. The case containing the engine is also different from those on other airliners. It has been designed to cut down the noise from the engine, making it less noisy for passengers in the cabin as well as for people on the ground.

In addition to a quieter cabin, passengers will also benefit from windows which are 65 percent larger than those on other airliners, giving them a much better view of the world passing by below them. The windows also have a unique facility which allows passengers or cabin crew to control the amount of light that enters them. This is thanks to a liquid in the window which reacts to an electric current. When a passenger or cabin crew member presses a button, the current causes a chemical reaction in the window which darkens the liquid.

tasks.title: Complete labels (1–7) on the diagram
tasks.type: NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER from the passage
tasks.instr: Eng qiyin mashq: belgilar uzun, paraphrase ko'p. Har belgida kalit so'zni tagiga chizing.
items: Composite fuselage material is much ___ than traditional aluminium sheets.
Composite fuselage material reduces the amount of ___ that the airliner needs.
Engineers can fit a new engine in a ___ than it takes on other airliners.
The size of the windows has increased by ___.
Window glass can be made darker by passing an ___ through them.
why: "It also makes it a lot lighter". "Much" = "a lot"; "than" dan oldin qiyosiy daraja keladi.
"The 787 uses 20 percent less fuel". "Reduces the amount" = "uses less".
"Carrying 210 passengers or more". "At least" = "or more", "accommodate" = "carrying".
"The engines can be changed in a much shorter time". "Fit a new engine" = "engines can be changed".
"Designed to cut down the noise from the engine". "Reduces" = "cut down". "Noise" yoki "engine noise" — ikkalasi to'g'ri.
"Windows which are 65 percent larger". "Increased by" = "larger".
"A liquid in the window which reacts to an electric current ... darkens the liquid". PAROSAT: "an" artikli unli harf bilan boshlanadigan so'zni ko'rsatadi.
tasks.note: Matnda ikkita foiz bor: 20 percent (yoqilg'i) va 65 percent (derazalar). 6-belgi derazalar haqida — shuning uchun 65.

homework_intro: Bugun chizmadagi belgini matndan topishni birga mashq qildik — uyga vazifada xuddi shu ishni endi yolg'iz o'zingiz, ustozsiz bajarasiz.
Birinchi vazifa — "The parts of a traditional water mill" matni: soatga qarab 10 daqiqa vaqt oling va 9 ta belgini to'ldiring, javob ONE WORD ONLY, ya'ni faqat bitta so'z.

Ikkinchisi — "O'z chizmangiz": uyingizdagi bitta qurilmani (choynak, velosiped, fen) chizib, 8 qismini inglizcha belgilaysiz va har biriga kamida 6 ta predlog ishlatib joylashuv gapini yozasiz, bu 20 daqiqacha vaqt oladi; uchinchisi — 15 gapli predlog testi, doskadagi ro'yxatdan foydalanasiz va 15 tadan 13 tasi to'g'ri bo'lsa bajarilgan hisoblanadi.

Eng ko'p qilinadigan xato shu yerda: chizmada allaqachon yozilgan so'z bo'sh joyga yana ko'chiriladi — "the ___ stone" ga "bed stone" deb ikki so'z yoziladi, to'g'risi esa faqat "bed"; va javob har doim ot bo'lsin, fe'l emas.
Uchala vazifa ham bitta daftarda bo'ladi, chizmangizni daftarga yopishtirasiz va keyingi darsga olib kelasiz: birinchi 10 daqiqada javoblarni juftlikda solishtiramiz, keyin daftarlarni yig'ib olaman.

lessons.book_ref: Jony Academy materiali — ustoz bergan audio va chizmalar (Track 17 Ferry facilities; Track 08 Sunshine Express — eng qiyin, oxirida) va 3 ta mualliflik skripti.

materials: Audio: Track 17 (ielts5_08_ferry.mp3) va Track 08 (ielts5_08_train.mp3) — darsdan oldin ochib, ovoz balandligi tekshirilsin; ikkalasi ham sinfda FAQAT BIR MARTA qo'yiladi.

Sinf mashqi (Joy iboralari mashqi) uchun 6 ta kartochka: opposite the entrance; just above the handle; at the far end of the corridor; on your left as you come in; between the pump and the tank; running along the back wall.
Har o'quvchida oddiy qalam va o'chirg'ich (audio vaqtida chizmaga belgi qo'yiladi), ustozda 4 ta skript transkripti va joy iboralarini bo'yash uchun marker.

intro: Listeningdagi diagram labelling — reading bilan bir xil mantiq, lekin BIR MARTA eshitiladi, shuning uchun chizmani oldindan o'qish shart.
So'zlovchi chizma bo'ylab TARTIB bilan yuradi: odatda yuqoridan pastga yoki chapdan o'ngga. Shu tartibni kuting.
Joy iboralari javobni belgilaydi: "on the left", "at the far end", "just above", "in the middle", "next to", "opposite".
Chalg'ituvchi: "The office used to be near the entrance, but now it's opposite the café." Javob — hozirgi holat.
Javob deyarli har doim ot: part, room, machine nomlari.
Eshitayotganda chizmaga qalam bilan belgi qo'ying; javobni keyin to'liq yozasiz.
presentation: Chizmani qachon o'qiyman?
Audio boshlanishidan oldin beriladigan 20–30 soniyada.
So'zlovchi qaysi tartibda yuradi?
Odatda chizma bo'ylab: yuqoridan pastga yoki chapdan o'ngga.
"Opposite the café" nimani bildiradi?
Kafening ro'parasi — chizmada qarama-qarshi tomon.
Eski va yangi joy aytilsa?
Hozirgi holatni oling: "used to be ... but now".
Javobni eshitib ulgurmasam?
Belgi qo'yib, keyingisiga o'ting; oxirida to'ldirasiz.
Javob fe'l bo'lishi mumkinmi?
Kam. Diagram labelling javoblari deyarli har doim ot.
notes: Ustoz avval chizmani doskaga chizadi va o'quvchilardan "qaysi tartibda aytiladi?" deb so'raydi.
Skriptni birinchi marta to'liq o'qing; ikkinchi marta faqat tekshirish uchun bo'laklab o'qing.
Transkriptni tarqatgandan keyin joy iboralarini marker bilan belgilatish foydali.
Har skriptdan keyin: "qaysi so'z javobni ochdi?" — signal so'zni toping.

listenings.title: Track 17. Ferry facilities — Pride of Poole
intro: Kemadagi yo'lovchilar uchun e'lon. Avval chizmani 1 daqiqa o'rganing: "Reception: you are here" — boshlanish nuqtasi. A, B, C Deck qayerda ekanini toping va har bo'sh joy turini ayting.
Ko'rsatma: Write ONE WORD ONLY for each answer. Diagramma javoblari USUALLY tartibda keladi — e'lon sizni kema bo'ylab "yurgizadi".
transcript: Good evening and welcome aboard the Pride of Poole. In this recorded announcement, we'll give you details of some of the facilities available on board this ship.

You're currently standing in the reception area in the centre of B Deck. If you're feeling hungry after a long day's travelling, go up the stairs to A Deck, where you'll find the restaurant. The restaurant caters for all appetites, with anything from a light snack to a full three-course meal. The restaurant will be open from the moment the ship leaves port to half an hour before arrival.

Next to the restaurant on A Deck in the lounge, there are reclining seats with music headphones if you want to relax. The headphones are free, but people using this area are encouraged to keep noise to a minimum so that other passengers can enjoy themselves and sleep or read if they wish.

For those of you who'd like some entertainment, just next door to us on this deck is a 40-seat cinema showing the latest full-length feature films. The cinema programme is available here at reception, but you'll have to buy the tickets themselves at the cinema entrance just before you go in.
Just next to the cinema is the staircase leading down to the cabins on C Deck. To access your cabin, just show your boarding pass to a steward, who will give you the key.
On this deck, that is B Deck, you'll also find an area where you can either play games in our special electronic games arcade or do your shopping.

Just beyond that on the same level, people who want a bit of fresh air or just want to see the sea can go out onto the viewing deck, which is in the open air. Make sure you wear a jacket or coat, as it can be quite cold and windy.

listenings.title: Guided tour of a small factory
intro: Kichik shokolad fabrikasi bo'ylab ekskursiya. Chizmada zal rejasi bor. BIR MARTA tinglang.
transcript: GUIDE: Welcome to Brookfield Chocolate. Before we go in, let me show you the plan of the building, so you know where everything is.

GUIDE: We're standing at the main entrance, at the bottom of the plan. As you come in, on your left there's the reception desk, and behind that a small shop where you can buy our products at the end of the tour.
GUIDE: Directly opposite the entrance, at the far end of the corridor, is the tasting room. That's where we finish, so remember the way.

GUIDE: Now, the working area. On the right of the corridor, the first door leads to the store room, where the cocoa beans arrive in large sacks. Next to the store room, going up the plan, is the roasting area — you'll smell it before you see it.
GUIDE: Above the roasting area, in the top right corner, is the grinding room. The nibs are ground there into a thick liquid. Please don't touch the machines; they are hot.

GUIDE: In the middle of the building, between the grinding room and the tasting room, you'll find the mixing hall. Sugar and milk powder are added there. The large silver tanks you can see through the window are in that hall.

GUIDE: The last production area, in the top left corner, is the moulding section, where liquid chocolate is poured into shapes and cooled. It's kept at eighteen degrees, so take a jacket if you feel the cold.
GUIDE: Finally, next to the shop, there's the packing area. It used to be upstairs, but we moved it down last year so that visitors can watch through the glass. Any questions before we start?

listenings.title: How a rainwater system works
intro: Uy uchun yomg'ir suvini yig'ish tizimi haqida ma'ruza. Chizmada tizim kesimi. BIR MARTA tinglang.
transcript: SPEAKER: Right, let's look at how a domestic rainwater system actually works. I'll follow the water from the roof down to the tap.
SPEAKER: Rain falls on the roof and runs into the gutter along the edge. Nothing unusual so far. The gutter takes the water to a vertical pipe at the corner of the house — that's the downpipe.
SPEAKER: At the bottom of the downpipe, before anything else, there's a leaf filter. It's a simple mesh basket. Most people forget to clean it, and that's the commonest cause of problems.

SPEAKER: After the filter the water reaches the first flush device. The idea is simple: the first few litres carry dust and bird droppings, so they are sent away and not stored. Once that small chamber is full, the clean water passes on.
SPEAKER: The water then enters the tank, which is usually underground, where the temperature stays low and the water keeps better. A typical family tank holds five thousand litres.
SPEAKER: Inside the tank, notice that the inlet pipe has a smooth curve at the end, called a calmed inlet. It slows the water so that the dirt at the bottom is not stirred up.
SPEAKER: The pump sits either in the tank or beside it; in our diagram it's outside, in the small chamber on the right. It sends water to the house through the supply line.

SPEAKER: Near the top of the tank there's an overflow, which takes extra water away in heavy rain. And finally, at the house end, there's a backflow valve, which makes sure rainwater can never enter the drinking water pipes.

listenings.title: The new library building
intro: Yangi kutubxona binosining rejasi tanishtiriladi. Uyda bir marta tinglang.
transcript: LIBRARIAN: Good afternoon, everyone. I'd like to explain the layout of the new building, because it's quite different from the old one.
LIBRARIAN: You come in from Park Street, through the main doors at the bottom of the plan. Straight in front of you is the help desk; if you're lost, that's where to go.

LIBRARIAN: To the right of the help desk is the self-service area, with four machines for borrowing and returning books. To the left, behind the glass wall, is the children's section. It has its own small entrance from the garden, so families don't have to walk through the quiet areas.

LIBRARIAN: Now, the ground floor. Along the whole of the left-hand wall are the study rooms — six of them, bookable online for up to two hours. Opposite them, on the right-hand side, you'll find the newspaper corner and, beyond it, the café. The café has a separate door to the street, so it stays open after the library closes.
LIBRARIAN: At the back, in the middle, is the lift, with the stairs immediately to its left.

LIBRARIAN: Upstairs, the plan is simpler. The whole front half is the reading hall, with sixty desks. Behind it, on the right, is the computer room — twenty machines, no food or drink. And in the far left corner, next to the window, is the local history collection. That used to be in the basement, but the damp damaged some books, so we moved it up.
LIBRARIAN: Finally, the toilets are on both floors, next to the lift.

listenings.title: Track 08. The Sunshine Express — train facilities
listenings.qtype: Diagram labelling (1–5) — eng qiyin, oxirgi mashq
intro: Poyezd menejeri Jane Sharpe yo'lovchilarga e'lon qilmoqda. Chizmada "Observation deck: you are here" — boshlanish nuqtasi. Avval har vagon qaysi tomonda ekanini (oldinda — lokomotiv, orqada — oxirgi vagon) aniqlang.
Ko'rsatma: Write ONE WORD ONLY for each answer. Bu mashq qiyinroq: yo'nalish so'zlari (below us, at the front, behind, at the back) tez-tez almashadi.
transcript: Hello, everyone, and welcome aboard the Sunshine Express on our journey from London to Naples. I'm Jane Sharpe, the train manager, and I hope you'll all enjoy the trip.

Before we depart, I'd like to tell you a bit about the train and its facilities. Now, we're here on the observation deck, which is where you'll probably spend most of your trip, as it offers the best views, and directly below us is a, well, we call it our leisure centre. There are some games machines, a television, a small library and so on. If you've brought a laptop or computer with you, you can also get onto the Internet here, as it has full wi-fi capability. There's also a small bar where you can get tea, coffee and light meals. For lunch and dinner, you'll use the restaurant car, which is at the front of the train. You'll have breakfast in your cabins, by the way, which will be brought to you by your steward.

The two cars behind the restaurant are where you'll find the second-class cabins. Each cabin has seats which are changed into beds at night. You'll also find a simple basin for washing, and a small fold-down table. First-class passengers, your cabins are at the back of the train. To get to them, you'll need to pass through the lounge. This can be used by everyone during the day, but is exclusive to first-class passengers after 6 p.m.

Right at the back of the train, basically as far as you can go, is my office. If anyone needs to see me, though, please use the phone in your cabin rather than coming to the office. Just press one and you'll get me. If I'm not there, tell your steward you need to see the manager, and he or she will look for me.

"For lunch and dinner, you'll use the restaurant car, which is at the front of the train". Midday and evening meals = lunch and dinner. Tuzoq: breakfast — kabinada.
"A simple basin for washing". Basic = simple. Tuzoq: "beds" va "fold-down table" — ular ham kabinada, lekin "___ facilities" = washing.
"Pass through the lounge ... exclusive to first-class passengers after 6 p.m." Only = exclusive; in the evening = after 6 p.m.
"Use the phone in your cabin ... you'll get me" — "me" = Jane Sharpe, the train manager. "Her" — ayol. Tuzoq: "steward" — menejer bo'lmasa stewardga aytiladi; lekin chizma "her"ni so'raydi.

lessons.title: Listening: Multiple Choice
lessons.grammar_topic: Multiple choice — uch variantdan bittasini tanlash
lessons.book_ref: Jony Academy materiali — ustoz bergan audiolar (Track 18 Ferry — further details; Track 09 Sunshine Express) va 3 ta mualliflik skripti.
objectives: Savol va uchta variantni audio boshlanishidan oldin o'qib ulgurish.
Uchala variant ham audioda eshitilishini bilish: eshitilgani emas, MOS kelgani tanlanadi.
Chalg'ituvchi turlarini tanish: eski ma'lumot, boshqa odamning fikri, qisman to'g'ri variant.
Variantni o'chirib borish usuli bilan ishlash (elimination).
Javobni belgilab, keyingi savolga o'tishda kechikmaslik.
materials: Audio: ielts5_09_ferry_details.mp3 (Track 18, Ferry) va ielts5_09_train_trip.mp3 (Track 09, Sunshine Express) — dars boshlanishidan oldin telefon yoki kolonkaga yuklab, orqa partadan eshitiladigan qilib sinab qo'ying; ikkalasi ham faqat BIR MARTA qo'yiladi.

"Choosing a part-time job" va "A talk about the city bike scheme" skriptlari — bu ikkisining audiosi yo'q, ustoz o'zi ovoz chiqarib o'qiydi: skriptni chop etib, MAYA va TOM repliklarini ikki xil belgilab chiqing.
Savol varag'i: Ferry 6–10, Sunshine Express 1–5, part-time job 1–5 va city bike 1–6 savollari A/B/C variantlari bilan — har o'quvchiga bitta nusxa, audio boshlanishidan OLDIN tarqatiladi.
Sekundomer yoki telefon taymeri — har mashq oldidan savollarni o'qishga 45 soniya berasiz; shu bilan uyga vazifadagi "Tez o'qish mashqi" ham tekshiriladi.

Transkript nusxalari (Ferry va Sunshine Express) — har juftlikka bitta, faqat tekshirish bosqichida tarqatiladi; har o'quvchida ikki xil rangli qalam bo'lsin: javob joyi bir rang, chalg'ituvchi joyi boshqa rang.

[class] "Chalg'ituvchi turlari" uchun 6 ta gap alohida qog'ozchalarga yozib, kesib qo'yiladi (o'quvchi kartochkani tortib oladi va turini aytadi); doskaga esa dars boshlanishidan oldin uch tur — ESKI ma'lumot / BOSHQA odamning fikri / QISMAN to'g'ri — va signal so'zlar yozib qo'yiladi: but, however, actually, though, in the end, only.
timeline: Salomlashish, o'tgan darsdagi savol turini 3 savolda eslatish
Ustoz doskada: qoida, bosqichlar, tipik xatolar
Savol turiga oid mashq birga bajariladi, har javob izohlanadi
Matndagi va savoldagi so'zlar jadvali; o'quvchilar ovoz chiqarib topadi
Mustaqil bajariladi, keyin javoblar izoh bilan tekshiriladi
Skript ustoz tomonidan o'qiladi yoki audio qo'yiladi, keyin transkript bilan tekshiriladi
Xatolar daftari: har xato javob sababi bilan yoziladi

intro: Multiple choice — eng ko'p vaqt oladigan tur, chunki o'qish kerak: savol + 3 variant.
Oltin qoida: audioda uchala variant ham aytiladi. Faqat bittasi savolga to'liq mos keladi.
Chalg'ituvchi 1 — ESKI ma'lumot: "It used to be on Mondays, but now it's on Thursdays."
Chalg'ituvchi 2 — BOSHQA odamning fikri: "My friend liked the food, but I thought the service was better."
Chalg'ituvchi 3 — QISMAN to'g'ri: variantda ikkita narsa aytiladi, audio faqat bittasini tasdiqlaydi.
Savolni o'qiyotganda kalit so'zni belgilang; variantlarni qisqa belgilab qo'ying (masalan: A = tez, B = arzon, C = yaqin).
Javob topilgach darhol belgilang va keyingi savolga qarang: audio to'xtamaydi.
Ishonchingiz komil bo'lmasa, eng ehtimolli variantni belgilang — bo'sh javob har doim 0.
formulas: A tez / B arzon / C yaqin
Ko'z bilan tez qamrab olish uchun
presentation: Uchala variant ham eshitildi. Qaysi biri javob?
Savolga TO'LIQ mos kelgani. Qolganlari chalg'ituvchi.
"It used to be..." degan gap eshitildi. Bu javobmi?
Yo'q, bu eski ma'lumot. Hozirgi holatni kuting.
Do'stining fikri aytildi, javob shumi?
Savol kimning fikrini so'rayotganiga qarang.
Savolni o'qishga ulgurmadim.
Variantlarning faqat farqli so'zini o'qing: tez / arzon / yaqin.
Ikkita variant to'g'ridek.
Savolning aniq so'ziga qayting: "main reason", "most", "first".
Javobni o'zgartirsam bo'ladimi?
Ha, lekin faqat aniq yangi ma'lumot eshitilsa.
notes: Ustoz skriptni o'qishdan oldin 45 soniya beradi: savol va variantlarni o'qish uchun.
Tekshirishda har chalg'ituvchi uchun "nega noto'g'ri" izohi aytilsin — bu darsning asosiy ishi.
Transkriptda javob joyini va chalg'ituvchi joyini ikki xil rangda belgilang.
Kuchsiz o'quvchilarga: avval faqat 3 savol, keyin 6 savol.

class_ex.title: Chalg'ituvchi turlari
class_ex.instr: Ustoz gap o'qiydi, o'quvchi chalg'ituvchi turini aytadi.
items: "The course was on Mondays last year, but now it's on Thursdays."
"My sister found it easy; I struggled with the writing."
"The hotel was clean and quiet, though the food was poor."
"We wanted to go by train, but in the end we drove."
"It's not the price that matters, it's the time."
"Almost everyone said yes — only two people disagreed."
why: Javob — Thursdays.
Savol kim haqida ekanini tekshiring.
Variantda "clean and good food" bo'lsa — noto'g'ri.
Javob — mashina.
Javob — vaqt.
"Hamma" emas.
class_ex.note: Har misolda "signal so'z" ni ayting: but, though, in the end, only, not ... it's.

listenings.title: Track 18. Ferry — further details
intro: 8-darsdagi "Pride of Poole" kemasi e'lonining davomi. Avval savollarni o'qing va har savolda kalit so'zni belgilang (what time, children, reduced price, lounge, special event). Keyin BIR MARTA tinglang.
Ko'rsatma: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C. MCQ da uchala variant ham audioda tilga olinadi — faqat bittasi savolga aniq javob.
transcript: Now for some further details. This voyage is an overnight trip. The ship leaves port at 7 p.m. and the journey takes just over 12 hours and 45 minutes, reaching our destination at about eight tomorrow morning. This is for the convenience of those wishing to catch the nine o'clock train, which leaves from the ferry terminal.

Passengers with children in their party are informed that there is a special section in the restaurant with kids' food and a play area. People with children are encouraged to turn up early to get a place, as the section is very popular.

Make this a trip to remember. Here at the information desk, you can obtain a souvenir ship's key ring for four euros fifty; you can upgrade from a tourist-class cabin to a first-class cabin; and you can get your train tickets here, which will save you time queuing in the station tomorrow morning. If you buy them on the ship, you can get them for 20 percent off.

For those using the lounge and wishing to check their email, there's a wireless connection, but you'll have to bring your own laptop. You can also watch the latest TV programmes there or in the coffee bar next to the restaurant.

Finally, a unique feature on this crossing only: anyone who buys a fashion item from our wonderful range of men's and women's clothes in the shopping area has the chance to win a free holiday. All you have to do is complete a sentence starting 'I like Sealand Ferries because ...' and the best sentence wins the prize of a holiday in Switzerland with tickets to a three-day music festival included. Talk to any member of staff for more details.

tasks.title: Questions 6–10: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C
tasks.instr: Savollar audio tartibida (ALWAYS). Uchala variant ham eshitiladi — "qaysi biri SAVOLGA javob?" deb so'rang.
items: 6 At approximately what time will the ship arrive? A) at 7 a.m. B) at 8 a.m. C) at 9 a.m.
7 Which of these can children have in the restaurant? A) a children's menu B) earlier mealtimes C) a children's party
8 What are available at a reduced price? A) souvenirs of the ship B) first-class cabins C) train tickets
9 Which of these is situated in the lounge? A) a computer B) a coffee machine C) a television
10 What special event will happen during the voyage? A) a fashion show B) a concert C) a competition
why: "Reaching our destination at about eight tomorrow morning". A tuzoq: "7 p.m." — jo'nash vaqti (kechqurun). C tuzoq: "the nine o'clock train" — poyezd vaqti, kema emas.

"A special section in the restaurant with kids' food". Kids' food = children's menu. B tuzoq: "turn up early to get a place" — joy olish uchun erta kelish, ovqat vaqti erta emas. C — "play area" bor, bayram yo'q.

"If you buy them on the ship, you can get them for 20 percent off" — them = train tickets. Reduced price = 20 percent off. A tuzoq: key ring narxi aytilgan (4.50), lekin chegirma yo'q. B — upgrade qilish mumkin, arzonroq emas.

"You can also watch the latest TV programmes there" — there = the lounge. A tuzoq: wireless bor, lekin "bring your own laptop" — kompyuter yo'q. B tuzoq: "coffee bar next to the restaurant" — boshqa joy.

"Complete a sentence ... the best sentence wins the prize" — bu tanlov (competition). A tuzoq: "fashion item" — kiyim sotib olish sharti, ko'rgazma emas. B tuzoq: "a three-day music festival" — sovrin ichida, kemada emas.
tasks.note: Ustoz kaliti: 6 B, 7 A, 8 C, 9 C, 10 C. Bu mashq Listening MCQ ning asosiy qonunini ko'rsatadi: har savolda UCHALA variant ham audioda tilga olinadi — 7 p.m./8/9 o'clock; kids' food/early/play; souvenir/first-class/tickets; laptop/coffee bar/TV; fashion/festival/sentence.

tasks.title: Nega boshqa variantlar emas?
tasks.instr: Har tuzoq variant audioda qanday eshitildi?
why: Soat to'g'ri, lekin p.m. va jo'nash — savol kelish vaqtini so'raydi.
Narx aytildi, chegirma emas.
Joy boshqa.
Sovrin — kemadagi voqea emas.

listenings.title: Track 09. The Sunshine Express — trip information
intro: London — Neapol poyezdi haqida e'lonning davomi (8-darsdagi Track 08 dan keyin). Avval savollarni o'qing va kalit so'zlarni tagiga chizing: how long, passports, dinner, Italian border, NOT do.
Ko'rsatma: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C. 5-savolda "NOT" bor — nima QILMASLIK kerakligini qidiring.
transcript: Right, let me give you a bit more information about the trip. The first part of our journey is from London to Paris, going through the Channel Tunnel. It will take us just over an hour to get to the Tunnel, including a short stop before we get there to pick up some more passengers. From there, it'll be another three hours to Paris, so we're looking at four hours altogether, give or take a few minutes.

A quick bit of advice about passports. You won't need these until we get to the Italian border, so I suggest you keep them in the safe which you'll find in your cabin. Ask your steward – that's the person in charge of your carriage – for a key. That way, you won't need to carry them with you all the time.

Now, meals. As I said earlier, breakfast tomorrow morning will be in your cabins, and this will be served at about 7.30, 7.45, so you'll be able to enjoy it as we travel along the southern French coast. Lunch is at 1 o'clock in the restaurant car, and dinner is at 8 o'clock, although we'd like you all to be at your table about fifteen minutes earlier, at a quarter to, if you could.

When we get to the Italian border tomorrow morning, our train will change engines, and we'll also be getting a new crew. We'll be taking advantage of the stop to have a look around. I've arranged a visit to the local market, a museum and a castle. This will take about four hours, with a break for coffee in a local café, and we'll be back on the train in time for lunch.

A few quick rules. Some of you might have brought your own food or drink on board. That's fine, but could we ask that you consume it in your cabins and not in the restaurant or lounge? Could we also ask you to make sure your cabin windows are closed when you're not in your cabin? And whatever you do, don't get off the train until we reach the Italian border. Apart from the border and one or two other places, which I'll tell you about, any stops we make will only be for a few minutes. I'd hate to leave anyone behind.
All right, so, moving on from the Italian border, we'll be heading ... [fade]

tasks.title: Questions 1–5: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C
tasks.instr: Savollar audio tartibida. Har savolda uchala variant ham eshitiladi.
items: 1 How long will it take to get to Paris? A) about one hour B) about three hours C) about four hours
2 What should passengers do with their passports? A) leave them with their steward B) lock them away C) carry them at all times
3 When should passengers be in the restaurant car for dinner? A) 7.45 p.m. B) 8.00 p.m. C) 8.15 p.m.
4 What will the passengers do when the train gets to the Italian border? A) change trains B) go on a tour C) have lunch in a local café
5 What should passengers NOT do? A) eat their own food on the train B) open their cabin window C) leave the train before it gets to Italy
why: "We're looking at four hours altogether". A tuzoq: "just over an hour to get to the Tunnel" — birinchi qism. B tuzoq: "another three hours to Paris" — ikkinchi qism. Jami: 1 + 3 = 4.
"Keep them in the safe which you'll find in your cabin" — safe = qulflanadi. A tuzoq: stewarddan faqat KALIT so'raladi. C teskari: "you won't need to carry them with you all the time".

"Dinner is at 8 o'clock, although we'd like you all to be at your table about fifteen minutes earlier, at a quarter to" — 7.45. B tuzoq: rasmiy vaqt. 7.45 nonushta vaqti sifatida ham eshitiladi (7.30, 7.45) — ehtiyot bo'ling.
"I've arranged a visit to the local market, a museum and a castle" — bu tur (tour). A tuzoq: poyezd emas, "change ENGINES". C tuzoq: kafeda QAHVA, tushlik esa poyezdda.

"Whatever you do, don't get off the train until we reach the Italian border". A tuzoq: o'z ovqatini yeyish mumkin — faqat kabinada. B tuzoq: oyna kabinada YO'Q bo'lganda yopiq bo'lsin — ochish umuman taqiqlanmagan.
tasks.note: Kitob kaliti: 1 C 2 B 3 A 4 B 5 C. 1 va 3-savollar — hisoblash tuzog'i: javob to'g'ridan-to'g'ri aytilmaydi (1 + 3 soat; 8 dan 15 daqiqa oldin).

tasks.title: Tuzoq turlari
why: Yo'lning bir qismi vaqti.
"Be at your table ... at a quarter to".
change engines ≠ change trains.
"fine, but in your cabins"; "closed when you're not in your cabin".

listenings.title: Choosing a part-time job
intro: Ikki talaba yarim kunlik ish haqida gaplashmoqda. BIR MARTA tinglang, har savolda A, B yoki C ni tanlang.
transcript: MAYA: Have you found a job yet, Tom?
TOM: I've got two offers, actually. One is in the university café, and the other is at the bookshop in town.
MAYA: The café pays well, doesn't it?
TOM: It's nine pounds an hour, and the bookshop is eight fifty. But the café shifts start at seven in the morning, and I have lectures at nine, so I'd be running across town every day.
MAYA: So you'll take the bookshop?
TOM: I think so. It's not the money — half an hour of sleep matters more to me right now.
MAYA: Fair enough. How many hours a week?
TOM: The bookshop wants twelve, but they said ten is possible during exams. The café wanted sixteen, which is too many.
MAYA: My job is only eight hours, but I work every Saturday, and I hate that.
TOM: Yes, weekends are the problem. The bookshop is closed on Sundays, and they rotate Saturdays, so I'd work two Saturdays a month.
MAYA: That's better than mine. What about the people?
TOM: I met the manager. She seemed strict — she talked a lot about being on time — but the other staff said she's fair, and she lets people swap shifts.
MAYA: My manager is friendly but hopeless at organising. Last week nobody knew who was working.
TOM: That sounds worse. Oh, and the bookshop gives a staff discount — thirty per cent on books.
MAYA: Thirty? That's dangerous for you.
TOM: I know. I'll probably spend my wages there.

tasks.title: Multiple choice
items: 1 Why does Tom prefer the bookshop? A) It pays more B) The hours suit him better C) It is nearer his home
2 How many hours a week will Tom probably work? A) eight B) ten C) twelve
3 What does Tom say about Saturdays? A) He will work every Saturday B) He will work two a month C) He will never work Saturdays
4 What do the staff say about the manager? A) She is fair B) She is disorganised C) She is unfriendly
5 What extra benefit does the bookshop offer? A) free meals B) a discount C) transport
why: "The café shifts start at seven ... I have lectures at nine". A noto'g'ri: kafe ko'proq to'laydi.
Do'kon 12 soat so'radi; 10 faqat imtihon paytida. 8 — Mayaning ishi.
"They rotate Saturdays, so I'd work two Saturdays a month".
"The other staff said she's fair". Tartibsizlik — Mayaning menejeri.
"A staff discount — thirty per cent on books".

tasks.title: Chalg'ituvchi izohi
tasks.instr: Har savolda nega boshqa variant noto'g'ri?
why: Pul ko'proq, lekin Tom pulni tanlamadi.
Boshqa odam haqida.
"I work every Saturday" deb u aytdi.
Boshqa odamning fikri.

listenings.title: A talk about the city bike scheme
intro: Shahar velosiped tizimi haqida qisqa ma'ruza. BIR MARTA tinglang.
transcript: SPEAKER: Good evening. I'm here to explain how the city bike scheme works, and to answer the question everyone asks: is it actually cheaper than the bus?
SPEAKER: The scheme opened three years ago with 200 bikes at 20 stations. Today there are 1,400 bikes at 130 stations, and we add about ten stations a year.

SPEAKER: Now, prices. A single ride of up to thirty minutes costs one pound fifty. A day pass is five pounds, and an annual membership is sixty. For most people the annual pass pays for itself after about six weeks of daily use.

SPEAKER: The most common complaint is not price, though — it's finding an empty space to leave the bike. In the morning everybody cycles towards the centre, so the central stations fill up. We move bikes back out by van at night, but the vans themselves are unpopular with residents.

SPEAKER: We are testing a solution: users who return a bike to an empty station in the centre get a free ride credit. In the trial, this cut the number of full stations by about a third, which is better than we expected.

SPEAKER: Safety. Helmets are not provided — we know some cities do this, but hygiene rules make it difficult. Instead we spend the money on lights, which are now fitted to every bike and switch on automatically.

SPEAKER: Finally, who uses the bikes? You might expect students, but our data shows that the largest group is people aged between thirty and forty-five, travelling to work. Students actually prefer walking, because the campus is close to the centre.

tasks.title: Multiple choice
items: 1 How many stations are there now? A) 20 B) 130 C) 1,400
2 An annual pass becomes cheaper than daily rides after about: A) six weeks B) thirty minutes C) three years
3 What do users complain about most? A) the price B) nowhere to park the bike C) the vans
4 What was the result of the trial? A) worse than expected B) as expected C) better than expected
5 Why are helmets not provided? A) they are too expensive B) for hygiene reasons C) they are not needed
6 Who uses the bikes most? A) students B) people aged 30–45 C) tourists
why: "1,400 bikes at 130 stations". 20 — boshlang'ich, 1,400 — velosiped soni.
"Pays for itself after about six weeks of daily use".
"The most common complaint ... it's finding an empty space to leave the bike".
"Which is better than we expected".
"Hygiene rules make it difficult".
"The largest group is people aged between thirty and forty-five".

tasks.title: Chalg'ituvchi izohi
answers: narx eng ko'p shikoyat emas; furgonlar aholiga yoqmaydi
why: Savol stansiyalar haqida.
"Not price, though".
Sabab — gigiyena.
"Students actually prefer walking".

listenings.title: Tutorial: choosing a project topic
intro: Talaba va ustoz loyiha mavzusi haqida gaplashmoqda. Uyda bir marta tinglang.
transcript: TUTOR: So, Leyla, you wanted to talk about your project topic.
LEYLA: Yes. I had three ideas: school uniforms, screen time in children, and food waste in supermarkets.
TUTOR: Which one attracts you most?
LEYLA: Screen time, I think. But I'm worried there's too much written about it already.

TUTOR: That's a real risk. The uniform topic is narrower, but honestly, students write about it every year and the tutors get tired of it. Food waste is the one I'd choose in your place — you can collect your own data locally.
LEYLA: Collect it how?
TUTOR: Two supermarkets near campus have agreed to talk to students this term. You could interview a manager and count what goes into the bins for a week.
LEYLA: That sounds like a lot of work.
TUTOR: It is, but it's original. And your mark comes mostly from method, not from the amount of reading.
LEYLA: How long should the project be?
TUTOR: Four thousand words. Some students hand in six and lose marks for going over.
LEYLA: And the deadline is in May?
TUTOR: The 12th of May for the written part. But there's an outline due much earlier — the 3rd of March. That's only two pages, but it's compulsory; without it we can't approve your topic.
LEYLA: Should I start with the reading or the interviews?
TUTOR: The interviews, definitely. Managers change jobs, and if you wait until April they may say no. Do the reading while you wait for their replies.
LEYLA: All right. One more thing — can I work with Dmitri? He's doing something similar.
TUTOR: You can share the data collection, but the writing must be completely separate. Two identical projects fail, even if the data is the same.

tasks.title: Multiple choice
items: 1 Which topic does the tutor recommend? A) school uniforms B) screen time C) food waste
2 Why does the tutor not recommend uniforms? A) it is too narrow B) tutors are tired of it C) there is no data
3 What gives most of the mark? A) the method B) the reading C) the length
4 What is the length of the project? A) two pages B) four thousand words C) six thousand words
5 What must Leyla do by 3 March? A) hand in the outline B) finish the interviews C) submit the project
6 What does the tutor say about working with Dmitri? A) it is not allowed B) they may share data only C) they may write together
why: "Food waste is the one I'd choose in your place".
"Students write about it every year and the tutors get tired of it".
"Your mark comes mostly from method, not from the amount of reading".
"Four thousand words". 6,000 — ball yo'qotadiganlar; 2 bet — reja.
"There's an outline due much earlier — the 3rd of March".
"You can share the data collection, but the writing must be completely separate".

tasks.title: Signal so'zlar
why: Tavsiya signali.
Sabab aytiladi.
Qarama-qarshi qo'yish.
Muddat va majburiylik.

homework_intro: Bugun biz chalg'ituvchining uch turini ajratishni o'rgandik; uyda endi ularni o'zingiz topasiz — shunda bu bilim sizniki bo'ladi.

Birinchi vazifa — "Tutorial: choosing a project topic" skripti: bir marta tinglang, to'xtatmang, 6 ta javobni belgilang, faqat shundan keyin transkriptni ochib tekshiring; hammasi 20 daqiqa vaqt oladi.
Ikkinchisi — "Chalg'ituvchi daftari": bugungi uch skriptdan 12 ta chalg'ituvchini ko'chiring va har birining yoniga turini yozing — eski ma'lumot, boshqa odamning fikri yoki qisman to'g'ri.
Eng ko'p qilinadigan xato shu: gap ko'chiriladi-yu, turi yozilmaydi — turi ko'rsatilmagan qator qabul qilinmaydi, u qator uchun ball yo'q.

intro: Matching headings — matnning har xatboshisiga ro'yxatdan sarlavha tanlanadi. Sarlavhalar soni xatboshidan ko'p bo'ladi: ortiqchalari ishlatilmaydi.
Bu tur TARTIBSIZ: i, ii, iii raqamlari matn tartibida kelmaydi. Shuning uchun har xatboshi alohida o'qiladi.
Ishlash yo'li: avval xatboshini o'qing, asosiy g'oyani O'Z so'zingiz bilan bir gapda ayting, keyingina sarlavhalar ro'yxatiga qarang.
Aksincha qilsangiz (avval sarlavhalarni o'qisangiz), ko'zingiz matndan o'sha so'zni qidiradi va tuzoqqa tushasiz.
Asosiy g'oya odatda birinchi yoki oxirgi gapda bo'ladi, lekin har doim emas: butun xatboshini qamrab oluvchi fikrni qidiring.
Tafsilot tuzog'i: sarlavha faqat bitta gapga mos kelsa — noto'g'ri. Sarlavha butun xatboshiga mos kelishi kerak.
O'xshash sarlavhalarni yonma-yon qo'ying va FARQLI so'zini belgilang: "problems of X" va "solutions to X".
Oson xatboshilardan boshlang, qiyinlarini oxiriga qoldiring va ishlatilgan sarlavhani o'chirib boring.
presentation: Qaysi tartibda ishlayman?
Xatboshi → o'z gapingiz → sarlavhalar ro'yxati.
Sarlavhalar tartibdami?
Yo'q, bu turda tartib yo'q.
Sarlavha faqat birinchi gapga mos keladi. Olamanmi?
Yo'q, bu tafsilot tuzog'i. Sarlavha butun xatboshiga mos bo'lsin.
Ikkita sarlavha o'xshash. Nima qilaman?
Farqli so'zini belgilang va xatboshidan shu so'zni qidiring.
Ortiqcha sarlavhalar nega beriladi?
Tuzoq uchun. Hamma sarlavha ishlatilmaydi.
Vaqtim kam. Nimadan boshlayman?
Eng oson va aniq xatboshidan; qiyinlari oxirida qoladi.
notes: Bu tur o'quvchilarni eng ko'p qiynaydi: ustoz har xatboshi uchun "bir gapda nima haqida?" savolini majburiy qilsin.
Doskada ikki ustun: "asosiy g'oya" va "tafsilot" — o'quvchilar gaplarni ajratadi.
Vaqt: har xatboshiga 1.5 daqiqa; 6 xatboshi — 9 daqiqa.
mistakes: Bir xil so'z bor deb tanlash

readings.title: Reading #12. Traffic Jams — No End in Sight
text: A. There are no easy answers to the problems of traffic congestion. Traffic congestion affects people throughout the world. Traffic jams cause smog in dozens of cities across both the developed and developing world. In the U.S., commuters spend an average of a full work week each year sitting in traffic, according to the Texas Transportation Institute. While alternative ways of getting around are available, most people still choose their cars because they are looking for convenience, comfort and privacy.

B. The most promising technique for reducing city traffic is called congestion pricing, whereby cities charge a toll to enter certain parts of town at certain times of day. In theory, if the toll is high enough, some drivers will cancel their trips or go by bus or train. And in practice it seems to work: Singapore, London and Stockholm have reduced traffic and pollution in city centers thanks to congestion pricing.

C. Another way to reduce rush hour traffic is for employers to implement flexitime, which lets employees travel to and from work at off-peak traffic times to avoid the rush hour. Those who have to travel during busy times can do their part by sharing cars. Employers can also allow more staff to telecommute (work from home) so as to keep more cars off the road altogether.

D. Some urban planners still believe that the best way to ease traffic congestion is to build more roads, especially roads that can take drivers around or over crowded city streets. But such techniques do not really keep cars off the road; they only accommodate more of them.

E. Other, more forward-thinking, planners know that more and more drivers and cars are taking to the roads every day, and they are unwilling to encourage more private automobiles when public transport is so much better both for people and the environment. For this reason, the American government has decided to spend some $7 billion on helping to increase capacity on public transport systems and upgrade them with more efficient technologies. But environmentalists complain that such funding is tiny compared with the $50 billion being spent on roads and bridges.
paraphrases: a solution which is no solution
do not really keep cars off the road
such funding is tiny compared with
across both the developed and developing world

tasks.title: Questions 1–5: Choose the correct heading for each paragraph
tasks.instr: Har xatboshini alohida o'qing (NEVER guruhi — tartib yo'q). Avval asosiy g'oyani o'z so'zingiz bilan ayting, keyin ro'yxatga qarang.
answers: i A solution which is no solution
why: "Traffic congestion affects people throughout the world ... across both the developed and developing world". "Global" = "throughout the world". Asosiy g'oya — muammo hamma joyda.
"Charge a toll to enter certain parts of town". "Paying" = "charge a toll", "get in" = "enter". Tuzoq: iii "Closing city centres" — markaz yopilmaydi, faqat pullik bo'ladi.
Flexitime, mashinani birga ishlatish, uydan ishlash — hammasi ish tartibini o'zgartirish. "Employers" so'zi uch marta.
Ko'proq yo'l qurish yechim deb o'ylanadi, lekin "do not really keep cars off the road; they only accommodate more of them".
Hukumat 7 mlrd sarflaydi, lekin "such funding is tiny compared with the $50 billion" — yetarli emas.
tasks.note: Ishlatilmagan sarlavhalar: iii "Closing city centres to traffic" (B dagi tuzoq — pullik kirish, yopish emas) va iv "Making cars more environmentally friendly" (matnda mashinani ekologik qilish haqida gap yo'q, E da jamoat transporti haqida).

iii Closing city centres to traffic

readings.title: Reading #13. Pedestrians only
text: How traffic-free shopping streets developed

A. The concept of traffic-free shopping areas goes back a long time. During the Middle Ages, traffic-free shopping areas known as souks were built in Middle Eastern countries to allow people to shop in comfort and, more importantly, safety. As far back as 2,000 years ago, road traffic was banned from central Rome during the day to allow for the free movement of pedestrians, and was only allowed in at night when shops and markets had closed for the day. In most other cities, however, pedestrians were forced to share the streets with horses, coaches and, later, with cars and other motorised vehicles.

B. The modern, traffic-free shopping street was born in Europe in the 1960s, when both city populations and car ownership increased rapidly. Dirty exhaust fumes from cars and the risks involved in crossing the road were beginning to make shopping an unpleasant and dangerous experience. Many believed the time was right for experimenting with car-free streets, and shopping areas seemed the best place to start.

C. At first, there was resistance from shopkeepers. They believed that such a move would be bad for business. They argued that people would avoid streets if they were unable to get to them in their cars. When the first streets in Europe were closed to traffic, there were even noisy demonstrations, as many shopkeepers predicted they would lose customers.

D. However, research carried out afterwards in several European cities revealed some unexpected statistics. In Munich, Cologne and Hamburg, visitors to shopping areas increased by 50 percent. On Copenhagen's main shopping street, shopkeepers reported sales increases of 25-40 percent. Shopkeepers in Minneapolis, USA, were so impressed when they learnt this that they even offered to pay for the construction and maintenance costs of their own traffic-free streets.

E. With the arrival of the traffic-free shopping street, many shops, especially those selling things like clothes, food and smaller luxury items, prospered. Unfortunately, it wasn't good news for everyone, as shops selling furniture and larger electrical appliances actually saw their sales drop. Many of these were forced to move elsewhere, away from the city centre. Today they are a common feature on the outskirts of towns and cities, often situated in out-of-town retail zones with their own car parks and other local facilities.
paraphrases: goes back a long time / 2,000 years ago
the time was right for experimenting

tasks.title: Match the headings i–vii with paragraphs A–E
tasks.instr: Har xatboshining asosiy g'oyasini bir gapda ayting, keyin mos sarlavhani tanlang.
answers: vi An idea from ancient history
why: "Goes back a long time ... Middle Ages ... 2,000 years ago ... central Rome". "Ancient history" = "2,000 years ago".
Aholi va mashina ko'paydi, xarid qilish "unpleasant and dangerous" bo'ldi — "the time was right" = o'zgarish kerak edi.
"Resistance from shopkeepers ... noisy demonstrations". "Opposition" = "resistance", "local" = shahar do'kondorlari.
Tashrif 50% ga, savdo 25–40% ga oshdi — muvaffaqiyat dalillari. Tuzoq: vii "North America learns from Europe" — Minneapolis faqat oxirgi gapdagi tafsilot, butun xatboshi emas.
Kiyim va oziq-ovqat do'konlari "prospered" (g'oliblar), mebel va katta texnika do'konlari "saw their sales drop" (yutqazganlar).

readings.title: Reading #14. Future of money: a currency that helps people make friends
text: A. In one of America's poorest cities, a new use of technology has been attracting attention. The 92,000 people who live in Macon, Georgia, USA know each other a little better than they did, thanks to an online computer game. Since October, the locals - college students and elderly people alike - have been playing Macon Money, a 'social impact game' that uses 'virtual money' to bring people from different economic backgrounds closer together by encouraging them to meet.

B. In the game, winning players receive 'bonds', which they can then exchange for bank notes of Macon Money. These notes can be spent at local shops and businesses. But the game is not as simple as it sounds. Each person receives just half a bond and must find the person with the other half so that they can spend it. People often find their other half by searching for them on the social networking sites Facebook and Twitter. Matching players then meet in person to redeem the bond and get their Macon Money. The bonds range in value from $10 to $100.

C. Pairs might spend their money separately, or do something together like share a meal or give the money to someone who needs it more, says Beverly Blake of the John S. and James L. Knight Foundation, the non-profit group based in Miami, Florida, that funded the game. 'These are meetings and conversations that might not happen naturally at all,' she said. The game's designers are hoping Macon Money will bring members of the community together who wouldn't normally meet each other.

D. Although Macon Money is quite a new innovation, early signs are positive. The first round of the game has seen $65,000-worth of bonds given out and 2,688 participants so far spending $48,000 in Macon Money. Recently, Macon Money's Executive Producer Kati London accepted the 2011 FutureEverything Award for outstanding innovation in art, society and technology in Manchester, UK. It isn't just technology for technology's sake, London said in an interview with FutureEverything after receiving the award, 'It's about putting those tools, that craft, to work in the community.'

E. Whether such a game can bring lasting economic growth remains to be seen, however. An independent research firm will now evaluate how much economic activity the game has caused, with results due later this year.

a 'social impact game' ... to bring people closer together
winning players receive 'bonds' ... must find the person with the other half
members of the community who wouldn't normally meet each other

readings.title: Why city birds sing differently
text: A. Anyone who has walked in a park at dawn knows that birds are noisy in the morning. What fewer people notice is that the same species sounds different in the city and in the countryside. Over the last twenty years biologists in Europe, Asia and North America have recorded thousands of hours of birdsong and found the same pattern almost everywhere.

B. The pattern is simple: city birds sing higher and louder. Traffic produces a deep, low noise, and a low song disappears inside it, like a voice in a busy room. By raising the pitch, a bird lifts its song above the traffic. Great tits in Amsterdam, for example, sing about two hundred hertz higher than great tits in nearby woods.

C. Singing higher solves one problem and creates another. Female birds usually prefer deep songs, which show that a male is large and strong. A male who sings high may be heard, but he may also be judged as weak. Researchers in Germany found that city females took longer to choose a partner, and some pairs produced fewer eggs.

D. Time of day matters as well. In quiet villages, birds begin singing at first light. In cities they often start up to two hours earlier, using the only period when the streets are silent. Street lighting adds to this: under bright lamps, robins sometimes sing through the night, which is exhausting for them.

E. Not every bird can adapt. Species that sing naturally low, such as pigeons, cannot raise their pitch, and they are disappearing from the noisiest districts. Species with flexible voices, like blackbirds and sparrows, are doing well. Over time this changes which birds live around us — noise acts like a filter.

F. Some cities are now responding. Planting trees along busy roads reduces noise by several decibels, and quiet surfaces on roads help too. In one Dutch experiment, after a road was resurfaced, the local great tits lowered their songs again within two years — proof that the change is behaviour, not evolution.

readings.title: The return of the wolf
text: A. A hundred years ago wolves had disappeared from most of Western Europe. Farmers had hunted them, governments had paid rewards for dead animals, and the forests they needed had been cut down. By 1970 only a few hundred survived, mainly in Italy, Spain and Poland.

B. Then the law changed. In 1979 European countries signed an agreement that made killing wolves illegal, and at the same time millions of people were leaving the countryside for the cities. Fields returned to forest, deer and wild boar multiplied, and the wolves followed the food. Today there are more than twenty thousand wolves in Europe, and packs have been photographed within fifty kilometres of Paris and Berlin.

C. Scientists were especially interested in what happened in one American park, where wolves were reintroduced in 1995. Deer had eaten so many young trees that the riverbanks were bare. With wolves present, the deer moved more often and stopped feeding in open valleys; trees grew back, birds returned, and even the rivers changed shape because the banks became stronger.

D. Farmers see the story from another side. A single wolf pack can kill sheep, and in some mountain regions attacks have risen sharply. Governments pay compensation, but the money arrives late and does not cover the fear of losing animals that a family has raised for years. In several countries this has become a political question, not a scientific one.

E. Protection that works is usually old-fashioned. Electric fences help, but the most effective tool is a large guard dog that lives with the flock from birth. In Portugal, farms with such dogs report up to 90 per cent fewer attacks. The problem is cost: a trained dog is expensive, and small farms cannot always afford one.

F. The debate is likely to continue, because both sides are partly right. Wolves make forests healthier, and they are protected by law; but the people who lose animals are real, and telling them that a predator is "good for the ecosystem" solves nothing. Most experts now argue for money and training rather than for new laws.

readings.title: Sleep and the teenage brain
text: A. Parents often complain that teenagers cannot get up in the morning and will not go to bed at night. For a long time this was treated as laziness. Sleep research over the past thirty years suggests something different: the teenage body clock really does move.

B. The clock is controlled by a hormone called melatonin, which tells the body that it is time to sleep. In children, melatonin is released at about nine in the evening. In teenagers it appears one to three hours later, and it also disappears later in the morning. A fifteen-year-old asked to sleep at ten is being asked to sleep while their body is still in "day" mode.

C. The effects of missing sleep are easy to measure. Teenagers who sleep fewer than seven hours make more mistakes in tests of attention, remember less of what they studied, and report more arguments at home. Some studies also link short sleep to weight gain, because tiredness changes the hormones that control hunger.

D. Screens make the situation worse, though perhaps not for the reason most people think. The blue light of a phone does delay melatonin a little, but the bigger problem is what the phone contains: messages that demand an answer and videos designed never to end. A book in bed rarely keeps a teenager awake until two in the morning.

E. Some schools have tried the obvious experiment. In one English town, lessons began at ten instead of nine for two years. Attendance improved, and the number of top grades rose by about twelve per cent. However, parents who started work at eight found the new times difficult, and after the study ended the school returned to the old timetable.

F. Researchers suggest small changes that families can make: the same bedtime every day, including weekends; no screens for an hour before sleep; bright light in the morning to reset the clock. These are less dramatic than changing the school day, but they are free, and every family can try them tonight.

readings.title: Reading #15. Air conditioning
text: The history of an invention that makes life more pleasant
Willis Carrier designed the first air-conditioning unit in 1902, just a year after graduating from Cornell University with a Masters in Engineering.

At a Brooklyn printing plant, _fluctuations in heat and moisture_ were causing the size of the printing paper to keep changing slightly, making it hard to align different colours. Carrier's invention made it possible to control temperature and humidity levels and so align the colours. The invention also allowed industries such as film, processed food, textiles and pharmaceuticals to improve the quality of their products.

In 1914, the first air-conditioning device was installed in a private house. However, its size, similar to that of an early computer, meant it _took up too much space_ to come into widespread use, and later models, such as the Weathermaker, which Carrier brought out in the 1920s, _cost too much_ for most people. Cooling for human comfort, rather than industrial need, really took off when three air conditioners were installed in the J.L. Hudson Department Store in Detroit, Michigan. People crowded into the shop to experience the new invention. The fashion spread from department stores to cinemas, whose income rose steeply as a result of the comfort they provided.

To start with, money-conscious employers regarded air conditioning as a luxury. They considered that if they were paying people to work, they should not be paying for them to be comfortable as well. So in the 1940s and '50s, the industry started _putting out a different message_ about its product: according to their research, installing air conditioning _increased productivity_ amongst employees. They found that typists increased their output by 24% when transferred from a regular office to a cooled one. Another study into office working conditions, which was carried out in the late '50s, showed that the majority of companies cited air conditioning as the single most important contributor to efficiency in offices.

However, air conditioning has its critics. Jed Brown, an environmentalist, complains that air conditioning is _a factor in global warming_. Unfortunately, he adds, because air conditioning leads to higher temperatures, people have to use it even more. However, he admits that it provides _a healthier environment_ for many people in the heat of summer.

2 What problem did the Brooklyn printing plant have? A) Changes in heat and moisture changed the size of the paper. B) The colours of the ink were too dark. C) The machines were too hot for workers. D) The paper was too expensive.

3 Why did early air conditioners not come into widespread use in homes? A) People did not like the noise. B) There was not enough electricity. C) They were too big and later too expensive. D) Department stores bought them all.

4 What was the purpose of the research done in the 1940s and '50s? A) to make office workers produce more B) to compare different types of air conditioner C) to persuade businesses to buy air conditioners D) to encourage employees to change offices

5 What does Jed Brown say about air conditioning? A) In future, everyone will need it. B) Turning it off will not reduce global warming. C) It can seriously damage people's health. D) It is good for people, but bad for the environment.
why: "Just a year after graduating from Cornell University". C tuzoq: 1914 — uyga birinchi o'rnatilgan yil.
"Fluctuations in heat and moisture were causing the size of the printing paper to keep changing". Fluctuations = changes.

Ish beruvchilar AC ni "luxury" deb bilardi, shuning uchun sanoat "putting out a different message" — ya'ni sotib olishga ko'ndirish. A tuzoq: unumdorlik oshgani — tadqiqot NATIJASI, maqsadi emas.
"A factor in global warming" (atrof-muhitga zarar) + "provides a healthier environment for many people" (odamlarga foyda). C teskari: u sog'liqqa foydali deydi.

readings.title: Reading #16. The ballpoint pen
text: Most of us have at least one, but how did this popular item evolve?

One morning in 1945, a crowd of 5,000 people jammed the entrance of Gimbels Department Store in New York. The day before, Gimbels had placed _a full-page advertisement_ in the New York Times for a wonderful new invention, the ballpoint pen. The advertisement described the pen as _'fantastic' and 'miraculous'_. Although they were expensive, $12.50 each, all 10,000 pens in stock were sold on the first day.

In fact, this 'new' pen was not new at all. In 1888, John Loud, a leather manufacturer, had invented a pen with a reservoir of ink and a rolling ball. However, his pen was _never produced_, and efforts by other people to produce a commercially successful one failed too. The main problem was with the ink. If it was too thin, the ink _leaked out_ of the pen. If it was too thick, it _didn't come out of the pen at all_.

Almost fifty years later, in 1935, a newspaper editor in Hungary thought he spent too much time filling his pens with ink. He decided to invent a better kind of pen. With the help of his brother, who was a chemist, he produced a ballpoint pen that _didn't leak when the pen wasn't being used_. The editor was called Ladislas Biro, and it was his name that people would associate more than any other with the ballpoint pen.

By chance, Biro met Augustine Justo, the Argentinian president. Justo was so impressed with Biro's invention that he invited him to set up a factory in Argentina. In 1943, the first Biro pens were produced.

Unfortunately, they were not popular, since the pen _needed to be held in a vertical position_ for the ink to come out. Biro redesigned the pen with a better ball, and in 1944 the new product was on sale throughout Argentina.

It was a North American, Milton Reynolds, who introduced the ballpoint pen to the USA. Copying Biro's design, he produced the version that sold so well at Gimbels. Another American, Patrick Frawley, _improved the design_ and in 1950 began producing a pen he called the Papermate. It was _an immediate success_, and within a few years, Papermates were selling in their millions _around the world_.
