Opposite + left.
Go past + right.
Turn left + at the end.
D, C — javob emas.

listenings.title: Riverside Park — welcome at the gate
intro: Park xodimi darvoza oldida tashrif buyuruvchilarga yo'l ko'rsatmoqda. Avval "main gate" ni toping. Skriptni ustoz bir marta o'qiydi.
transcript: Welcome to Riverside Park. You're standing at the main gate, so let me tell you where everything is.
As soon as you come in, you'll see the café straight away on your right. It's a good place for a hot drink on a cold day. The toilets are just opposite, on your left.

If you walk straight up the main path, just before you reach the crossroads, you'll see the pond on your right. That's where you can hire a boat — the boat hire hut is right next to the pond, on your right.
For those of you with children, the playground is a little further. When you get to the crossroads, turn left, and at the end of that path, on your right, you'll find the playground.

tasks.title: Write the correct letter, A–F
why: "As soon as you come in ... straight away on your right". Tuzoq: A — "just opposite, on your left" — hojatxona.
"Just before you reach the crossroads ... the pond on your right ... right next to the pond". Tuzoq: C — chapda.
"Turn left, and at the end of that path, on your right". G'arbga yursangiz, o'ng tomon — shimol; yo'l oxiri — E.

tasks.title: Chap yoki o'ng?
why: B.
E.

listenings.title: Westgate Shopping Centre — ground floor
intro: Savdo markazi ma'lumot xodimi (Part 2). Avval "West entrance" va koridorni toping. Skriptni bir marta tinglang.
transcript: Good morning and welcome to Westgate Shopping Centre. If you've come in through the west entrance, you're at the start of our main corridor.
The first shop on your left is a sports shop, and the second shop on your left is the bookshop, which has a small café inside.
Directly opposite the bookshop, on your right, is the bank, where you'll also find cash machines.
If you're here to see a film, the cinema is at the very end of the corridor, on your right, next to the bank.
The pharmacy, by the way, is the first shop on your right as you come in.

tasks.title: Write the correct letter, A–F
tasks.instr: Sharqqa qarab yuring: chap — shimol (A B C), o'ng — janub (D E F).
why: "The second shop on your left". Birinchisi A (sports shop), ikkinchisi — B.
"Directly opposite the bookshop, on your right". B ning qarshisi — E.
"At the very end of the corridor, on your right, next to the bank". Tuzoq: D — dorixona ("first shop on your right").

tasks.title: Tartib so'zlari

listenings.title: Getting around the town centre
intro: Turistik ma'lumot xodimi vokzaldan chiqqanlarga yo'l ko'rsatmoqda. Uyda bir marta tinglang.
transcript: Welcome to Kingsford. When you leave the station, walk straight ahead up the main road.
The first building you'll pass on your left is the post office, and opposite it, on your right, is a small supermarket.
At the top of the road there's a T-junction. The building directly opposite you is the town museum, which is free to enter.
To get to the hotel, turn right at the junction and it's the first building on your left, just past the museum.
If you need the bus station, it's also on this road, but on your right, across from the hotel.

tasks.title: Write the correct letter, A–F
why: "The first building you'll pass on your left". Tuzoq: B — "opposite it, on your right" — supermarket.
"At the T-junction ... directly opposite you". Junction qarshisi — D.

"Turn right at the junction ... the first building on your left, just past the museum". Sharqqa yursangiz, chap — shimol; D dan keyin — E. Tuzoq: F — avtobus bekati ("on your right, across from the hotel").

turn right + first on your left, just past

Hotel.

listenings.title: Track 13. College plan — for visiting students
listenings.qtype: Plan labelling (1–5) — eng qiyin, oxirgi mashq
intro: Kollejga kelgan talabalarga bino rejasi tushuntirilmoqda. Bu eng qiyin mashq: ko'p xona, koridorlar va eshiklar. Avval rejada "College entrance", "Reception", "Sports Hall" va "Parking area for bicycles" ni toping. Keyin BIR MARTA tinglang.
Ko'rsatma: Write the correct letter, A–K, next to questions 1–5.
transcript: OK, now, we've got some students here from Bardwell College who have joined us for today's events. Hello to you all, and welcome.

Now, before our day begins, you'll need to get a guest badge, which you'll have to wear while you're on the college premises. You can get these from the administration office. To get there from the main hall, leave the hall by the door opposite reception, turn left, and just follow the corridor to the end. The administration office is on your right. Don't go any further, or you'll be in the sports hall. If you show your guest badge in the café, by the way, you'll get a 20% discount on drinks and sandwiches.

To get there from the main hall, walk along the corridor between the main hall and reception and turn right. The café is through the first door on your left. Directly opposite the café, on the same corridor, is the student common room, where you can go to relax and perhaps meet some of our own students.

If you have any valuables that you don't want to carry around with you, I suggest you put these in a locker. These are next to the sports hall, opposite the administration office. You can get a key for a locker when you get your guest badge from the administration office.

And if you want to use our library, leave the main hall by the door opposite the one you came in – that's the door by the bicycle parking area – and walk to the end of the corridor. The library is through the door straight ahead of you.

tasks.title: Questions 1–5: Write the correct letter, A–K
tasks.instr: Eng qiyin mashq: har yo'nalishdan keyin qayerdaligingizni qalam bilan belgilang.
why: "Leave the hall by the door opposite reception, turn left, and just follow the corridor to the end. The administration office is on your right. Don't go any further, or you'll be in the sports hall". Koridor oxirida, sport zali oldida o'ngda — D.
"Walk along the corridor between the main hall and reception and turn right. The café is through the first door on your left". O'ngga burilgach, chap tomondagi birinchi eshik — E.
"Directly opposite the café, on the same corridor". E ning qarshisi — K.
"Next to the sports hall, opposite the administration office". D ning qarshisi, sport zali yonida — C.
"Leave the main hall by the door ... by the bicycle parking area – and walk to the end of the corridor. The library is through the door straight ahead of you". Koridor oxirida to'g'ri oldinda — B.
tasks.note: Ustoz kaliti: 1 D · 2 E · 3 K · 4 C · 5 B. Bu mashq qiyin, chunki 3 va 4-savol boshqa joyga NISBATAN beriladi (opposite the café, opposite the administration office) — oldingi javob xato bo'lsa, keyingisi ham xato bo'ladi.

why: "Directly opposite the café" — E qarshisi K.
"Opposite the administration office" — D qarshisi C.
D ni tasdiqlaydi.

lessons.title: Reading: Pick from a List (Choose TWO)
lessons.grammar_topic: Pick from a list — ro'yxatdan ikki (yoki uch) javob tanlash
lessons.book_ref: Jony Academy materiali — ustoz matnlari (#21, #22) va mualliflik matnlari.
objectives: "Choose TWO letters" savolida ikkala javobni ham matndan isbotlash.
Savol qaysi mavzuni so'rayotganini aniqlab, matnning tegishli qismini tez topish.
Har bir variantni alohida tekshirish: matnda bormi? savolga javobmi? aynan shundaymi?
Tuzoqlarni ajratish: matnda bor, lekin boshqa narsa haqida; qisman to'g'ri; teskari.
5 ta matnda ishlash: ustozning 2 matni + 3 ta Jony Academy matni.
materials: Reading #21 "Humpback whale breaks migration record" matni va 1–14 savollari (7 juft "Choose TWO") — har o'quvchiga bitta nusxa, javobsiz; javob kaliti va rad etish izohlari faqat ustozda qoladi.

Reading #22 "On the trail of the honey badger" matni 1–5 savollari bilan, shuningdek "Why birds fly in a V" va "The dance of the honeybee" matnlari savollari bilan — har o'quvchiga bittadan nusxa (chop etiladi yoki ekranda).
Uyga beriladigan "How animals sleep" matni 1–6 savollari bilan — har o'quvchiga bitta nusxa, javobsiz; dars oxirida tarqatiladi.

readings.title: Reading #21. Humpback whale breaks migration record
text: A whale surprises researchers with her journey.
A lone humpback whale travelled more than 9,800 kilometres from breeding areas in Brazil to those in Madagascar, setting a record for the longest mammal migration ever documented.

Humpback whales (Megaptera novaeangliae) are known to have some of the longest migration distances of all mammals, and this huge journey is about 400 kilometres _farther_ than the previous humpback record. The finding was made by Peter Stevick, a biologist at the College of the Atlantic in Bar Harbor, Maine.

The whale's journey was unusual not only for its _length_, but also because it travelled across almost 90 degrees of longitude _from west to east_. Typically, humpbacks move in a north-south direction between _cold feeding areas_ and _warm breeding grounds_ - and the longest journeys which have been recorded until now have been between breeding and feeding sites.

The whale, a female, was first spotted off the coast of Brazil, where researchers _photographed_ its tail fluke and _took skin samples_ for chromosome testing to determine the animal's sex. Two years later, a tourist on a whale-watching boat snapped a photo of the humpback near Madagascar.

To match the two sightings, Stevick's team used an extensive international catalogue of photographs of the undersides of tail flukes, which have distinctive markings. Researchers routinely _compare the markings_ in each new photograph to those in the archive.

The scientists then estimated the animal's shortest possible route: an arc _skirting the southern tip of South Africa_ and heading north-east towards Madagascar. The minimum distance is 9,800 kilometres, says Stevick, but this is likely to be an underestimate, because the whale probably took a detour to feed on krill in the Southern Ocean _near Antarctica_ before reaching its destination.

Most humpback-whale researchers focus their efforts on the Northern Hemisphere because the Southern Ocean near the Antarctic is _a hostile environment_ and it is _hard to get to_, explains Rochelle Constantine, who studies the ecology of humpback whales at the University of Auckland in New Zealand. But, for whales, oceans in the Southern Hemisphere are wider and easier to travel across, says Constantine. Scientists will probably observe more long-distance migrations in the Southern Hemisphere as _satellite tracking_ becomes increasingly common, she adds.

Daniel Palacios, an oceanographer at the University of Hawaii at Manoa, says that the record-breaking journey could indicate that migration patterns are shifting as populations begin to recover from near-extinction and the population increases. But the reasons why the whale did not follow the usual migration routes remain a mystery. She could have been _exploring new habitats_, or simply have _lost her way_. 'We generally think of humpback whales as very well studied, but then they surprise us with things like this,' Palacios says. 'Undoubtedly there are a lot of things we still don't know about whale migration.'

took skin samples for chromosome testing

readings.title: Reading #22. On the trail of the honey badger
readings.qtype: Pick from a list (1–5) — qo'shimcha mashq
text: Researchers learn more about this fearless African predator

On a recent field trip to the Kalahari Desert, a team of researchers learnt a lot more about honey badgers. They were rewarded with a detailed insight into how these fascinating creatures live and hunt.

The team employed a local wildlife expert, Kitso Khama, to help them locate and follow the badgers across the desert. Their main aim was _to study the badgers' movements and behaviour_ as discreetly as possible, without frightening them away or causing them to change their natural behaviour. They also planned _to trap a few and study them close up before releasing them_. In view of the animal's reputation, this was something that even Khama was reluctant to do.

'The problem with honey badgers is they are naturally _curious_ animals, especially when they see _something new_,' he says. 'That, combined with their _unpredictable_ nature, can be a dangerous mixture. If they sense you have food, for example, they won't be shy about coming right up to you for something to eat. They're actually quite sociable creatures around humans, but as soon as they feel they might be in danger, they can become extremely vicious. Fortunately this is _rare_, but it does happen.'

The research confirmed many things that were already known. As expected, honey badgers ate any creatures they could catch and kill. Even poisonous snakes, feared and avoided by most other animals, were not safe from them. The researchers were surprised, however, by the animal's fondness for local _melons_, probably because of their _high water content_. Previously researchers thought that the animal got all of its liquid requirements from its prey. The team also learnt that, contrary to previous research findings, the badgers occasionally formed _loose family groups_. They were also able to confirm certain results from previous research, including the fact that female badgers never socialised _with each other_.

Following some of the male badgers was a challenge, since they can cover large distances in a short space of time. Some hunting territories cover _more than 500 square kilometres_. Although they seem happy to share these territories with other males, there are _occasional fights_ over an important food source, and male badgers can be as aggressive towards each other as they are towards other species.

As the badgers became accustomed to the presence of people, it gave the team the chance to get up close to them _without being the subject of the animals' curiosity_ - or their sudden aggression. The badgers' eating patterns, which had been disrupted, returned to normal. It also allowed the team to observe more closely some of the other creatures that form working associations with the honey badger, as these seemed to _adopt the badgers' relaxed attitude_ when near humans.

readings.title: Why birds fly in a V
text: Anyone who has watched geese crossing an autumn sky has noticed their V-shaped formation. For a long time, scientists suspected that the shape helped birds save energy, but it was very difficult to prove, because it is hard to measure what a bird is doing in the air.

In 2014, a team from the Royal Veterinary College in London found a solution. They attached tiny data recorders to a group of northern bald ibises, rare birds that had been trained to follow a light aircraft on their migration. The recorders measured the position of each bird and every beat of its wings.

The results were surprising. Each bird flew in exactly the place where the air pushed up by the wings of the bird in front could help lift it. The birds also timed their wing beats to match the bird ahead, so that they always met rising air rather than falling air. Earlier research on pelicans had shown that birds flying in formation have lower heart rates than those flying alone.

Flying at the front is the hardest job, and no single bird does it all the time. The ibises regularly changed places, and each bird spent roughly as long leading as it did following — a kind of fair sharing that researchers had not expected.

Energy is not the only reason for the shape. A V also allows every bird to see the others clearly, which helps the group stay together and avoid collisions. Young birds on their first migration can follow experienced adults who know the route.

readings.title: The dance of the honeybee
text: When a honeybee discovers a good source of food, it returns to the hive and performs a dance. For centuries, beekeepers noticed this strange movement, but it was the Austrian scientist Karl von Frisch who first explained what it meant. His work on bee communication won him a share of the Nobel Prize in 1973.

Von Frisch found that bees use two main dances. If the flowers are close to the hive, a bee performs a "round dance", running in small circles. This tells the other bees that food is nearby, but not the exact direction. For food further away, the bee performs a "waggle dance": it runs forward in a straight line while shaking its body from side to side, then circles back and repeats the movement.

The waggle dance contains surprisingly precise information. The angle of the straight run compared with a vertical line on the honeycomb shows the direction of the food compared with the position of the sun. The length of time the bee spends waggling shows how far away the food is: the longer the waggle, the greater the distance.

The dancer also shares other clues. Other bees touch it with their antennae and learn the smell of the flowers it has visited, and they may taste samples of nectar it brings back. Because the sun moves across the sky during the day, bees also adjust the angle of their dance as time passes.
Not every scientist accepted von Frisch's ideas at first. Some believed that bees found food only by smell, and it took several decades of experiments before the dance language was widely accepted.

readings.title: How animals sleep
text: All animals with a brain seem to need some form of sleep, but the way they sleep varies enormously. Some of the most unusual examples come from animals that cannot simply lie down and close their eyes.

Dolphins, for example, must come to the surface to breathe, so they can never become fully unconscious. Instead, they rest one half of the brain at a time, while the other half stays awake to control breathing and watch for danger. During this kind of sleep, a dolphin often keeps one eye open.

Frigatebirds, which fly over the ocean for weeks without landing, use a similar method. In 2016, scientists fitted small devices to their heads and discovered that the birds slept in the air, sometimes with one half of the brain and sometimes with both. However, they slept for only about forty minutes a day in flight, compared with more than twelve hours on land.
At the other extreme, some bats sleep for up to twenty hours a day. Scientists believe this saves energy and keeps them away from danger at times when the insects they eat are not active.

Large grazing animals sleep much less. Giraffes and elephants in the wild may sleep for only two to four hours, often in short periods, because they need to spend a long time eating and must stay alert to predators. Why sleep is so necessary is still not fully understood, but its loss causes serious problems in every animal that has been studied.

intro: Yes / No / Not Given — 6-darsdagi True / False / Not Given ning "fikr" varianti. Savol faktni emas, MUALLIF NIMA DEB O'YLASHINI so'raydi.
YES — gap muallif fikriga mos. NO — gap muallif fikriga qarshi. NOT GIVEN — muallif bu haqda fikr bildirmagan (balki umuman gapirmagan).
Muallif fikri odatda baho so'zlari bilan beriladi: kindness, unusual, better off, the truth is, not good news, should. Shu so'zlarni belgilang.
Tuzoq 1 — gapda baho bor, matnda yo'q: "Into the Wild is a GOOD title" — muallif nom haqida baho bermagan → NOT GIVEN.
Tuzoq 2 — miqdor: "MANY young people make the same decisions" — matn "most would not do the same thing" deydi → NO.
Tuzoq 3 — taqqoslash: "more adventurous THAN OTHERS" — matn "more conventional than others" deydi → NO.
Savollar matn tartibida keladi (ALWAYS). NOT GIVEN javobi ham ikki qo'shni javob orasidagi joyda qidiriladi.

readings.title: Reading #23. Making a change
text: How easy is it for us to change our lives – and why?

In 1990, a young American named Christopher McCandless gave up his career plans, left behind everyone he knew, including his family, and went off on an adventure. He was 22 at the time. _In an act of kindness_, he donated all his savings to the famous charity, Oxfam International, and hitchhiked his way through America to Alaska. His decisions were so unusual for his age that Jon Krakauer wrote a book about them called Into the Wild, and Sean Penn directed a film that had the same title.

Of course, this is an unusual story. _Most college graduates would not do quite the same thing._ However, studies do show that _in teenage years, people are more likely to try out new experiences_. Instead of following the family career path, for example, and working his way up the same organization like his grandfather did, a 15-year-old may dream about becoming a traveller - only to find _in his early 20s that this fascination with new places is declining_ and change is less attractive. This age-related trend can be observed in all cultures.

The reason why people all over the world become less keen to change as they get older may be because people's lives generally _follow similar patterns and involve similar demands_. Most people, _wherever they are_, aim to find a job and a partner. As they get older, they may have young children to look after and possibly elderly family members. These responsibilities cannot be achieved without some degree of consistency, which means that new experiences and ideas may not have a place in the person's life. New experiences may bring excitement but also insecurity, and so most people prefer to stay with the familiar.

However, not every individual is the same. One toddler may want to play a different game every day and _get fed up if nothing changes_ at the nursery. Another may seek out and play with the same children and toys on every visit. _Young children who avoid new experiences will grow up to be more conventional than others._ Psychologists argue that those who have more open personalities as children are more open than others might be when they are older. They also suggest that young men have a greater interest in novelty than women, although, as they age, this desire for new experiences fades more quickly than it does in women.

The truth is that, as we get older, we prefer the things we know. We tend to order the same meals in restaurants, sit on the same side of the train when we commute to work, go on holiday to the same places and construct our day in the same way. If you are older than 20, remember that your openness to new experiences is slowly declining. So _you are better off making a new start today than postponing it until later_.

readings.title: Reading #24. Breaking the habit
readings.qtype: Yes / No / Not Given (1–7) — qo'shimcha mashq
text: We all think we can break our bad habits — but they can stay with us for life

What is a bad habit? The most common definition is that it is something that we do regularly, almost without thinking about it, and which has some sort of negative consequence. This consequence could affect those around us, or it could affect us personally. Those who deny having bad habits are probably lying. Bad habits are part of what makes us human.

Many early habits, like sucking our thumb, are _broken when we are very young_. We are either _told to stop doing it by our parents, or_ we consciously or subconsciously _observe that others do not have the same habit_, and we gradually grow out of it. It is when we intentionally or unintentionally _pick up new habits in our later childhood or early adulthood_ that it becomes a problem. Unless we can break that habit early on, it becomes a part of our life, and becomes 'programmed' into our brain.

A recent study of human memory suggests that no matter how hard we try to change our habits, it is the old ways that tend to win, especially in situations where we are _rushed, stressed or overworked_. Habits that we thought we had got rid of can _suddenly come back_. During the study programme, the researchers showed a group of volunteers several pictures, and gave them words to associate with them (for example, see a picture of tea, and associate it with 'breakfast'). They then showed the volunteers the same pictures again, and gave them new words to associate with them (see a picture of tea, and say 'afternoon').

A few days later, the volunteers were given a test. The researchers showed them the pictures, and told them to respond with one of the words they had been given for each one. _It came as no surprise_ that their answers were split between the first set of words and the second. Two weeks later, they were given the same test again. This time, most of them only gave the first set of words. They appeared to have completely forgotten the second set. The study confirms that _the responses we learn first are those that remain strongest over time_. We may try to change our ways, but after a while, the response that comes to mind first is usually the first one we learned. The more that response is used, the more automatic it becomes and the harder it becomes to respond in any other way.

The study therefore suggests that over time, our bad habits also become automatic, learned behaviour. This is _not good news for people who picked up bad habits early in life and now want to change or break them_. Even when we try to put new, good intentions into practice, those previously learned habits remain stronger in more automatic, unconscious forms of memory.

readings.title: Should every child learn to code?
text: In the last ten years, many governments have added computer programming to the school curriculum, sometimes for children as young as five. Supporters say that coding is the new literacy: just as every child learns to read and write, every child should learn to give instructions to a computer. I think this comparison is only partly true.

There are real benefits. Writing a program teaches children to break a large problem into small steps, to test their ideas and to accept that mistakes are normal. These are valuable habits, and they are useful far outside computer science. A child who has learnt to find the error in ten lines of code has also learnt patience.

However, I do not believe that every child needs to become a programmer. Most adults will never write code at work, and the programming languages taught today may look very different in twenty years' time. What will last is not the language but the way of thinking behind it — and that can also be taught through mathematics, science and even music.

My main concern is time. The school day is not getting longer, and every new subject pushes another one out. In some schools, coding lessons have replaced art or physical education, which I consider a serious mistake. Children need to move and create as much as they need to calculate.

The best approach, in my view, is to teach the ideas of programming inside other subjects, and to offer coding as an option for those who enjoy it. That way, every child meets the key skills, and nobody loses the subjects that make school a complete education.
paraphrases: people who agree with an idea

readings.title: In praise of boredom
text: Most of us now carry a device that means we never have to be bored. In a queue, on a bus or in a waiting room, we take out a phone and fill every empty minute. This seems harmless, but I believe we are losing something valuable.

Boredom is uncomfortable, and that is exactly why it is useful. When the mind has nothing to do, it begins to wander, and wandering thoughts often lead to new ideas. In one well-known experiment, people who first completed a dull task, copying numbers from a telephone book, later produced more creative answers in a problem-solving test than people who had not been bored.

Children, in particular, benefit from unstructured time. Parents today often fill every afternoon with lessons, clubs and screens, sometimes because they fear their children will fall behind. In my opinion, this is a mistake. A child who is left alone with nothing to do will eventually invent a game, build something or start a story — and learn that they can create their own entertainment.

I am not suggesting that phones are evil or that every moment should be empty. Technology gives us information and connection, and I use it every day. But I think we should protect a few moments each day when we allow ourselves to be bored — a walk without headphones, a journey without a screen.

It may feel strange at first. After a week, however, many people who try this say that they notice more around them and think more clearly. Boredom, it seems, is not a problem to be solved, but a space in which our best ideas can grow.

readings.title: Why we should walk more
text: For most of human history, walking was simply how people got from one place to another. Today, many of us walk less than a thousand steps a day, moving from the house to the car and from the car to the office. I believe this change has cost us more than we realise.

The health benefits of walking are well known. Regular walking strengthens the heart, helps control weight and improves sleep. What is less often mentioned is its effect on the mind. A study at Stanford University found that people produced more creative ideas while walking than while sitting, and the effect continued for a short time after they sat down.

Walking also changes the way we see a city. From a car window, streets are something to get through as quickly as possible. On foot, we notice small shops, trees and faces, and we are more likely to talk to neighbours. In my experience, neighbourhoods where people walk feel safer and friendlier.

Of course, not every journey can be made on foot, and it would be unfair to blame people who live far from their workplace. The real responsibility lies with city planners. Too many cities have been designed for cars, with wide roads, few pavements and long distances between homes and shops.

Cities that have made walking easier, by widening pavements and closing some streets to traffic, have often seen local shops do better, not worse. Changing a city takes years, but individuals can start today: get off the bus one stop early, or take the stairs instead of the lift.

lessons.title: Reading: Summary Completion with a Box
lessons.grammar_topic: Summary completion (box) — xulosani ro'yxatdagi so'zlar bilan to'ldirish
lessons.book_ref: Jony Academy materiali — ustoz matnlari (Reducing errors in memory, #26) va mualliflik matnlari.
objectives: Box (A–J ro'yxat) bilan ishlashda ortiqcha so'zlarni o'chirib borish.
Bo'sh joy grammatikasini aniqlab, ro'yxatdagi so'zlarni turiga ko'ra guruhlash (son, sifat, fe'l, ot).
Box so'zi matnda boshqa shaklda yoki teskari ma'noda berilishini tanish ("fewer incorrect" = "more correctly").
Inkor tuzoqlarini ajratish: "did not move very ___" + "started very slowly" = quickly.
5 ta matnda ishlash: ustozning 2 matni + 3 ta Jony Academy matni.
materials: Reading #25 "Reducing errors in memory" matni, glossariysi va 1–5 xulosasi A–J ro'yxati bilan — har o'quvchiga bitta nusxa (asosiy matn, sinfda birga bajariladi).

Reading #26 "Fighting fear using virtual reality" matni va uning A–J ro'yxati — har o'quvchiga bitta nusxa; shu ro'yxatdagi 10 so'z alohida qirqilgan kartochka qilib ham tayyorlansin, har juftlikka bitta to'plam (guruhlash stolda so'zlarni ko'chirib bajariladi).

Uyga vazifa matni "Why the Leaning Tower leans" A–J ro'yxati bilan — har o'quvchiga bitta nusxa, dars oxirida tarqatiladi.

intro: Summary with a box — xulosa va 8–10 ta so'zdan iborat ro'yxat (A–J) beriladi. Bo'sh joylar 5 ta, demak kamida 3–5 ta so'z ortiqcha.
Javob sifatida HARF yoziladi (G, C, H...), so'z emas. Ko'rsatmani o'qing: "Write the correct letter, A–J".

Birinchi qadam — ro'yxatni guruhlang: sonlar (12, six, ten, three, twelve), sifatlar (different, complex, the same), miqdor (more, less, fewer). Bo'sh joy qaysi guruhni talab qiladi — faqat shu guruhdan tanlaysiz.
Box so'zlari matnda deyarli hech qachon aynan bo'lmaydi: "observed" = "just looked at it"; "different times" = "10 a.m. ... at night".
Eng xavfli tuzoq — inkor va teskari: "did not have as many problems ... chose fewer incorrect words" → "remembered MORE words correctly". "Fewer" ro'yxatda bor, lekin gap mantiqiga to'g'ri kelmaydi.
Ikkinchi tuzoq — raqamlar: matnda bir nechta son bo'ladi (twelve sessions, three-month period, six hours). Qaysi son nimaga tegishli ekanini tekshiring.
Xulosa odatda matn tartibida boradi (USUALLY), lekin ba'zan bir xatboshini qisqa qilib aytadi.

Ko'rsatma "letter" desa — faqat harf. So'z yozilsa ball berilmasligi mumkin.

Odatda yo'q — har harf bir marta.
Ro'yxatdagi so'z matnda yo'q.

Ikki so'z ham mos keladi (quickly / slowly).

Odatda ha (USUALLY).

readings.title: Reading #25. Reducing errors in memory
text: Sleep may reduce mistakes in memory, according to a first-of-its-kind study led by a scientist at Michigan State University.

The findings, which appear in the September issue of the journal Learning & Memory, have practical implications for many people, from students doing multiple-choice tests to elderly people confusing their medicine, says Kimberly Fenn, principal investigator and assistant professor of psychology.

'It's easy to muddle things in your mind,' Fenn says. 'This research suggests that after sleep, you're better able to pick out the incorrect parts of that memory.' Fenn and colleagues from the University of Chicago and Washington University in St Louis studied the presence of incorrect or false memory in groups of college students. While previous research has shown that sleep improves memory, this study is the first one that looks at errors in memory, she said.

Study participants were 'trained' by being shown or listening to lists of words. Then, _twelve hours later_, they were shown individual words and asked to identify which words they had seen or heard in the earlier session. One group of students was trained _at 10 a.m._ and tested at 10 p.m. _after the course of a normal sleepless day_. Another group was trained _at night_ and tested twelve hours later in the morning, after about six hours of sleep. _Three experiments were conducted. In each experiment_, the results showed that students who had slept _did not have as many problems_ with false memory and _chose fewer incorrect words_.

How does sleep help? The answer isn't known, Fenn said, but she suspects it may be due to sleep strengthening the source of the memory. The source, or context in which the information is acquired, is a vital element of the memory process. In other words, it may be easier to remember something if you can also remember where you first heard or saw it. Or perhaps the people who didn't sleep as much during the study received so much other information during the day that this affected their memory ability, Fenn said.

Further research is needed, she said, adding that she plans to study different population groups, particularly the elderly. 'We know older individuals generally have worse memory performance than younger individuals. We also know from other research that elderly individuals tend to be more prone to false memories,' Fenn said. 'Given the work we've done, it's possible that sleep may actually help them to reject this false information. And potentially this could help to improve their quality of life.'
paraphrases: in each experiment, the results showed

readings.title: Reading #26. Fighting fear using virtual reality
readings.qtype: Summary completion with a box (1–5) — qo'shimcha mashq
text: Computers are not just for entertainment, shopping or research purposes - as one woman found out when she tried to cure her fears

Most people have at least one thing they are afraid of. A fear of things like snakes, spiders, dogs, heights or open spaces affects over 90% of the population. In extreme cases, a fear can develop into a phobia, where the fear of something is so powerful it can affect the way the sufferer lives their life. About 10% of people suffer from a phobia. Most sufferers never seek treatment, because the most common type of cure - 'exposure therapy' - involves them being exposed to the object of their fear, and this is the last thing many of them are prepared to do.

There is now a new cure for phobias, using something called virtual reality exposure therapy (VRET). The concept is simple. The person with the phobia wears a virtual reality headset. A computer, controlled by a therapist, then simulates a variety of situations in which the sufferer is gradually exposed to the object of their fear, which they view on the headset's screen. At the same time, the therapist explains why they should not be afraid of it. The technique is surprisingly successful, as this case demonstrates.

Sara Considine had a serious spider phobia, and had developed several spider-related behaviour patterns. Before going to bed, for example, she would check her room for spiders, then seal the windows with tape so none could get in. She had frightening dreams about spiders every night. Eventually, she decided to get treatment.

During twelve one-hour virtual reality sessions over a _three-month period_, Ms Considine _started very slowly_. First, she stood a long way from the virtual spider and _just looked at it_. Slowly, she moved a little closer. The therapist controlling the computer programme then made the virtual spider move. After just two sessions, Ms Considine reported that although she still saw spiders in her dreams, they were _no longer frightening_, and she had even managed to have an amusing 'conversation' with one of them. A few sessions later, the therapist encouraged her to hold the virtual spider in her virtual hand, and put it in places where the presence of a real spider would cause her fear. The next stage was to _introduce touch_. A large toy spider was placed next to her. Ms Considine then reached out to touch the virtual spider she could see on the screen, and at the same time her real hand touched the toy spider.

After her sessions were over, Sara Considine was able to stop her spider-related behaviour. She even took up camping, something she would never have considered before therapy. More recently she has appeared on a television nature programme, where for the first time she was able to hold a real spider in her hands.
paraphrases: introduce touch / her real hand touched

tasks.title: Questions 1–5: Complete the summary using the list A–J
tasks.instr: Treating a phobia using VRET. Harfni yozing.

At first, the sessions did not move very (2) ___.

why: "Over a three-month period". J twelve tuzoq: 12 — mashg'ulotlar soni, oylar emas.
"Started very slowly" = "did not move very quickly". G slowly tuzoq: inkor bilan gap teskari ma'no beradi.
"Just looked at it" = "observed". D held tuzoq: ushlash keyinroq bo'lgan.
"They were no longer frightening". B amused by tuzoq: "amusing conversation" bor, lekin "stop being amused" ma'nosi teskari.
"The next stage was to introduce touch ... her real hand touched the toy spider". "Make physical contact" — tabiiy birikma; H touch grammatikaga to'g'ri kelmaydi ("make physical touch" deyilmaydi).

why: Sessiyalar soni.
"did not move very slowly" — matnga qarshi.
U endi qo'rqmaydi, "zavqlanmay qo'ydi" emas.

readings.title: The power of a short nap
text: In many countries, sleeping during the working day is seen as a sign of laziness. Yet a growing amount of research suggests that a short sleep in the afternoon can make people more alert, more accurate and even more creative.

One of the best-known studies was carried out by NASA in the 1990s. Pilots on long flights were divided into two groups. One group was allowed to rest in their seats for forty minutes, while the other group stayed awake as usual. The pilots who rested slept for an average of twenty-six minutes. Afterwards, their performance was about a third better than that of the other group, and their alertness had improved by more than half.

The length of the nap is important. Experts recommend between ten and thirty minutes. A longer sleep allows the brain to enter deep sleep, and a person who wakes up from deep sleep often feels heavy and confused for some time. This feeling, called sleep inertia, can last for half an hour.

The timing also matters. Most people feel a natural drop in energy in the early afternoon, between about one and three o'clock, and this is the easiest time to fall asleep quickly. A nap taken late in the evening, on the other hand, can make it harder to sleep well at night.

Some companies have started to take this seriously, providing quiet rooms or special chairs where employees can rest. Critics say the evidence is still limited, and that a nap cannot replace a full night's sleep. Even so, for people who are short of sleep, twenty minutes with their eyes closed may be one of the cheapest ways to work better.

tasks.title: Complete the summary using the list A–J
items: In a NASA study, pilots who rested slept for about (1) ___ minutes.
After a long sleep, people may feel (3) ___.
The best time for a nap is in the early (4) ___.
For tired people, a short nap may be a (5) ___ way to work better.
why: "Slept for an average of twenty-six minutes". A forty tuzoq: dam olishga berilgan vaqt.
"About a third better". D half — hushyorlik haqida.
"Feels heavy and confused for some time".
"Between about one and three o'clock". H evening teskari: kechki uyqu tunda uxlashga xalaqit beradi.
"One of the cheapest ways to work better".
tasks.note: Ortiqcha so'zlar: A forty, D half, E worse, H evening, J expensive.

readings.title: How the Rosetta Stone was read
text: In 1799, French soldiers who were rebuilding a fort near the town of Rashid, in Egypt, found a large broken stone covered in writing. Known today as the Rosetta Stone, it became one of the most important discoveries in the history of language.

The stone carries the same official message in three kinds of writing: ancient Egyptian hieroglyphs, a later Egyptian script called Demotic, and ancient Greek. Scholars could already read Greek, so for the first time they had a real chance to understand hieroglyphs, which nobody had been able to read for more than a thousand years.

The work was slow. The English scientist Thomas Young made important early progress, showing that some hieroglyphs inside oval shapes spelled the names of rulers such as Ptolemy. But it was the French scholar Jean-François Champollion who solved the problem. He realised that hieroglyphs were not simply pictures of ideas: many of them also represented sounds. In 1822, he announced that he could read the system.

Champollion's success depended partly on his knowledge of Coptic, a late form of the Egyptian language that was still used in some churches. By comparing Coptic words with the sounds of the hieroglyphs, he was able to read whole sentences.

After the French were defeated in Egypt, the stone was taken by the British, and it has been displayed in the British Museum in London since 1802. It is one of the most visited objects in the museum, and Egypt has asked several times for it to be returned.
paraphrases: nobody had been able to read

tasks.title: Complete the summary using the list A–J

It has the same text in (2) ___ types of writing.
Researchers could understand the (3) ___ part of the text.
Champollion discovered that many hieroglyphs stood for (4) ___.
He was helped by his knowledge of (5) ___.
why: "French soldiers who were rebuilding a fort ... found".
"In three kinds of writing".
"Scholars could already read Greek".
"Many of them also represented sounds". E pictures tuzoq: "not simply pictures of ideas".
"His success depended partly on his knowledge of Coptic".
tasks.note: Ortiqcha so'zlar: B scholars, D two, E pictures (teskari), I 1802 (muzey), J 1822 (e'lon yili — xulosada so'ralmagan).

readings.title: Why the Leaning Tower leans
text: The bell tower of Pisa cathedral, in Italy, is famous for one reason: it is not straight. Few visitors realise, however, that it began to lean while it was still being built, and that the problem is hidden under the ground.

Construction began in 1173. Five years later, when the builders reached the second floor, the tower started to sink on its south side. The ground there is soft, made of clay, sand and shells, and the foundations were only three metres deep — far too shallow for such a heavy building.

The tower was then left unfinished for almost a century, because Pisa was involved in wars with neighbouring cities. This long pause turned out to be lucky: it gave the soil time to become firmer. Without it, experts believe, the tower would almost certainly have fallen. When work continued, the builders tried to correct the lean by making the upper floors slightly taller on one side, which is why the tower is actually a little curved.

The tower was completed in the fourteenth century, but the lean continued to increase slowly. By 1990 it was so dangerous that the tower was closed to the public. Engineers carefully removed soil from under the north side, allowing the building to settle back by more than forty centimetres. It reopened in 2001.
Today the tower is considered safe for at least two hundred years. The engineers were careful not to make it straight: without its lean, Pisa would lose its most famous attraction.

tasks.title: Complete the summary using the list A–J
items: The tower began to lean because the ground was (1) ___.
Building stopped for almost a hundred years because of (3) ___.
This long break was (4) ___ for the tower.
Engineers took soil from under the (5) ___ side.
why: "The ground there is soft, made of clay, sand and shells".
"Only three metres deep — far too shallow".
"Pisa was involved in wars with neighbouring cities". F money aytilmagan.
"This long pause turned out to be lucky". H dangerous — 1990-yil holati.
"Removed soil from under the north side". J south tuzoq: minora janubga egilgan.
tasks.note: Ortiqcha so'zlar: B hard, C deep, F money, H dangerous, J south.

homework_intro: Bugun ro'yxatdagi ortiqcha so'zlarni birma-bir o'chirib borishni va so'zni gap mantiqiga qarab tanlashni mashq qildik — uyda xuddi shu qadamlarni yolg'iz o'zingiz takrorlaysiz.
Birinchi vazifa — "Why the Leaning Tower leans" matni: soatga qarab 10 daqiqa qo'ying, avval A–J ro'yxatini guruhlarga ajrating, keyin 1–5 bo'sh joyga faqat HARF yozing.

Ikkinchi vazifa — bugungi beshta box ro'yxatini daftarda son / sifat / ot / fe'l guruhlariga ajratasiz va har bo'sh joy qaysi guruhni talab qilishini yozasiz; uchinchisi — tuzoq daftariga har matndan bittadan eng yaxshi tuzoqni ko'chirasiz (masalan fewer → more, slowly → quickly) va nega tuzoq ekanini bir gap bilan izohlaysiz; ikkalasi birga 20 daqiqacha oladi.

Eng ko'p uchraydigan xato — ro'yxatdagi so'z matnda ko'ringani uchun uni darrov tanlash: minora matnida "south" ham, "dangerous" ham bor, lekin savol boshqa narsani so'raydi — gapni oxirigacha o'qing va inkor bor-yo'qligini tekshiring.
Uchala vazifani keyingi dars boshida daftar ochiq holda stolga qo'yasiz, javoblarni birga tekshiramiz va men har matn uchun "ortiqcha qolgan beshta so'z nega mos emas?" deb so'rayman.

intro: Listening matching — ro'yxatda odamlar yoki joylar (1–4), qutida variantlar (A–F). Har odamga bitta harf. Qutida 2 ta ortiqcha variant bor.
Savollar (1–4) audio tartibida keladi: avval 1-odam haqida, keyin 2-odam haqida gapiriladi. Odamning ISMI — langar.

Variantlar audioda DEYARLI HECH QACHON aynan aytilmaydi. "A relative's influence" — audioda "his uncle was a film student and because of that...". Shuning uchun tinglashdan oldin har variantning sinonimini o'ylab qo'ying.
Bir odam haqida bir necha variant tilga olinishi mumkin, lekin faqat bittasi savolga javob. Savolni eslang: "What helped each person to become successful?" — sabab so'raladi, natija emas.
Chalg'ituvchi: "Anna Pavlova's parents weren't wealthy" — "a lot of money" (B) tilga olinadi, lekin inkor qilinadi. Javob — uning shaxsiy uslubi (A).
Ikki so'zlovchi bo'lsa, kim kim haqida gapirayotganini kuzating — lekin javob faqat odam haqidagi faktga bog'liq.

transcript: MAN: So we have to do a presentation on a successful person at our next seminar.

MAN: So what made him successful?
WOMAN: Apparently his uncle was a film student and because of that, he started making short films when he was only 16.
MAN: That's quite young ... and were they good?
WOMAN: Yup. He won a scholarship to go to Canada and study film, and that's how his career developed.
MAN: Great. Um ... here's one of my suggestions. She was a ballet dancer – born in St Petersburg in Russia in 1881.
WOMAN: Anna Pavlova. OK – why have you picked her?
MAN: Well, firstly, because her parents weren't wealthy – they were very poor, in fact – and yet she still went to the School of Imperial Ballet at ten years of age.
WOMAN: That's so young! Was she very talented?
MAN: Yes, she was, but she didn't follow the rules of ballet. She was very individual and did things that were different from other ballerinas at the time.
WOMAN: Ah – and that's what made her stand out ...
MAN: Yes.
WOMAN: OK. I've got another woman – Marie Curie.
MAN: She's very famous. Wasn't she Polish?
WOMAN: Yeah, born in 1867, but did you know that she was the first woman professor at the University of Paris and the first woman to win a Nobel prize?
MAN: Yes – amazing!
WOMAN: There were many brilliant scientists around when she was working.
MAN: So why did she do better?
WOMAN: Other scientists couldn't get ahead of her because she sensibly published her ideas straight away.
MAN: What a clever thing to do!
WOMAN: Yeah – everyone does it automatically these days, but all those years ago, people often didn't think about it.
MAN: Great! Well, here's one more.
WOMAN: OK – who is it?
MAN: This is an African-American guy who worked as a chef in the 1850s. His name was George Crum.
WOMAN: Did he make a famous dish or something?
MAN: Not exactly – but without him, we wouldn't have the potato chip. Or crisps, as the British call them.
WOMAN: Oh!

MAN: Yeah. Apparently, he had a customer who was annoyed because his French fries were too fat and soft. So he sliced a new potato as thinly as he could and fried it until it was hard and crunchy. Added lots of salt ...
WOMAN: ... and a new snack was created.
MAN: Well, I, I think we've got some interesting people here ...

tasks.title: Questions 1–4: What helped each person to become successful?
tasks.instr: Har odamga bitta harf. 2 ta variant ortiqcha.
why: "His uncle was a film student and because of that, he started making short films". Uncle = relative. Tuzoq: "scholarship to Canada" — natija, sabab emas.

"She was very individual and did things that were different from other ballerinas ... that's what made her stand out". Individual = personal style. Tuzoq: B — "her parents weren't wealthy" — pul INKOR qilingan.
"She sensibly published her ideas straight away" — "What a clever thing to do!" Sensibly / clever = wise decision.
"Without him, we wouldn't have the potato chip ... a new snack was created". Ixtiro. Tuzoq: F — kasbini o'zgartirmagan, oshpaz bo'lib qolgan.
tasks.note: Ustoz kaliti: 1 C · 2 A · 3 E · 4 D. Ortiqcha variantlar: B (a lot of money — Pavlova uchun inkor qilingan) va F (a change of job).

tasks.title: Paraphrase juftlari
answers: "sensibly published ... a clever thing to do"
why: 1-savol.
2-savol.
3-savol.
4-savol.

listenings.title: Track 14. What makes people happy?
intro: Amy va Matt psixologiya topshirig'i haqida gaplashmoqda: mutaxassislar baxt haqida nima deydi. Avval variantlarni o'qing, keyin BIR MARTA tinglang.
Ko'rsatma: Choose FOUR answers from the box and write the correct letter, A–F, next to Questions 1–4.
transcript: AMY: Hey, Matt, are you coming out tonight?
MATT: I'd love to, Amy, thanks, but I've got too much work. I need to get this psychology assignment in by Thursday.
AMY: Oh, what's it on?
MATT: Happiness, or specifically, the things that make people happy.
AMY: Wow, that's a big area. How are you approaching it?
MATT: Well, I've been looking on the Internet to see what various experts have to say on the subject.
AMY: Did you find anything interesting?
MATT: Well, yes, I did.
AMY: Like?

MATT: Like, for example, there's a professor at Nottingham University, a guy called Richard Tunney, and he suggests that the more close friends we have, the happier we are. And if you see these friends regularly, go out with them and so on, well, that's even better.
AMY: I'd have thought that was fairly obvious.
MATT: I guess so. The next one is a bit more interesting, though. Martin Seligman, a professor of psychology at an American university, conducted a happiness experiment with his students.
AMY: What did he do? Give everyone huge amounts of cash and then see how much they smiled? That would help, wouldn't it?

MATT: Well, perhaps it would. For a short while, anyway. No, what he did was tell half his students to take part in fun activities, like playing video games or going to the cinema, and the other half to do good things.
AMY: Good things?
MATT: You know, like visiting elderly people at a care home, or some other kind of voluntary work. And it was those students who reported a more lasting feeling of happiness.
AMY: That's interesting.
MATT: Then there's George Vaillant, a psychiatrist and professor at Harvard Medical School. He's spent the past 60 years studying people.
AMY: So, I guess he probably knows a bit about them.
MATT: He certainly does. According to him, the thing that really makes people happy is having something to aim for, you know, a goal in the future.
AMY: Right, so I can say 'By the time I'm 30, I'm going to be a millionaire,' and that will make me happy.
MATT: Ah, but Vaillant has a warning here. He says: You need to be realistic. It's no good setting yourself impossible goals, because, well ...
AMY: Because you'll only make yourself unhappy trying to achieve them.
MATT: Exactly.
AMY: So, does anyone mention anything that people normally assume brings happiness? Like a healthy bank account, or an expensive house, something more, er, material?

MATT: Funnily enough, those things aren't mentioned much. Here's another interesting one, though. Melanie Hodgson, she's a professor at Westbrook University, claims that people are happier when they're getting ready to go on holiday.
AMY: Oh, I love that. Sitting on a beach, relaxing, sightseeing ...
MATT: No, not the actual holiday itself, which professor Hodgson says can sometimes be quite stressful ...
AMY: That's true, they can.
MATT: ... but the things you do leading up to it. Deciding what you're going to take with you, what you're going to see and do, packing your case, that kind of thing.
AMY: I get it. Yes, I can see how that would work.

tasks.title: Questions 1–4: What do these experts say makes people happy?
tasks.instr: Har mutaxassisga bitta harf. 2 ta variant ortiqcha.
why: "The more close friends we have, the happier we are ... see these friends regularly, go out with them". Social life. Tuzoq: D — "making NEW friends" emas, bor do'stlar bilan uchrashish.
"Visiting elderly people at a care home, or some other kind of voluntary work ... a more lasting feeling of happiness". Helping others.
"Having something to aim for ... a goal in the future ... You need to be realistic". Achievable ambition = realistic goal.

"Not the actual holiday itself ... but the things you do leading up to it. Deciding what you're going to take ... packing your case". Planning a trip. Tuzoq: B — "being on holiday" — INKOR qilingan ("not the actual holiday").
tasks.note: Ustoz kaliti: 1 F · 2 C · 3 A · 4 E. Ortiqcha variantlar: B (being on holiday — Hodgson uchun inkor qilingan) va D (making new friends — Tunney uchun yaqin, lekin "new" yo'q).

tasks.title: Chalg'ituvchi tahlili
why: Yangi emas, bor do'stlar.
Inkor.
Qutida yo'q; javob — voluntary work.

listenings.title: Three famous travellers
intro: Ikki talaba sayohatchilar haqida taqdimot tayyorlamoqda. Savol: What was special about each traveller's journey? Avval variantlarni o'qing, keyin bir marta tinglang.
transcript: WOMAN: So, for our talk on travellers, I've found four people.
MAN: Go on, then.
WOMAN: The first is Ibn Battuta. In the fourteenth century he travelled for almost thirty years, from Morocco as far as China. No one before him had written about so many countries.
MAN: That's a long time. What about the second?
WOMAN: Nellie Bly. She was an American journalist, and in 1889 she tried to go round the world faster than the hero of a famous novel. She did it in 72 days — it was a race against the clock.
MAN: Brilliant. And the third?
WOMAN: Thor Heyerdahl. He built a raft from wood and rope, using only materials that ancient people could have had, and sailed it across the Pacific.
MAN: I've heard of him. And the last one?
WOMAN: Freya Stark. She went into areas of the Middle East where no European woman had been before, and she did it alone, which people thought was very dangerous at the time.

tasks.title: What was special about each traveller's journey?
why: "He travelled for almost thirty years".
"A race against the clock ... in 72 days".
"Using only materials that ancient people could have had". Old technology.
"She did it alone".
tasks.note: Ortiqcha variantlar: D (paid for by a king) va F (filmed).
box: D it was paid for by a king

tasks.title: Paraphrase juftlari
answers: "materials that ancient people could have had"

listenings.title: Choosing a holiday destination
intro: Turagent mijozga to'rtta shaharni tavsiya qilmoqda. Savol: What is each city best known for? Avval variantlarni o'qing, keyin bir marta tinglang.
transcript: AGENT: So you're interested in a city break. Let me tell you about four options.
CLIENT: Great.
AGENT: Samarkand is wonderful if you love history. The Registan square and the old mosques are among the finest buildings in Central Asia.
CLIENT: Sounds beautiful. And the next one?
AGENT: Lyon, in France. People say it's the food capital of the country — the restaurants are fantastic, and quite cheap, too.
CLIENT: Mm, tempting. What else?
AGENT: Barcelona is perfect if you want both a city and the sea. You can spend the morning in a museum and the afternoon on the beach.
CLIENT: And the last one?
AGENT: Vienna. It's famous for its music — you can go to a concert almost every night. It's not a cheap city, though, so it depends on your budget.

tasks.title: What is each city best known for?
why: "The Registan square and the old mosques are among the finest buildings".
"The food capital of the country". Tuzoq: C — "quite cheap, too" — qo'shimcha, asosiy emas.
"A city and the sea ... the afternoon on the beach".
"It's famous for its music". Tuzoq: C — "not a cheap city" — inkor.
tasks.note: Ortiqcha variantlar: C (low prices — Lyon uchun qo'shimcha, Vienna uchun inkor) va F (nightlife).

tasks.title: Asosiy va qo'shimcha
why: Asosiysi — food.
Asosiysi — music.

listenings.title: Four study tips from students
intro: Radio ko'rsatuvida to'rt talaba imtihonga tayyorlanish usullarini aytmoqda. Savol: What does each student recommend? Uyda bir marta tinglang.
transcript: PRESENTER: Today four students tell us how they prepare for exams. Aziz, you first.
AZIZ: I always study with two friends. We test each other, and explaining things to someone else helps me remember them.
PRESENTER: Thanks. Lola?
LOLA: For me, the most important thing is sleep. I used to stay up all night, but now I go to bed early before an exam, and my marks have really improved.
PRESENTER: Interesting. Ben?
BEN: I make a plan. I write down every topic and give each one a day in my calendar, so I never have to rush at the end.
PRESENTER: And finally, Madina?
MADINA: I put my phone in another room. Without messages and social media, I can concentrate for much longer. I don't use any special apps — I just remove the problem.

tasks.title: What does each student recommend?
why: "I always study with two friends. We test each other".
"The most important thing is sleep ... go to bed early". Tuzoq: F — "used to stay up all night" — eski odat, endi emas.
"Give each one a day in my calendar".
"I put my phone in another room ... I just remove the problem". Tuzoq: C — "I don't use any special apps" — inkor.
tasks.note: Ortiqcha variantlar: C (study app — Madina inkor qilgan) va F (studying at night — Lolaning eski odati).

tasks.title: Chalg'ituvchi daftari
answers: "I used to stay up all night"
why: Endi emas.
Inkor.

homework_intro: Bugun biz qutidagi variant audioda deyarli hech qachon aynan aytilmasligini ko'rdik — "a relative's influence" o'rniga "his uncle was a film student" eshitildi; uyda xuddi shu ishni yolg'iz o'zingiz bajarasiz.

Birinchi vazifa — 5-skript, "Four study tips from students": varaqning old tomonidagi A–F qutisini avval o'qing, har variantga bittadan sinonim o'ylang, keyin skriptni bir marta tinglang yoki uydagi birov sizga bir marta ovoz chiqarib o'qib bersin, 1–4 ga harflarni yozing va faqat shundan keyin varaqning orqasidagi transkriptni oching — bu 10 daqiqa oladi.

Ikkinchi vazifa — "Sinonim daftari": Track 5 va Track 14 qutilaridagi 12 ta variantni daftarga ko'chirib, har birining yoniga audioda qanday aytilganini yozasiz (a relative's influence — his uncle was a film student), ortiqcha variantlarga esa "aytilmagan" yoki "inkor qilingan" deb qo'yasiz; uchinchisi — "O'z matching mashqingiz": oilangizdagi 4 kishi haqida 4 gap va 6 variantli quti, 2 tasi ortiqcha bo'lsin.

Eng ko'p qilinadigan xato shu: so'z eshitilgani uchun harfni yozib qo'yish — Madina "I don't use any special apps" deydi, demak C javob emas; har harfni yozishdan oldin gap tasdiqmi yoki inkormi, bir tekshiring.

O'z mashqingizda variantlarni gapdagi so'zlar bilan bir xil yozmang, paraphrase qiling; uchala vazifa birga taxminan yarim soat oladi, daftarni keyingi darsga to'liq yozilgan holda olib keling — dars boshida sherigingiz sizning mashqingizni tinglab moslaydi, men esa sinonim daftaringizni yig'ib tekshiraman.

lessons.title: Listening: Pick from a List (Part 3 — discussion)
lessons.grammar_topic: Pick from a list (Part 3) — suhbatda ikki kishi KELISHGAN javoblarni tanlash
lessons.book_ref: Jony Academy materiali — ustoz bergan audiolar (CD2 Track 6 choosing a successful person, Track 15 personality tests) va 3 ta mualliflik skripti.
objectives: Part 3 suhbatida (2 kishi) "Choose TWO" savollarini ishlash.
Ikki so'zlovchi KELISHGAN fikrni ajratish: taklif — rad etish — kelishuv zanjirini kuzatish.
"Agree", "decide", "do next" kabi savol so'zlarini oldindan belgilash.
Kelishuv signallarini tanish: "Yeah, you're right", "I agree", "OK, let's...", "that's it".
13-darsdagi pick from a list ko'nikmasini qiyinroq, suhbat formatida mustahkamlash.
materials: Ikkala audio darsdan oldin ochib qo'yilsin: ielts5_22_choosing.mp3 (CD2 Track 6) va ielts5_22_personality.mp3 (Track 15) — kolonka ulangan, ovoz sinab ko'rilgan, ikkalasi ham 0:00 da to'xtatib turilsin, chunki har biri FAQAT BIR MARTA qo'yiladi.

Doskada dars boshlanmasdan turib: TAKLIF → RAD / KELISHUV uchta so'z katta qilib yozilsin ("Taklif, rad yoki kelishuv?" sinf mashqi shu uchtasiga quriladi), yoniga signal so'zlar ustuni — "Yeah, you're right / I agree / OK, let's... / That's a good idea" va "but / I'm not sure / I don't think we can ... yet".

Track 6 va Track 15 savol varaqasi (5–10 savollar, har biriga A–E variantlar) — har o'quvchiga bitta nusxa; variantlar qo'lda bo'lmasa "Choose TWO letters" ishlamaydi, shuning uchun bu varaqada transkript BO'LMASIN.
"Planning a class trip" va "Tutor meeting — improving an essay" skriptlarining 1–4 savollari — har juftlikka bitta nusxa.

Ustoz uchun o'sha ikki skriptning to'liq transkripti chop etilgan holda (bu ikkisida audio yo'q — ustoz ovoz chiqarib o'qiydi): KATE/SAM va DR HALE/NODIR gaplari ikki xil rang yoki belgi bilan ajratilsin, ikkinchi rolni kuchli o'quvchi o'qib bersa bo'ladi.

"Choosing a club at university" (5-skript) uyga vazifa varaqasi — har o'quvchiga bitta nusxa: 1-betda 1–4 savol va variantlar, 2-betda transkript (uyda kimdir o'qib berishi va tekshirish uchun, oldindan ochilmasin); o'quvchilar zanjir daftari va ruchka bilan kelsin.
timeline: Salomlashish, o'tgan darsdagi savol turini 3 savolda eslatish
Ustoz doskada: qoida, bosqichlar, tipik xatolar
Savol turiga oid mashq birga bajariladi, har javob izohlanadi
Matndagi va savoldagi so'zlar jadvali; o'quvchilar ovoz chiqarib topadi
Mustaqil bajariladi, keyin javoblar izoh bilan tekshiriladi
Skript ustoz tomonidan o'qiladi yoki audio qo'yiladi, keyin transkript bilan tekshiriladi
Xatolar daftari: har xato javob sababi bilan yoziladi

intro: 13-darsda pick from a list asosan bitta so'zlovchi (monolog) yoki oddiy suhbat edi. Bu darsda — Part 3: ikki talaba muhokama qiladi, takliflar beriladi, ba'zilari qabul, ba'zilari rad qilinadi.
Savolda "Which TWO things do the students AGREE..." — bu eng muhim so'z. Bittasining taklifi yetarli emas; ikkinchisi rozi bo'lishi kerak.
Zanjir: 1) taklif ("What about choosing a woman?") → 2) e'tiroz ("Is it fair to select someone because of their gender?") → 3) kelishuv ("Yeah, OK, let's pick a woman"). Javob — oxirgi kelishuv.
Rad etish signallari: "I'm not sure", "but", "I don't think we can ... yet", "maybe their fame won't last". Bunday variant — chalg'ituvchi.
Kelishuv signallari: "Yeah, you're right", "I agree", "OK, I think that's it", "that's a good idea".
Ba'zan javob ikki kishining gapini birlashtirishdan chiqadi: biri "natural ability" deydi, ikkinchisi "I agree" deb qo'shadi.
presentation: Bittasi taklif qildi, ikkinchisi indamadi. Javobmi?
Ehtiyot bo'ling — kelishuv signalini kuting. Savol "agree" desa, ikkalasi rozi bo'lishi kerak.
Taklif rad etilib, keyin qabul qilindi.
Oxirgi fikr hisoblanadi: "Is it fair...?" — "Oh, I see. OK, let's pick a woman" → qabul.
Variantdagi so'z audioda aytildi, lekin "not".
Bu chalg'ituvchi: "It isn't about money" → wealth emas.
Part 3 da nechta kishi?
Odatda 2–3 (talabalar va o'qituvchi).
Javoblar tartibdami?
Savollar (5–6, 7–8, 9–10) tartibda; harflar ichida tartib yo'q.
Ikkala harfni topolmadim.
Ishonchli bittasini yozing, ikkinchisiga eng ehtimollisini.
notes: Track 6 — 21-darsdagi Track 5 suhbatining davomi (o'sha ikki talaba to'rt kishidan birini tanlaydi). Track 15 — 21-darsdagi Track 14 (Amy va Matt) ning davomi.
Ustoz kaliti yuborilgan va kiritildi: Track 6 — 5–6 B,E; 7–8 B,C; 9–10 C,D. Track 15 — 5–6 B,C; 7–8 A,D; 9–10 A,E.
Har savoldan keyin o'quvchi zanjirni aytsin: kim taklif qildi → kim e'tiroz bildirdi → qanday kelishildi.

class_ex.title: Taklif, rad yoki kelishuv?
class_ex.instr: Ustoz gapni o'qiydi; o'quvchi "taklif", "rad" yoki "kelishuv" deydi.
items: "Is it fair to select someone because of their gender?"
"Oh, I see. Yeah, OK, let's pick a woman."
"Yeah, but maybe their fame won't last for ever."
"I don't think we can write the presentation yet, do you?" — "No"
why: Hali qaror yo'q.
Shubha.
Javob shu.
Fame — chalg'ituvchi.
Talk yozish — hozir emas.
Oldingi fikr qabul.
class_ex.note: Uch so'z doskada: TAKLIF → RAD / KELISHUV. Javob faqat KELISHUV.

listenings.title: CD2 Track 6. Choosing one of the four people
intro: 21-darsdagi ikki talaba endi to'rt kishidan birini tanlash uchun mezon (criteria) belgilaydi, keyingi qadamni va muvaffaqiyat sirini muhokama qiladi. Avval uch savol va variantlarni o'qing. Keyin BIR MARTA tinglang.
Ko'rsatma: Choose TWO letters, A–E, for each question.
transcript: WOMAN: OK, so we have to choose one of these four people.
MAN: It's going to be difficult.
WOMAN: Well, why don't we agree on some criteria that will help us?
MAN: Do you mean things like how old they were when they became successful?
WOMAN: Yeah – except I'm not sure how old they all were! Um, what about choosing a woman ...
MAN: Is it fair to select someone because of their gender? And look at celebrities – there are lots of women.
WOMAN: But it was different in the past.
MAN: Oh, I see. Yeah, OK, let's pick a woman.
WOMAN: Great. Right, well, they're all pretty talented, aren't they? Some have even won awards.
MAN: Yeah, but maybe their fame won't last for ever.
WOMAN: No ... so we should pick someone who's done something great on an international level.
MAN: Yeah, that changed the world ... OK, I think that's it. We've got our two criteria. So what do we need to do before we meet again?
WOMAN: Well, how much information have we got?
MAN: Quite a lot of detail about their lives, but not enough about what they did.
WOMAN: OK – so before we meet again, let's both find out as much as we can. It's always better to have too much information.
MAN: Yeah, you're right. What about pictures?
WOMAN: Yeah – I don't even know what this person looks like!
MAN: OK – well, we might get some from the library – but I can look on the Internet as well.
WOMAN: Once we've done that, we can get together and talk about the next stage.
MAN: Yeah – I don't think we can write the presentation for the seminar yet, do you?
WOMAN: No – anyway, it'll be fun working together.
MAN: Yeah! It's been quite an education doing this.
WOMAN: Yes – it's made me think about success and what it really means.
MAN: It isn't about money, is it?
WOMAN: No – and you don't have to be experienced to achieve it. It can just be luck.
MAN: But perhaps in most cases you need to have some natural ability.
WOMAN: Yeah – I agree. And I also think you do have to work hard and be determined.
MAN: Yeah – and really want to succeed.
WOMAN: No matter where you are or what you've done before.
MAN: Mm. It's quite a curious thing.

tasks.title: Questions 5–10: Choose TWO letters, A–E
tasks.instr: Faqat ikkala talaba KELISHGAN variantni tanlang.
items: 5–6 Which TWO criteria will the students use to choose a successful person? A) age B) gender C) individual talent D) fame E) global importance
7–8 Which TWO things do the students agree to do before they meet again? A) write a biography B) conduct more research C) find photographs D) write a talk E) plan a seminar
9–10 Which TWO things do the students agree are linked to success? A) wealth B) experience C) talent D) effort E) location
why: "Yeah, OK, let's pick a woman" (B — gender) va "someone who's done something great on an international level" — "Yeah, that changed the world" (E). A tuzoq: yosh taklif qilindi, lekin "I'm not sure how old they all were". C tuzoq: "they're all pretty talented" — hammasi iste'dodli, farqlamaydi. D tuzoq: "maybe their fame won't last for ever" — rad.

"Let's both find out as much as we can" — "Yeah, you're right" (B) va "What about pictures? ... we might get some from the library ... look on the Internet" (C). D tuzoq: "I don't think we can write the presentation yet" — "No" — rad. A, E aytilmagan.

"You need to have some natural ability" — "Yeah – I agree" (C) va "you do have to work hard and be determined" — "Yeah – and really want to succeed" (D). A teskari: "It isn't about money". B teskari: "you don't have to be experienced". E teskari: "no matter where you are".
tasks.note: Ustoz kaliti: 5–6 B,E · 7–8 B,C · 9–10 C,D. Bu mashqda har savolda taklif → rad → kelishuv zanjiri aniq ko'rinadi.

tasks.title: Zanjir tahlili
tasks.instr: Kim taklif qildi, kim rozi bo'ldi?
answers: W taklif — M e'tiroz — M rozi
W: "all talented, won awards" — M: "fame won't last"
M: "can't write yet, do you?" — W: "No"
why: "Oh, I see. Yeah, OK, let's pick a woman".
Rad.
Ikkalasi rad qildi.
Kelishuv.

listenings.title: Track 15. Amy, Matt and personality tests
listenings.qtype: Pick from a list (5–10) — qo'shimcha mashq
intro: 21-darsdagi Amy va Matt suhbatining davomi: shaxsiyat testlari, Amyni nima baxtli qiladi va Matt keyin nima qiladi. Avval savollarni o'qing, keyin BIR MARTA tinglang.
Ko'rsatma: Choose TWO letters, A–E, for each question.
transcript: MATT: I've also found one of those personality tests on the Internet. You know, answer these questions to find out how happy you are.
AMY: Oh, those. They're a bit of a waste of time, aren't they? I did one on 'How healthy are you?' and the results were completely wrong.
MATT: But they're quite good fun though, aren't they?
AMY: Well, yes, especially if you do them with friends. I think it's important that you shouldn't take them seriously, though.
MATT: That's true.

AMY: Anyway, why should I do a test that tells me how happy or healthy or successful I am? I mean, I already know the answers, don't I? So, I'm not likely to get any surprises, like, oh, according to this test I'm happy – I didn't expect that!
MATT: OK, I take your point. So what makes you happy?
AMY: Oh, I don't know. Spending time with people I know and like, I guess. I need people around me.
MATT: Me too. But I need time on my own, as well.

AMY: That doesn't really bother me. I grew up in a big family, so I'm used to someone always being in the room. If I wanted to be alone, to get away from people, I had to go out for a walk or something. I still do that occasionally. In fact, that's one thing that makes me happy. A long walk in the countryside. And the advantage is that you're getting some exercise too, which is something I don't usually do.
MATT: But you go running, don't you?
AMY: Sometimes, but only because I feel I have to. Anyway, back to your assignment. You've got all the information you need ...
MATT: Not quite. I need to do a bit more research first.
AMY: OK, so you'll be off to the library, then?
MATT: I would if I knew I could find something useful, but you know how disorganised it is there. It's impossible to find what you want, especially when it comes to psychology books.
AMY: Oh, I know.
MATT: No, give me a computer and the Internet any day.
AMY: Well, good luck with that. If you get bored and want a break, you know where to find me.
MATT: Thanks, but if I don't get this done, I'll be in trouble.
AMY: Why don't you email Tony? He did a similar assignment last year, so he might have a few suggestions.
MATT: That's a good idea. Have you got his email address?
AMY: Sure, give me a moment while I look it up.
MATT: Thanks.

tasks.title: Questions 5–10: Choose TWO letters, A–E
tasks.instr: Kimning fikri so'ralayotganini eslang: 5–8 — Amy, 9–10 — Matt.
items: 5–6 What does Amy think about personality tests? A) They take too much time to do. B) They are not accurate. C) They are entertaining. D) They are too serious. E) They tell you unexpected things.
7–8 What TWO things make Amy happy? A) being with friends B) having time on her own C) going out with her family D) spending time outside E) keeping fit
9–10 What TWO things is Matt going to do next? A) get more information B) go to the library C) try to find some useful books D) take a short break E) ask someone for help
why: "The results were completely wrong" (B) va "especially if you do them with friends" — "quite good fun" ga rozi (C). A tuzoq: "a waste of time" — vaqt ko'p ketishi emas, befoyda degani. D teskari: "you shouldn't take them seriously" — testlar emas, odamlar jiddiy qaramasin. E teskari: "I'm not likely to get any surprises".

"Spending time with people I know and like ... I need people around me" (A) va "A long walk in the countryside" (D). B tuzoq: bu MATTga kerak ("I need time on my own"); Amy: "That doesn't really bother me". E tuzoq: "going running ... only because I feel I have to".

"I need to do a bit more research first" (A) va "Why don't you email Tony?" — "That's a good idea" (E). B, C tuzoq: kutubxona "disorganised ... impossible to find what you want" — bormaydi. D teskari: "if I don't get this done, I'll be in trouble".
tasks.note: Ustoz kaliti: 5–6 B,C · 7–8 A,D · 9–10 A,E. Asosiy tuzoq — 7–8 B: "time on my own" Matt uchun, Amy uchun emas. Kim gapirayotganini kuzating!

listenings.title: Planning a class trip
intro: Ikki talaba (Kate va Sam) sinf sayohatini rejalashtirmoqda (Part 3). Avval savollarni o'qing, keyin bir marta tinglang.
transcript: KATE: So, Sam, we need to decide where to take the class for the end-of-year trip.
SAM: Right. What about the science museum? Everyone went last year, though.
KATE: Exactly — they'd be bored. How about the national park? It's not too far, and we could walk to the lake.
SAM: Yes, I like that. It's cheap, too. But what if it rains?
KATE: There's a visitor centre with a café, so we'd have somewhere to go inside.
SAM: Perfect. OK, national park it is. Now, how do we get there? A coach?
KATE: A coach would be expensive for just twenty people. What about the train?
SAM: The station is a long walk from the park. I think we should hire two minibuses — the teachers can drive.
KATE: Good idea, that's much cheaper. And what should people bring?
SAM: Their own lunch, definitely. And good walking shoes.
KATE: Yes, and I'll ask everyone to bring a raincoat, just in case. Money isn't necessary — the café is included in the ticket.

tasks.title: Choose TWO letters, A–E
items: 1–2 Which TWO reasons do Kate and Sam give for choosing the national park? A) nobody has been there B) it is not expensive C) there is somewhere to go if it rains D) it has a science centre E) it is near the station
3–4 Which TWO things should the students bring? A) money for the café B) their own lunch C) a map D) suitable shoes E) a camera
why: "It's cheap, too" (B) va "There's a visitor centre with a café ... somewhere to go inside" (C). A aytilmagan. E teskari: "The station is a long walk from the park".
"Their own lunch, definitely" (B) va "good walking shoes" (D). A teskari: "Money isn't necessary". Raincoat ham kerak, lekin variantlarda yo'q.

listenings.title: Tutor meeting — improving an essay
intro: Talaba (Nodir) o'qituvchi (Dr Hale) bilan insho haqida gaplashmoqda (Part 3). Avval savollarni o'qing, keyin bir marta tinglang.
transcript: DR HALE: Come in, Nodir. I've read your essay on city transport.
NODIR: Thank you. Was it all right?
DR HALE: The ideas are good, and your research is very thorough. You've used a lot of recent sources, which is excellent.
NODIR: Oh, good. I spent a long time in the library.
DR HALE: It shows. But there are two areas to work on. First, the introduction is too long — you tell the reader everything before you start. Keep it to one short paragraph.
NODIR: OK. And the second?
DR HALE: Your conclusion just repeats what you've already said. It should give your own opinion.
NODIR: I see. Should I add more examples too?
DR HALE: No, you have plenty. And your grammar is fine — don't worry about that.
NODIR: So, I'll rewrite the introduction and the conclusion. Can I also make the charts clearer?
DR HALE: The charts are fine. Just focus on those two parts and send it to me by Friday.

tasks.title: Choose TWO letters, A–E
items: 1–2 What TWO things does Dr Hale praise? A) the research B) the introduction C) the charts D) the use of recent sources E) the conclusion
3–4 What TWO things does Nodir agree to change? A) the introduction B) the grammar C) the examples D) the conclusion E) the charts
why: "Your research is very thorough" (A) va "used a lot of recent sources, which is excellent" (D). C tuzoq: "the charts are fine" — maqtov emas, oddiy "yaxshi". B, E — o'zgartirish kerak.
"I'll rewrite the introduction and the conclusion" — "Just focus on those two parts". B teskari: "grammar is fine". C teskari: "you have plenty". E teskari: "the charts are fine".
