objectives: Passage 3 ning eng qiyin uch turini bitta matnda ishlash: MCQ (muallif maqsadi), sentence endings, Yes/No/Not Given.

Matching sentence endings da grammatika + ma'no bo'yicha variantlarni o'chirish.
Muallif fikrini (views) baho so'zlaridan topish: "fortunately", "justifiably", "hideous", "an enormous achievement".
Passage 3 vaqt rejasi: 20 daqiqa, 14 savol.
materials: Reading #33 "The Pompidou Centre" matni 1–14 savollari bilan (MCQ 1–4, A–F sentence endings 5–8, Yes / No / Not Given 9–14) — har o'quvchiga bitta nusxa, javobsiz; A–F oxirlar ro'yxati va glossary matn bilan bir varaqda bo'lsin, javob kaliti va tuzoq izohlari faqat ustozda qoladi.

Reading #34 "The man who tried to destroy Paris" matni xuddi shu tuzilishdagi 1–14 savoli bilan — har o'quvchiga bitta nusxa; bu matnda o'quvchilar birinchi matndagi usulni mustaqil qo'llaydi, shuning uchun stolda taymer yoki sekundomer tursin (20 daqiqa). Ustoz varag'ida 14-savolning ikki tomoni yozib qo'yilgan bo'lsin — "modern houses that look like they are much older" nega NO va nega NOT GIVEN emas; muhokama shu qog'ozdan yuritiladi.

"The Sydney Opera House" va "The Eiffel Tower: from eyesore to icon" matnlari savollari va glossary bilan — har o'quvchiga bittadan nusxa; bu darsda audio yo'q, Listening bosqichi shu ikki yengilroq (Band 4–5) matn bilan to'ldiriladi.

"Learning to love concrete" uy vazifasi varaqasi — har o'quvchiga bitta nusxa, javobsiz; dars oxirida tarqatiladi, sinfda ochilmaydi; orqa tomonida "MCQ / sentence endings / Yes-No-Not Given uchun necha daqiqa ketdi" deb yoziladigan uchta bo'sh qator qoldiring.

Doskada qo'ng'iroqdan oldin ikki narsa tayyor tursin: xatboshi vazifasi so'zlari — tasvirlash, tushuntirish, taqqoslash, tanqid, baholash, misol keltirish (sinf mashqi ham, ikkinchi uy vazifasi ham shu ro'yxatdan ishlaydi); yonida Passage 3 vaqt rejasi: MCQ 7 + endings 5 + Y/N/NG 6 + tekshirish 2 = 20 daqiqa. intro: Passage 3 — eng uzun va eng qiyin matn. Ko'pincha muallif fikri va maqsadi so'raladi, faktlar kamroq.
MCQ "about the Xth paragraph" — savol qaysi xatboshini aytsa, faqat shu xatboshini o'qing. Javob tartibda (ALWAYS).

"Main purpose" savoli: xatboshining vazifasini aniqlang. Masalan, xatboshi "critics swiftly changed their tune" bilan tugasa — maqsad: fikr nega o'zgarganini ko'rsatish. Faqat bir detalni aytgan variant — tuzoq.

Matching sentence endings: gap boshi va A–F oxirlari. Avval GRAMMATIKA: "The escalators and lifts ..." (ko'plik) → "were ..." oxiri; keyin MA'NO. Ro'yxatda 2 ta ortiqcha oxir bor. Tartib odatda matn bo'yicha (USUALLY).
Yes / No / Not Given (19-dars): muallif fikri. "It is hard to call it a building" → "building so'zi yaxshiroq mos keladi" — NO.
Tavsiya etilgan tartib: MCQ (tartibli) → sentence endings → Y/N/NG. MCQ matnning birinchi yarmini "o'qitib" beradi.
presentation: "Main purpose" savolida nima qilaman?
Xatboshi oxirgi gapiga qarang — u odatda xulosa va maqsadni ko'rsatadi.
Sentence endingsda ikki oxir mos kelsa?
Gap boshining aniq mavzusini matndan toping va o'sha gap bilan solishtiring.
Endings tartibdami?
Odatda (USUALLY) ha.
Muallif boshqa odam fikrini aytsa?
"Traditionalists regarded it as ugly" — bu ular fikri; muallif esa "an enormous achievement" deydi.
Passage 3 ga necha daqiqa?
20 daqiqa: MCQ 7, endings 5, YNNG 6, tekshirish 2.
Matn juda qiyin bo'lsa?
Savollarni o'qing — ular matnning qaysi qismini o'qish kerakligini aytadi. Hamma so'zni tushunish shart emas.
notes: Ikkala ustoz matni (Pompidou va Le Corbusier) bir xil tuzilishga ega: MCQ 1–4, endings 5–8, YNNG 9–14. Ikkinchi matnda o'quvchilar birinchisidagi usulni mustaqil qo'llaydi.
Bu matnlar uchun javob kaliti berilmagan edi — barcha 28 ta javob Jony Academy tomonidan yechildi va har biri matn bilan isbotlandi.
Asl matndagi xatolar tuzatildi: "most outstanding now building" → "new building", "a James Bond 1 film" → "a James Bond film", "enabled wider audience" → "a wider audience", "Europe s" → "Europe's".

Le Corbusier 14-savoli munozarali: matn "modern houses that look like they are much older" deydi — "old houses" emas, shuning uchun NO. Ba'zi o'quvchilar NOT GIVEN deyishi mumkin — ikki variantni solishtirib muhokama qiling.

readings.title: Reading #33. The Pompidou Centre
readings.qtype: Passage 3: MCQ (1–4) + Sentence endings (5–8) + Yes/No/Not Given (9–14)
text: More than three decades after it was built, the Pompidou Centre in Paris has survived its moment at the edge of architectural fashion and proved itself to be one of the most remarkable buildings of the 20th century.

It was the most outstanding new building constructed in Paris for two generations. It looked like an explosion of brightly coloured service pipes in the calm of the city centre. However, when in 1977 the architects Richard Rogers and Renzo Piano stood among a large crowd of 5,000 at the opening of the Centre Culturel d'Art Georges Pompidou (known as the Pompidou), _no one was really aware of the significance of this unusual building_.

Rogers was only 38 when he and Piano won the competition to design a new cultural centre for Paris in the old market site. Young, unknown architects, they had been chosen from a field of nearly 700 to design one of the most prestigious buildings of its day. After six difficult years, with 25,000 drawings, seven lawsuits, battles over budgets, and _a desperate last-minute scramble to finish the building_, it had finally been done.

Yet the opening was a downbeat moment. The Pompidou Centre had been rubbished by the critics while it was being built, there was no more work in prospect for the architects, and their partnership had effectively broken down. But this was just a passing crisis. The Centre, which combined the national museum of modern art, exhibition space, a public library and a centre for modern music, proved an enormous success. It attracted six million visitors in its first year, and _with its success, the critics swiftly changed their tune_.

The architects had been driven by the desire for ultimate flexibility, for _a building that would not limit the movement of its users_. All the different parts were approached through the same enormous entrance hall and served by the same escalator, which was free to anyone to ride, whether they wanted to visit an exhibition or just admire the view. With all the services at one end of the building, _escalators and lifts at the other_, and the floors hung on giant steel beams providing uninterrupted space the size of two football pitches, their dream had become a reality.

The image of the Pompidou pervaded popular culture in the 1970s, making appearances everywhere - _on record-album covers and a table lamp_, and even acting as the set for a James Bond film. This did much to overcome the secretive nature of the architectural culture of its time, as it enabled a wider audience to appreciate the style and content of the building and so moved away from the strictly professional view.

The following year, Rogers was commissioned to design a new headquarters for Lloyd's Bank in London and went on to create one of Britain's most dynamic architectural practices. Piano is now among the world's most respected architects. But what of their shared creation?

It was certainly like no previous museum, with its plans for a flexible interior that not only had movable walls but _floors that could also be adjusted up or down_. _This second feature did not in the end survive_ when the competition drawings were turned into a real building. In other ways, however, the finished building demonstrated a remarkable degree of refinement - of craftsmanship even - in the way the original diagram was transformed into a superbly detailed structure. It was this quality which, according to some critics, suggested that the Pompidou should be seen as _closer to the 19th-century engineering tradition_ than the space age.

Nevertheless, as a model for urban planning, _it has proved immensely influential_. The Guggenheim in Bilbao and the many other major landmark projects that were built in the belief that innovatively designed cultural buildings can bring about urban renewal are all following the lead of the Pompidou Centre.

Other buildings may now challenge it for the title of Europe's most outlandish work of architecture. However, more than a quarter of a century later, this construction - _it is hard to call it a building_ when there is no façade, just a lattice of steel beams and pipes and a long external escalator snaking up the outside - still seems extreme.

Today, the Pompidou Centre itself _still looks much as it did when it opened_. _The shock value of its colour-coded plumbing and its structure has not faded with the years._ But while traditionalists regarded it as an ugly attack on Paris when it was built, _they now see it for what it is - an enormous achievement_, technically and conceptually.
paraphrases: no one was really aware of the significance
there was a hurry to complete it
a desperate last-minute scramble to finish
the critics swiftly changed their tune
allow visitors to use it freely
would not limit the movement of its users
record-album covers and a table lamp
did not in the end survive
reminded people of past building styles
influenced the way cities are designed
immensely influential as a model for urban planning
(opposite of) shock value has not faded
(opposite of) still looks much as it did

tasks.title: Questions 1–4: Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D
tasks.instr: Har savol ko'rsatgan xatboshini o'qing. Javoblar tartibda.
items: 1 What does the writer say in the first paragraph about the opening of the Pompidou Centre? A) The elderly did not like it. B) The architects were not present. C) The atmosphere was very noisy. D) The people did not realise its importance.

2 What does the writer say in the second paragraph about the construction of the Pompidou? A) There was a hurry to complete it. B) It cost less than expected. C) Other experts helped draw the plans. D) The market location was criticised.

3 What is the writer's main purpose in the third paragraph? A) to explain the multi-functional role of the centre B) to praise the architects for their design ideas C) to say why some people's opinions quickly altered D) to show how the media benefited from its success

4 What was the architects' 'dream', referred to in the fourth paragraph? A) to become famous B) to provide entertainment C) to allow visitors to use it freely D) to build the biggest museum in the world
why: "No one was really aware of the significance of this unusual building". B teskari: arxitektorlar olomon ichida turgan.
"A desperate last-minute scramble to finish the building". B tuzoq: "battles over budgets" — arzon bo'lgani aytilmagan.
Xatboshi tushkun ochilishdan boshlanib, "with its success, the critics swiftly changed their tune" bilan tugaydi. A tuzoq: markazning vazifalari faqat detal sifatida tilga olingan.
"Ultimate flexibility ... a building that would not limit the movement of its users"; eskalator "free to anyone to ride".

readings.title: Reading #34. The man who tried to destroy Paris
readings.qtype: Passage 3: MCQ (1–4) + Sentence endings (5–8) + Yes/No/Not Given (9–14) — qo'shimcha mashq
text: Le Corbusier was one of the most influential architects of the 20th century. But many may wish he had never built anything

Born Charles-Edouard Jeanneret in Switzerland in 1887, the architect Le Corbusier used his grandfather's name when he went to Paris at the age of 29. As Jeanneret, he had been a fairly successful small-town architect; as Le Corbusier, he had bigger ideas. He disliked the architectural styles that were popular at the time, and considered them to be out of date in an industrial age. _He believed that the 20th century deserved a brand-new style of architecture. "We must start again from zero,"_ he said.

The new style of architecture was called the International Style, and _it attracted many followers in the architectural world_. However, _nobody was as enthusiastic about it as Le Corbusier at the beginning_. He worked hard to promote his ideas at exhibitions, at talks, in books and in his own magazine. He loved machines, and believed that, like a machine, a building should have a function. He is famous for saying: "A house is a machine for living in."

The machines he admired the most were ships, and his early buildings tried to capture the spirit of the sea with their white walls, exposed rooms, shining glass and flat roofs. He called this style of architecture 'purism'. The first building to embrace this style was the Villa Savoye in France. Le Corbusier believed that it was one of the best, most functional houses ever built. _Unfortunately, this turned out to be an exaggeration._ The flat roof was a particular problem, as water poured in every time it rained, and it needed constant repairs. Nevertheless, _its design was revolutionary, and it should be considered a significant piece_ of early 20th-century architecture.

In 1935, Le Corbusier visited New York City. He loved the city, and especially its tall buildings. He had only one reservation, which he explained to a journalist for the Herald Tribune newspaper. American skyscrapers were the biggest, tallest buildings in the world at that time, but Le Corbusier was a man who always thought big, and as far as he was concerned, they were "just too small". Le Corbusier had always admired tall buildings. _Now, inspired by his visit, he abandoned purism._ _It is doubtful that he could have created anything as grand_ as the skyscrapers he had seen in the city, but from now on Le Corbusier started designing buildings that sent out a more powerful message.

He first started using bright colours, and then experimented with concrete. _Le Corbusier loved the look and flexibility of concrete_, and found it hard to hide it behind brick or paint, _preferring to leave it on full view_. At a time when concrete was seen as modern and exciting, his designs made him world famous, and he was asked to design several important buildings around the world. Altogether, he designed about 60 major buildings worldwide, in a style that became known as 'modernism'.

However, while _many admired and copied his new style of architecture, many more hated it_. They turned against him, and tried to block his plans. Buildings should inspire people and make them feel good, they said, and Le Corbusier's ugly, depressing buildings often had the opposite effect. In this respect, the people of Paris had a lucky escape. Early in his career, Le Corbusier had wanted to knock down the centre of Paris and replace the old buildings with huge towers. _Fortunately, his plan was rejected._ Justifiably, in view of his plans to transform one of the world's most beautiful cities into _a hideous concrete jungle_, Le Corbusier is still known as 'the man who tried to destroy Paris'.

Despite the criticism, he had an enormous effect on the world of architecture, and _attracted a large number of followers. As a result, many places were subjected to his style._ In the Paris suburbs of Bobigny, for example, huge towers were built to house some of the city's poorer inhabitants. Other European cities such as London, Berlin and Dublin also felt his influence.

Apart from the buildings that were directly influenced by Le Corbusier, something else happened that the architect never planned: there was a return to older styles of architecture. Today, many people live in _modern houses that look like they are much older_. This look may represent a return to traditional tastes and values. More likely, however, it represents a reaction against modernist architecture.

2 What does the writer say about the International Style in the second paragraph? A) A lot of other architects liked it. B) At first, people did not like it very much. C) It took a lot of hard work to get people to accept it. D) The buildings looked like machines.

readings.title: The Sydney Opera House
readings.qtype: Passage 3: MCQ + Sentence endings + Yes/No/Not Given
text: Few buildings are as instantly recognisable as the Sydney Opera House, with its white roofs rising above the harbour like the sails of a ship. Yet the story of how it was built is one of conflict, delay and enormous cost, and the architect who designed it never saw it finished.

In 1957, a young Danish architect, Jørn Utzon, won an international competition with a design that was little more than a set of bold sketches. The judges admired its imagination, but nobody, including Utzon himself, knew exactly how the curved roofs could be built. Construction began in 1959, before the engineering problems had been solved, a decision that caused many of the troubles that followed.

It took years of experiments before Utzon found the answer: every roof shell would be cut from the surface of the same imaginary sphere, so that the pieces could be produced in a standard way. It was a brilliant solution, but by then the project was already far behind schedule.

Costs rose far beyond the original estimate of seven million Australian dollars. A new state government, elected in 1965, began to question every payment, and in 1966 Utzon resigned and left Australia, never to return. The interiors were completed by a team of local architects, and the building finally opened in 1973 — ten years late and at a cost of 102 million dollars.

Today it is hard to imagine Sydney without it. In 2007 it became a UNESCO World Heritage Site, one of very few buildings to receive this honour while its architect was still alive. In my view, the story is a reminder that great buildings are rarely easy ones: the problems are soon forgotten, but the achievement remains.

readings.title: The Eiffel Tower: from eyesore to icon
readings.qtype: Passage 3: MCQ + Sentence endings + Yes/No/Not Given
text: Today the Eiffel Tower is the symbol of Paris and one of the most visited monuments in the world. It is easy to forget that when it was built, many Parisians hated it.

The tower was designed for the World's Fair of 1889, which celebrated the hundredth anniversary of the French Revolution. Gustave Eiffel's company, which had already built bridges and railway stations, won the competition with a plan for an iron tower 300 metres high — by far the tallest structure in the world at that time. It was built in just over two years, a remarkable speed for such a project.

Even before construction began, a group of well-known artists and writers published a letter of protest in a Paris newspaper. They called the tower "useless and monstrous" and claimed it would dominate and spoil the beautiful city. Some of them later changed their minds; others never did.

The tower was only meant to stand for twenty years, after which it was to be taken down. Eiffel, determined to save it, encouraged scientists to use it for experiments, and in the early 1900s it proved valuable as a giant radio aerial. During the First World War, it was used to intercept enemy messages. Its usefulness saved it, and the permit was extended.

It remained the tallest building in the world until 1930. Today around six million people visit it every year. In my opinion, the story of the tower shows that a city's taste can change completely within a single lifetime, and that the buildings we hate today may become the ones we love tomorrow.

readings.title: Learning to love concrete
readings.qtype: Passage 3: MCQ + Sentence endings + Yes/No/Not Given
text: For decades, the large concrete buildings of the 1950s, 60s and 70s were among the least loved buildings in Europe. The style, known as brutalism, took its name from the French phrase béton brut, meaning "raw concrete", and many people felt the name suited buildings that looked heavy, grey and unfriendly.

Many of these buildings were built after the Second World War, when cities needed large numbers of homes, schools and hospitals quickly and cheaply. Concrete was ideal: it was strong, inexpensive and could be shaped into almost any form. Architects also believed that honest, undecorated materials expressed a modern, democratic spirit.

By the 1980s, however, public opinion had turned. Some housing estates had become associated with crime and poverty, and poor maintenance left concrete stained and cracked. Local governments demolished many brutalist buildings, often with public support.

In the last twenty years, something unexpected has happened. A new generation, too young to remember the problems, has begun to admire the bold shapes of these buildings. Photographs of brutalist towers are popular on social media, and flats in well-kept examples, such as the Barbican in London, are now expensive and highly desired.

I believe this change is welcome, but it should not make us forget why people once hated these buildings. The best brutalist architecture was imaginative and well built; the worst was cheap and badly managed. The lesson is not about concrete itself, but about the care a building receives after it is finished.

homework_intro: Bugun bitta matnda uch turni — MCQ, sentence endings va Yes / No / Not Given ni — ketma-ket ishladik va har turga o'z vaqtini ajratdik; uyda endi xuddi shu ishni yolg'iz o'zingiz bajarasiz.

Birinchi vazifa — 5-matn "Learning to love concrete": soatga qarab 15 daqiqa qo'ying, avval ikkita MCQ ni, keyin sentence endingsni, oxirida Yes / No / Not Given ni ishlang va har javob yoniga matndagi isbot gapni qisqa ko'chirib qo'ying.

Ikkinchisi — "Xatboshi vazifalari": Le Corbusier matnining 8 xatboshisiga doskadagi ro'yxatdan bittadan vazifa so'zini yozasiz (tasvirlash, tushuntirish, taqqoslash, tanqid, baholash, misol) — 8 qator; uchinchisi — "Muallif fikri daftari": Pompidou va Le Corbusier matnlaridan muallif fikrini bildirgan 10 ta so'z yoki iborani, har birining yoniga qaysi xatboshidan olinganini yozasiz; bu ikkalasi birga 20 daqiqacha oladi.

Eng ko'p qilinadigan xato — "main purpose" savolida xatboshining bitta detalini tanlash: variant matnda bor bo'lsa ham, savol xatboshi NIMA QILISHINI so'raydi, shuning uchun avval vazifa so'zini o'zingiz ayting, keyin variantni tanlang.

Uchala vazifani ham keyingi dars boshida daftar ochiq holda stolga qo'yasiz: "Learning to love concrete" javoblarini birga tekshiramiz, men MCQ 2 — "main purpose" savolining isbotini va muallif fikri daftaringizdan bir nechta iborani so'rayman.

intro: Part 4 — IELTS Listeningning oxirgi va eng qiyin qismi: bitta so'zlovchining ma'ruzasi (lecture). O'rtada pauza YO'Q — 10 savolni o'qishga faqat boshida vaqt beriladi. Shuning uchun boshidagi 30–45 soniyada barcha qaydlarni o'qib chiqing.

Qaydlar sarlavhalarga bo'lingan (Overall design / Roof / Supporting posts). Sarlavha — ma'ruzaning bo'limi. Ma'ruzachi yangi bo'limga o'tganda signal beradi: "Now, let's have a close look at the roof", "So how does the house stay upright?" (= Supporting posts).

listenings.title: CD2 Track 27. Traditional Samoan Houses
intro: Ma'ruzachi Samoa (Tinch okeani orollari) an'anaviy uylari haqida gapiradi. Avval 45 soniya barcha qaydlarni o'qing va uch sarlavhani belgilang: Overall design, Roof, Supporting posts. Pauza bo'lmaydi. Keyin BIR MARTA tinglang.
Ko'rsatma: Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.
transcript: Last week, we looked at some of the features of modern houses, and today we're going to turn the clock back and look at traditional house design. I've chosen to start with Samoa, which is part of a group of Polynesian islands in the South Pacific Sea, because the influence of culture and weather on house design is quite clear there.

Um, so let's have a look, first of all, at the overall design of a traditional Samoan house. Now, these days, houses in Samoa have become more modern and are usually rectangular, but traditional designs were round or sometimes they were oval in shape. Here's a picture. This traditional style is still used – often for guest houses or meeting houses – and most Samoan villages have at least one of these buildings.

As you can see, there are no walls, so the air circulates freely around the house – Samoa is a place that experiences high temperatures ... but the open design of the house also reflects the openness of Samoan society. If the occupants want shelter, there are several blinds made of coconut leaves that can be lowered during rainy or windy weather – or indeed the blinds can also be pulled down if people want some privacy.

The foundations of the house – that's the part beneath the floor – are raised slightly. Um, in the past, the height was linked to the importance of the occupants, which we'll talk about another time. However, the floor of the house was usually covered with river stones. Today, we have a range of methods for balancing the temperature inside a building, but the stones on the floor of a Samoan home are ideal for cooling the building on hot days.

Now, let's have a close look at the roof. This, as you can see in the picture, is dome-shaped and traditionally thatched, or covered with leaves from the sugar cane – that's an established crop in Samoa. This was a job for the women, and it involved twisting the leaves and then fastening them with a thin strip of coconut leaf before fixing them to the roof in several layers.

Now, the shape of the roof is important – you can see that the sides are quite steep, and that's done so that the rain falls straight to the ground without moisture going through the leaves and causing leaks or dampness inside the house. Then, you'll notice how high the top of the roof is – this is a way of allowing heat to rise on sunny days and go through the thatching, thereby cooling the house.

So how does the house stay upright? Well, there are a number of evenly spaced posts inside. They, um, they encircle the interior of the building and go up to the roof and support the beams there. They're also buried – er, usually about a metre and a half – in the ground to keep them firm. These posts are produced using local timber from the surrounding forests. They're cut by men from the family or village, and the number varies depending on the size and importance of the house.

Now, these posts were a very significant part of Samoan culture and did much more than hold up the roof. When there were meetings, people sat with their back to certain posts depending on their status in society. So there were posts for chiefs according to their status and posts for speakers and so on – and ordinary people sat around the side on mats.

The last area I want to look at today is the attachment of the beams and posts – what you call 'fixing' the construction. Traditionally, no nails or screws were used anywhere in such a building. Instead, coconut fibres were braided into rope to fix the beams and posts together. The old people of the village usually made and plaited the rope. This was a lengthy process – an ordinary house used about 40,000 feet of this rope – and as you can see in this picture, the rope was pulled very tightly and wound round the beams and posts in a complex pattern. And in fact, the process of tying it to the beams so that it was tight and strong enough to keep them together is one of the great architectural achievements of Polynesia.

listenings.title: Track 22. The Beijing Olympic Stadium
intro: 21-asr arxitekturasi turkumidagi ma'ruza: 2008-yil Pekin Olimpiada stadioni ("Qush uyasi"). Avval uch sarlavhani belgilang: Background details, General impressions, Inside. Keyin BIR MARTA tinglang.
Ko'rsatma: Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.
transcript: Good morning, everyone. Today, as part of our 21st century architecture series, I'm going to tell you a bit about a remarkable structure which I'm sure you're all familiar with, the stadium that was built for the 2008 Olympics in Beijing.

OK, let's start with a few background details. The stadium was designed by Herzog and de Meuron, a firm of architects from Switzerland. They studied Chinese ceramics, er, plates, cups and bowls, to get inspiration. The stadium is actually two structures, which are completely separate from each other. In the middle there's the seating area, which was originally designed for 100,000 spectators, but this had to be reduced to 90,000. Around this area is the frame, which is made of 110,000 tons of steel in horizontal beams and vertical columns. The architects wanted the roof to open and close, but they changed it because it could have been dangerous if there was an earthquake. The big advantage of changing it was that it reduced the cost by several million dollars, although the building still came to an incredible $423 million.

So, what makes this stadium such an amazing building? Let's start with the general impression it creates. For this, the best place to look at it is from a distance. Why from a distance? Well, that's where you'll really get an impression of what it looks like and how big it is. You'll also notice how it really stands out in its surroundings. This is not just because of its size – and it is big – but also because it stands on a low hill which helps make it higher than any other buildings in the area. Then there's its unusual shape, which has helped to give it its nickname of the Bird's Nest. The unusual shape of the stadium also does something else. You see, if you stare at it for long enough, you also get the impression that this structure isn't standing still, that it's moving in different directions, almost like it's a living, breathing creature. This is especially true at night, when the stadium is lit up from inside with lights that continually change colour.

In the stadium, everything changes. There are visitor entrances all around the outside, and as you enter, you get the impression that you're walking into a forest, and not just any forest, but something magical from a children's story. As you cross towards the spectator area, coloured light comes through the clear roof panels, creating strange pools of light and shadow. Now you're no longer in a forest, but on a set that's been built for a fantasy film. It really is a remarkable experience, and it's only once you're inside the spectator area that you finally realise you're in a sports stadium.

listenings.title: Lecture: the history of the umbrella
intro: Ma'ruza (Part 4 monolog). Avval qaydlarni o'qing va sarlavhalarni belgilang, keyin skriptni bir marta tinglang (ustoz o'qiydi, pauzasiz).
transcript: Good morning. Today I want to look at an everyday object with a surprisingly long history — the umbrella.

Let's begin with its origins. The first umbrellas were used about four thousand years ago in Egypt and China, but not against rain. They were used as protection from the sun, and only important people, such as kings and priests, were allowed to carry them.

Now, let's move on to how the umbrella became waterproof. It was the Chinese who first covered paper umbrellas with wax, so that they could be used in the rain. This idea slowly travelled west along the trade routes.

In Europe, however, the umbrella had a difficult start. For a long time, it was seen as an object for women only. That changed in the 1750s, when a traveller called Jonas Hanway carried one through the streets of London for thirty years. At first, people laughed at him, but by the end of his life, men were using umbrellas too.

The last area I'd like to talk about is design. Early European umbrellas were heavy, with frames made of wood or whalebone. In 1852, Samuel Fox designed a frame with steel ribs, which made the umbrella much lighter, and this basic design has hardly changed since.

listenings.title: Lecture: how bees make honey
intro: Biologiya ma'ruzasi (Part 4). Avval qaydlarni o'qing, keyin bir marta tinglang.
transcript: In today's lecture, I'd like to explain how honeybees produce honey.

First, the collection stage. Worker bees fly from flower to flower, collecting a sweet liquid called nectar. A single bee may visit up to fifteen hundred flowers in one trip. The nectar is stored in a special stomach, separate from the one the bee uses for its own food.

Next comes the processing stage. When the bee returns to the hive, it passes the nectar to younger bees, who chew it for about half an hour. During this time, chemicals called enzymes change the nectar into a simpler form of sugar.
Then there's the drying stage. The bees place the liquid in the cells of the honeycomb. At this point it's still too wet, so the bees fan it with their wings until most of the water evaporates.

Finally, the bees seal each cell with a lid made of wax. Stored this way, honey can last for an extremely long time — archaeologists have found honey in ancient Egyptian tombs that was still safe to eat.

listenings.title: Lecture: the Registan of Samarkand
intro: Arxitektura ma'ruzasi (Part 4). Uyda bir marta tinglang.
transcript: Today we're going to look at one of the most famous public squares in the world — the Registan in Samarkand, Uzbekistan.
Let's start with the name. "Registan" means "sandy place", because the square was originally covered in sand. It was the centre of the city, where people gathered to hear royal announcements.

The square is surrounded by three buildings called madrasahs, which were religious schools. The oldest, the Ulugh Beg Madrasah, was built in the fifteenth century by the ruler and astronomer Ulugh Beg. It's said that he taught mathematics there himself.

The other two buildings were added in the seventeenth century. The most striking is the Sher-Dor Madrasah, which is decorated with images of tigers chasing deer — very unusual, because Islamic art rarely shows animals.

Over the centuries, earthquakes badly damaged the buildings. In the twentieth century, a long programme of restoration was carried out, and one of the minarets, which was leaning dangerously, was straightened. Today the square is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and is visited by thousands of tourists every year.

lessons.grammar_topic: Matching sentence endings — gap boshini to'g'ri oxiri bilan ulash
lessons.book_ref: Jony Academy materiali — 5 ta mualliflik matni (osondan qiyinga). Takrorlash uchun: 29-dars, Pompidou 5–8 va Le Corbusier 5–8.
objectives: Matching sentence endings savol turining tuzilishini tushunish: gap boshi (1, 2, 3...) + oxirlar ro'yxati (A–G), ortiqcha oxirlar bor.
3 bosqichli filtrdan foydalanish: 1) GRAMMATIKA, 2) MATNDAN JOY, 3) MA'NO.
Gap boshidagi kalit so'zni matndan topish va javoblar tartibda kelishidan (USUALLY) foydalanish.
Asosiy tuzoqni tanish: oxir matnga ko'ra TO'G'RI, lekin boshqa gap boshiga tegishli.
5 ta matnda bosqichma-bosqich ishlash: Band 4 → Band 5.5.
materials: 1–2-matn ("The milkmaids and the first vaccine" va "Why the Titanic sank so quickly") savollari bilan — har o'quvchiga bittadan nusxa, javobsiz; A–G oxirlar qutisi matn bilan bir varaqda bo'lsin, javob kaliti va tuzoq izohlari faqat ustozda qoladi.

Doskada qo'ng'iroqqacha tayyor tursin: sinf mashqining besh oxiri — A to find a cure. B was built in 1912. C that the plan had failed. D were too expensive. Bu ikki ro'yxat dars oxirigacha o'chirilmaydi.

intro: Matching sentence endings — sizga gapning faqat BOSHI beriladi (masalan, "Women who milked cows"). Pastda A–G oxirlar ro'yxati bor. Har boshni bitta oxir bilan ulab, matnga mos TO'LIQ gap hosil qilasiz. Javob — harf.
Oxirlar ko'proq bo'ladi: 5 ta bosh — 7 ta oxir. Demak 2 ta oxir ortiqcha va ular ataylab "to'g'ridek" yozilgan.

1-FILTR — GRAMMATIKA (matnni o'qimasdan!). Bosh qanday tugaydi? "Women who milked cows" (ko'plik) → "rarely caught..." yoki "were..."; "The ship" (birlik) → "was...", "were" emas; "...realised" → "that + gap"; "...hoped" → "to + fe'l". Bu filtr ba'zi variantlarni darhol chiqarib tashlaydi.
2-FILTR — MATNDAN JOY. Gap boshidagi kalit so'zni (ism, sana, noyob so'z) matndan toping. Javoblar odatda (USUALLY) matn tartibida keladi: 3-savol javobi 2-savoldan keyinroq turadi.
3-FILTR — MA'NO. Qolgan 2–3 oxirni o'sha joy bilan solishtiring. Oxir matnda boshqa so'zlar bilan aytilgan bo'ladi (paraphrase).
ENG KATTA TUZOQ: oxir matnga ko'ra to'g'ri, lekin BOSHQA narsa, BOSHQA odam yoki BOSHQA vaqt haqida. Shuning uchun faqat "to'g'rimi?" emas, "AYNAN SHU bosh haqidami?" deb so'rang.
Tugagach butun gapni ovoz chiqarib o'qing: grammatik va mantiqiy jihatdan silliq bo'lishi kerak.
formulas: Har bosh yoniga mos oxirlarni yozing
presentation: Bitta oxirni ikki marta ishlatsa bo'ladimi?
Odatda yo'q. Har oxir bir marta; ortiqchalari ishlatilmaydi.
Grammatika bo'yicha ikki oxir mos kelsa?
Normal holat. Endi matndan joyni topib, ma'no bo'yicha tanlang.
Javoblar matn tartibidami?
Odatda (USUALLY) ha. Topilmasa, butun matnda kalit so'zni qidiring.
Oxirdagi so'z matnda aynan bor. Shumi?
Ehtiyot bo'ling — aynan so'z ko'pincha tuzoq. Ma'noni va kim haqida ekanini tekshiring.
Summary completion bilan farqi nima?
Summaryda bitta matn va bo'sh joylar; bu yerda har gap alohida va oxir butun ibora bo'ladi.
Vaqt qancha?
Har gapga 1–1.5 daqiqa. Grammatika filtri vaqtni ancha tejaydi.

readings.title: The milkmaids and the first vaccine
text: In the 18th century, smallpox was one of the most feared diseases in the world. It killed around a third of the people who caught it, and many survivors were left with deep marks on their faces.

Edward Jenner, a country doctor in England, heard a story that was common among farmers: milkmaids, the women who milked cows, rarely caught smallpox. Many of them had earlier caught cowpox, a mild disease that cows passed to humans, which caused only a few spots on the hands.

In 1796, Jenner decided to test the idea. He took material from a cowpox spot on the hand of a milkmaid called Sarah Nelmes and put it into a small cut on the arm of James Phipps, the eight-year-old son of his gardener. The boy became slightly ill for a few days and then recovered. Six weeks later, Jenner exposed him to smallpox. The boy did not become ill.

Other doctors were doubtful at first, and some newspapers laughed at the idea of putting material from cows into people. However, the method worked, and it spread quickly across Europe and America. Jenner called it "vaccination", from vacca, the Latin word for cow.

Almost two hundred years later, after a worldwide vaccination campaign, the World Health Organization declared in 1980 that smallpox had been completely eradicated. It remains the only human disease that has been wiped out in this way.

readings.title: Why the Titanic sank so quickly
text: On the night of 14 April 1912, the Titanic, the largest passenger ship in the world, hit an iceberg in the North Atlantic on its first voyage from England to New York. Less than three hours later, it was at the bottom of the sea.

The ship had been described as "practically unsinkable". It was divided into sixteen watertight compartments, and it could stay afloat if up to four of them were flooded. However, the iceberg damaged the side of the ship along a length of about ninety metres, and water entered five or six compartments. From that moment, the ship could not be saved.

There were other problems. The crew had received several warnings about ice from other ships that day, but the Titanic continued at high speed. When the lookouts finally saw the iceberg, it was too close to avoid.

The most serious problem was the lifeboats. The Titanic carried twenty lifeboats, enough for fewer than 1,200 people, although more than 2,200 were on board. The rules of the time were based on the size of a ship, not on the number of passengers, so the ship was not breaking the law. More than 1,500 people died.

The disaster led to important changes. In 1914, an international agreement required ships to carry enough lifeboats for everyone on board, and ships had to keep a radio watch for twenty-four hours a day.

readings.title: How computers learnt to play chess
text: For centuries, chess was seen as the ultimate test of human intelligence. When the first computer programs appeared in the 1950s, many scientists believed that a machine able to beat the world champion would prove that computers could really think.

Early programs were weak. They could calculate quickly, but they had no sense of which moves were important, and good amateur players beat them easily. Progress came slowly, mainly through faster computers that could examine more positions every second.

In 1996, IBM's computer Deep Blue played a six-game match against the world champion, Garry Kasparov. Deep Blue won the first game, but Kasparov won the match. A year later, after its engineers had improved it, Deep Blue won a rematch. Kasparov was angry and suggested that humans had helped the machine during the games, but IBM denied this and refused his request for a third match.

Deep Blue did not "understand" chess. It simply examined around 200 million positions per second and used rules written by human experts. In 2017, a program called AlphaZero took a completely different approach. It was given only the rules of the game and then played millions of games against itself. Within a day, it was stronger than any previous program, and experts described its style as creative and surprisingly human.
Today, the best programs are far stronger than any person. Yet chess has not died. More people play it than ever before, and top players use computers not as opponents but as training partners.

readings.title: The mould that changed medicine
text: In September 1928, the Scottish scientist Alexander Fleming returned to his laboratory in London after a summer holiday. Among the untidy piles of glass dishes on his bench, he noticed something strange: on one dish of bacteria, a blue-green mould had grown, and around it the bacteria had disappeared.

Fleming realised that the mould was producing a substance that killed bacteria, and he named it penicillin. He published his results in 1929, but he could not produce the substance in large amounts or in a pure form, and after a few years he moved on to other research. For almost a decade, his discovery attracted little attention.

The story continued at Oxford University, where Howard Florey and Ernst Chain began to study penicillin in 1939. Their team found a way to purify it, and in 1940 they showed that it could protect mice from deadly infections. The first human patient, a policeman, was treated in 1941. He began to recover, but the supply ran out and he died — which showed how much more of the drug was needed.

Mass production began in the United States, where companies learnt to grow the mould in huge tanks. By 1944, there was enough penicillin to treat the soldiers injured on D-Day. In 1945, Fleming, Florey and Chain shared the Nobel Prize in Medicine.

In his Nobel speech, Fleming gave a warning: if people used too little penicillin, or used it when it was not needed, bacteria could become resistant. Today, antibiotic resistance is one of the most serious problems in medicine, exactly as he predicted.

readings.title: The Silk Road: more than a road
text: The name "Silk Road" suggests a single highway along which camels carried silk from China to Europe. In reality, it was a changing network of routes, by land and by sea, that connected East Asia, Central Asia, the Middle East and the Mediterranean for more than 1,500 years. The name itself is surprisingly modern: it was introduced in 1877 by the German geographer Ferdinand von Richthofen.

Very few merchants travelled the whole distance. Goods usually moved in stages, passing from one trader to the next, and each city along the way took its profit. Cities such as Samarkand and Bukhara grew rich not only by selling goods but by providing markets, water and places to rest for the caravans that passed through them.

Silk was the most famous product, but it was far from the only one. Horses, spices, glass, paper, precious metals and medicines all travelled along the routes, in both directions. In many periods, the most valuable things that moved were not goods at all but ideas. Religions such as Buddhism and later Islam spread along the trade routes, and so did technologies: the knowledge of how to make paper reached Samarkand from China in the 8th century and later spread to the Middle East and Europe.

The exchange was not always positive. Diseases travelled with the merchants, and many historians believe that the plague which killed millions of people in the 14th century reached Europe partly through these trade networks.

In 2014, part of the network — the routes of the Chang'an-Tianshan corridor — became a UNESCO World Heritage Site. For the people of Uzbekistan, whose cities stood at the centre of the network, the Silk Road is not only a subject of history but a source of national pride.

intro: Listening testi taxminan 30 daqiqa: 4 section, har birida 10 savol. Audio BIR MARTA eshittiriladi. Qog'oz imtihonda oxirida javoblarni varaqqa ko'chirish uchun 10 daqiqa beriladi (kompyuterda — 2 daqiqa tekshirish).
Section'lar qiyinlashib boradi: S1 — kundalik suhbat (mehmonxona), S2 — monolog (hayvonot parki), S3 — o'quv suhbati (talabalar va o'qituvchi), S4 — akademik ma'ruza, PAUZASIZ.
Har section oldidan va S1–S3 ichidagi pauzalarda savollarni o'qishga vaqt beriladi. Bu vaqtni keyingi qismni o'qishga sarflang, o'tgan javobni o'ylashga emas.
S1 boshida namuna (Example) bor: "Arrival date — 23rd August". Namuna eshittirilgach, audio boshidan qayta boshlanadi — ovozlarga ko'nikish uchun.

Bu testdagi savol turlari: form completion (3, 23-dars), note completion (5-dars), map/plan labelling (17-dars), multiple choice (9, 24-dars), chart/graph tanlash (MCQ ning rasmli ko'rinishi), sentence completion (12-dars), Part 4 notes (30-dars).
Chart/graph savolida (26–27) so'zlarni emas, NISBATLARNI tinglang: "kichik foiz", "yarmidan ko'pi", "birinchi o'rinda", "eng kam foydali".
Test tugagach ustoz javoblarni o'qiydi; har o'quvchi to'g'ri javoblar sonini sanaydi va jadval bo'yicha band ballni topadi.
presentation: Audio necha marta eshittiriladi?
Bir marta. Test paytida to'xtatilmaydi va qayta qo'yilmaydi.

Test paytida savol varag'iga, oxirgi 10 daqiqada javob varag'iga ko'chiring.

To'xtamang, keyingi savolga o'ting. Oxirida taxminiy javob yozing — bo'sh joy aniq 0 ball.
Katta-kichik harf muhimmi?
Yo'q. "SCOTLAND" ham, "Scotland" ham to'g'ri. Imlo esa muhim.

Ikkalasi ham to'g'ri: raqamni raqam yoki so'z bilan yozish mumkin.
Kalitdagi qavs nimani anglatadi?
"(very) clean" — "clean" ham, "very clean" ham qabul qilinadi.
Qancha to'g'ri javob — qaysi band?
Pastdagi jadvalga qarang: 16–17 = 5.0, 23–25 = 6.0, 30–31 = 7.0.
notes: Bu dars — birinchi to'liq Listening testi. Maqsad — imtihon ritmini his qilish va zaif savol turlarini aniqlash.
Audio 4 faylga bo'lingan. Imtihon sharoiti uchun ketma-ket qo'ying, oralarida to'xtatmang — section ichidagi o'qish pauzalari audioning o'zida bor.

Uch shoxli Rothschild jirafalarini soat 12 va 3 da qo'l bilan boqish mumkin (13). Sigir va echkilarni silash mumkin bo'lgan joy kun bo'yi ochiq — bolalar uchun (14). Gepardlar har kuni 3.40 da soatiga 70 km gacha tezlikda "mashq yugurishi"ni bajaradi (15).

16–20. (Pauzadan keyin) Xodim va tinglovchilar asosiy kirishda turibdi, ma'lumot markazi o'ngda. Ertalabki sayr 10.45 da meerkatlar qo'rasidan boshlanadi: bolalar maydonchasi yonidan o'tadi, birinchi qo'rada — otters, keyingi qo'rada — Yangi Zelandiya qushlari (16), keyin sudralib yuruvchilar va yo'lbarslar. Afrika qishlog'i: kirishdan o'ngga buriling, birinchi avtobus bekatidan o'ting — Afrika yovvoyi itlari qo'rasidan oldin (17). Piknik joyi — parkning eng sharqida, bir tomonda tuyaqushlar, boshqa tomonda buffalo (18). Tushdan keyingi sayr: g'arbdagi sherlar maskaniga (Conservation Centre yonida) boring, ikki avtobus bekatidan o'ting, ikkinchisidan keyin taxminan yarim km — uchrashuv joyi; zebradan o'tib ketsangiz — uzoqlab ketgansiz (19). Safari avtobusining birinchi bekati — Jomo's Café: to'g'ri qarshida, jirafalar oldida (20).

intro: Ikki talaba — Sylvie va Daniel — o'qituvchi Mr Driver oldida o'tgan semestrdagi study-skills kursi bo'yicha so'rovnoma natijalarini taqdim qiladi. 26-savol — doiraviy diagramma (A–C), 27-savol — ustunli grafik (A–C): rasmga qarang.

homework_intro: Bugun birinchi marta to'liq Listening testini imtihon sharoitida bajardik va band ballni jadvaldan topdik; uyga vazifa esa ball haqida emas — maqsad qaysi savol turida yiqilganingizni aniqlash.

Birinchi vazifa — "Xato tahlili jadvali": har bir xatoingizni bitta qatorga yozing (savol raqami — savol turi — mening javobim — to'g'ri javob — sabab: eshitmadim / paraphrase'ni tanimadim / tuzoqqa tushdim / imlo / so'z chegarasi), bunga 10–15 daqiqa yetadi.

Ikkinchisi — "Part 3 ni qayta tinglash": CD2 Track 33 ni kitob transkripti bilan qayta tinglang va 21–27 savollarning har birida rad etilgan variant transkriptning qayerida aytilganini qalam bilan belgilang, taxminan 20 daqiqa; uchinchisi — "Zaif tur takrori": jadvalda eng ko'p takrorlangan tur bo'yicha bitta eski skriptni qaytadan bajaring (form — 3/23-dars, map — 17-dars, MCQ — 9/24-dars, Part 4 — 30-dars).

Eng ko'p qilinadigan xato — xatolarni shunchaki sanab, sabab o'rniga "e'tiborsizlik" deb yozib qo'yish: sabab aniq bo'lmasa jadval befoyda, shuning uchun har qatorga yuqoridagi beshta sababdan roppa-rosa bittasini tanlang.

Uchala vazifa ham bitta daftarga yoziladi va keyingi dars boshida tekshiraman: barcha xatolar sababi bilan yozilsa 2 coin, Part 3 ning yettita savolida rad etilgan variantlar belgilansa 1 coin, zaif tur takrori esa keyingi darslardagi mashqlarga asos bo'ladi.

lessons.title: Reading: Full Reading Test (Passage 1–3)
lessons.grammar_topic: To'liq Reading testi — 3 passage, 40 savol, 60 daqiqa
lessons.book_ref: Jony Academy materiali — ustoz bergan Full Practice Reading (William Kamkwamba; White mountain, green tourism; Reading in a whole new way).
objectives: To'liq IELTS Reading testini imtihon sharoitida 60 daqiqada bajarish (javob varag'iga ko'chirish uchun qo'shimcha vaqt YO'Q).
Vaqtni passage bo'yicha taqsimlash: P1 — 17–18 daqiqa, P2 — 20 daqiqa, P3 — 22 daqiqa.
1–31-darslarda o'rganilgan savol turlarini bitta testda qo'llash.
Natijani band ballga o'girish va o'z xatolarini savol turi bo'yicha tahlil qilish.
Keyingi mock testlar (34–35-darslar) uchun shaxsiy "zaif savol turlari" ro'yxatini tuzish.
materials: Savol varag'i: Full Practice Reading — uchala matn (William Kamkwamba; White mountain, green tourism; Reading in a whole new way) va 1–40 savollar bitta to'plamda, har o'quvchiga bitta nusxa; 1–5 uchun flow chart kataklari bo'sh, 19–22 uchun A–E variantlari va 37–40 uchun A–F oxirlari qutisi aniq ko'rinib tursin.
Javob varag'i (1–40) — har o'quvchiga bitta, qo'ng'iroqqacha stol ustida tayyor tursin: Reading'da ko'chirish uchun qo'shimcha vaqt yo'q, o'quvchi javobni darhol shu varaqqa yozadi.

Javoblar kaliti (1–40) — ustozdagi kitob nusxasidan; 5-bosqichda ovoz chiqarib o'qiladi. Kalitda 6-savol (FALSE), 24-savol (summer) va 32-savol (NOT GIVEN) oldindan belgilab qo'yilsin — bular testning eng ko'p xato qilinadigan uchtasi.

Xato tahlili jadvali: besh ustunli bo'sh varaqa (savol raqami, savol turi, mening javobim, to'g'ri javob, xato sababi) — har o'quvchiga bitta; 6-bosqichda to'ldiriladi va shu varaqa birinchi uyga vazifa bo'lib ketadi.

Doskada qo'ng'iroqqacha: vaqt rejasi soat raqamlari bilan (P1 — 17–18 daqiqa, P2 — 20 daqiqa, P3 — 22 daqiqa, testning tugash vaqti aniq yozilgan) va yonida yirik harflar bilan "KO'CHIRISH VAQTI YO'Q — javobni darhol varaqqa yoz". "To'g'ri javoblar → band" jadvali doskaning ikkinchi qanotiga yozilib, test tugaguncha yopiq tursin (yoki alohida qog'ozga yozib qo'yiladi va 5-bosqichda osiladi).

Ustozda soat yoki sekundomer — har 20 daqiqada vaqt e'lon qilinadi ("Passage 2 ga o'ting"). O'quvchilar xatolar daftari, qalam va o'chirg'ich bilan keladi; ikkinchi uyga vazifa uchun 6, 19, 25 va 31-darslarning uyga vazifa matnlari ustozda zaxira nusxada bo'lsin — dars oxirida o'quvchining zaif turiga qarab beriladi.

intro: Reading testi 60 daqiqa davom etadi va Listening'dan farqli ravishda javobni ko'chirish uchun qo'shimcha vaqt berilmaydi. Javoblarni to'g'ridan-to'g'ri javob varag'iga yozing.

Passage'lar qiyinlashib boradi: P1 — eng oson (faktlar), P2 — o'rta (matching, pick from list), P3 — eng qiyin (muallif fikri, MCQ, sentence endings). Shuning uchun P1 ni tezroq ishlab, P3 ga ko'proq vaqt qoldiring.

Bu testdagi savol turlari: flow chart (4-dars), T/F/NG (6-dars), short answer (4-dars), matching information (25-dars), pick from a list (18-dars), sentence completion (15-dars), MCQ (11-dars), Y/N/NG (19-dars), sentence endings (31-dars).
Har passage boshida 1 daqiqa: sarlavha, qism sarlavhasi va savol turlarini ko'rib chiqing, so'z chegaralarini belgilang (TWO WORDS / ONE WORD and/or a NUMBER).
Bitta savolga 2 daqiqadan ortiq vaqt sarflamang. Belgilab qo'ying va oxirida qayting. Bo'sh joy qoldirmang — noto'g'ri javob uchun ball olinmaydi.
Test tugagach ustoz javoblarni o'qiydi; har o'quvchi to'g'ri javoblar sonini sanaydi va jadval bo'yicha band ballni topadi.
presentation: Javob varag'iga qachon yozaman?
Darhol. Reading'da ko'chirish uchun qo'shimcha vaqt yo'q.
Savollarni qaysi tartibda ishlayman?
Passage tartibida. Passage ichida — avval tartibli turlar, keyin matching (NEVER guruhi).
Vaqt tugab qolsa?
Qolgan savollarga taxminiy javob yozing — bo'sh joy aniq 0 ball.
Katta-kichik harf muhimmi?
Yo'q. Lekin imlo muhim.
"39 feet" yoki "39"?
Ikkalasi ham to'g'ri: ko'rsatma "ONE WORD and/or a NUMBER".
Qancha to'g'ri javob — qaysi band?
Pastdagi jadvalga qarang: 23–26 = 6.0, 30–32 = 7.0.
notes: Bu dars — birinchi to'liq Reading testi. Maqsad ball emas, balki vaqtni boshqarish tajribasi va zaif savol turlarini aniqlash.
Test paytida ustoz har 20 daqiqada vaqtni e'lon qiladi: "Passage 2 ga o'ting".
Javoblar ustoz bergan kitob kaliti bilan tekshirildi. Eng qiyin savollar: 6 (FALSE — NOT GIVEN emas), 24 (summer — ski season tuzoq), 32 (NOT GIVEN).

Qo'shimcha matn berilmaydi: dars to'liq test + tahlildan iborat (60 + 40 daqiqa).

readings.title: Passage 1. William Kamkwamba
readings.source: Jony Academy materiali — Full Practice Reading
text: At only 14 years old, William Kamkwamba built a series of windmills that could generate electricity in his African village, Masitala, in Malawi, south-eastern Africa.

In 2002, William Kamkwamba had to drop out of school, as his father, a maize and tobacco farmer, could no longer afford his school fees. But despite this setback, William was determined to get his education. He began visiting a local library that had just opened in his old primary school, where he discovered a tattered science book. With only a rudimentary grasp of English, he _taught himself basic physics_ – mainly by studying photos and diagrams. Another book he found there featured windmills on the cover and inspired him to try and build his own.

He started by constructing a _small model_. Then, with the help of a cousin and friend, he spent many weeks searching _scrap yards_ and found old tractor fans, shock absorbers, plastic pipe and bicycle parts, which he used to build the real thing.

For windmill blades, William cut some _bath pipe_ in two lengthwise, then heated the pieces over hot coals to press the curled edges flat. To bore holes into the blades, he stuck a nail through half a corncob, heated the metal red and twisted it through the blades. It took three hours to repeatedly heat the nail and bore the holes. He attached the blades to a _tractor fan_ using proper nuts and bolts and then to the back axle of a bicycle. Electricity was generated through the bicycle dynamo. When the wind blew the blades, the bike chain spun the bike wheel, which charged the dynamo and sent a current through wire to his house.

What he had built was a crude machine that produced 12 volts and _powered four lights_. When it was all done, the windmill's wingspan measured more than eight feet and sat on top of a rickety tower 15 feet tall that swayed violently in strong gales. He eventually replaced the tower with a sturdier one that stands _39 feet_, and built a second machine that watered a family garden.

The windmill brought William Kamkwamba _instant local fame_, but despite his accomplishment, he was still unable to return to school. However, news of his magetsi a mphepo – electric wind – spread beyond Malawi, and eventually things began to change. An education official, who had heard news of the windmill, came to visit his village and was amazed to learn that William had been out of school for five years. He arranged for him to attend secondary school at the government's expense and _brought journalists to the farm_ to see the windmill. Then a story published in the Malawi Daily Mail caught the attention of bloggers, which in turn caught the attention of organisers for the Technology Entertainment and Design conference.

In 2007, William spoke at the TED Global conference in Tanzania and got a standing ovation. Businessmen stepped forward with offers to fund his education and projects, and with money donated by them, he was able to put his cousin and several friends back into school and pay for some medical needs of his family. With the donation, he also _drilled a borehole for a well and water pump_ in his village and installed drip irrigation in his father's fields.

The water pump has allowed his family to expand its crops. They have abandoned tobacco and now grow maize, beans, soybeans, potatoes and peanuts. The windmills have also brought big lifestyle and health changes to the other villagers. 'The village has changed a lot,' William says. 'Now, the time that they would have spent going to fetch water, they are using for doing other things. And also the water they are drinking is clean water, so _there is less disease_.' The villagers have also _stopped using kerosene_ and can use the money previously spent on fuel to buy other things.

William Kamkwamba's example has inspired other children in the village to _pursue science_. William says they now see that if they put their mind to something, they can achieve it. 'It has changed the way people think,' he says.
paraphrases: with the help of a cousin
raised the blades on a tower
sat on top of a tower
drilled a borehole for a well and water pump
inspired other children to pursue science

"He attached the blades to a tractor fan ... and then to the back axle of a bicycle". Fixed = attached.

readings.title: Passage 2. White mountain, green tourism
readings.qtype: Matching information (14–18) + Pick from a list (19–22) + Sentence completion (23–26)
readings.source: Jony Academy materiali — Full Practice Reading
text: The French Alpine town of Chamonix has been a magnet for tourists since the 18th century. But today, tourism and climate change are putting pressure on the surrounding environment. Marc Grainger reports.

A. The town of Chamonix-Mont-Blanc sits in a valley at 1,035 metres above sea level in the Haute-Savoie department in south-eastern France. To the north-west are the red peaks of the Aiguilles Rouges massif; to the south-east are the permanently white peaks of Mont Blanc, which at 4,810 metres is the highest mountain in the Alps. It's a typical Alpine environment, but one that is under increasing strain from the hustle and bustle of human activity.

B. Tourism is Chamonix's lifeblood. Visitors have been encouraged to visit the valley ever since it was discovered by _explorers_ in 1741. Over 40 years later, in 1786, Mont Blanc's summit was finally reached by a French doctor and his guide, and this gave birth to the sport of alpinism, with Chamonix at its centre. In 1924, it hosted the first Winter Olympics, and the cable cars and lifts that were built in the years that followed gave everyone access to the ski slopes.

C. Today, Chamonix is a modern town, connected to the outside world via the Mont Blanc Road Tunnel and a busy highway network. It receives up to 60,000 visitors at a time during the ski season, and _climbers, hikers and extreme-sports enthusiasts_ swarm there in the _summer in even greater numbers_, swelling the town's population to 100,000. It is the third most visited natural site in the world, according to Chamonix's Tourism Office and, last year, it had 5.2 million visitor bed nights – all this in a town with fewer than 10,000 permanent inhabitants.

D. This influx of tourists has put the local environment under severe pressure, and the authorities in the valley have decided to take action. Educating visitors is vital. _Tourists are warned not to drop rubbish_, and there are now recycling points dotted all around the valley, from the town centre to halfway up the mountains. _An internet blog reports environmental news_ in the town, and the 'green' message is delivered with all the tourist office's activities.

E. Low-carbon initiatives are also important for the region. _France is committed to reducing its carbon emissions by a factor of four by 2050._ Central to achieving this aim is a strategy that encourages communities to identify their carbon emissions on a local level and make plans to reduce them. Studies have identified that accommodation accounts for half of all carbon emissions in the Chamonix valley. Hotels are known to be inefficient operations, but those around Chamonix are now cleaning up their act. Some are using low-energy lighting, restricting water use and _making recycling bins available for guests_; others have invested in huge projects such as furnishing and decorating using locally sourced materials, using geothermal energy for heating and _installing solar panels_.

F. Chamonix's council is encouraging the use of renewable energy in private properties too, by making funds available for green renovations and new constructions. At the same time, public-sector buildings have also undergone improvements to make them more energy efficient and less wasteful. For example, _the local ice rink has reduced its annual water consumption_ from 140,000 cubic metres to 10,000 cubic metres in the space of three years.

G. Improving public transport is another feature of the new policy, as 80 percent of carbon emissions from transport used to come from private vehicles. While the Mont Blanc Express is an ideal way to travel within the valley – and see some incredible scenery along the route – it is much more difficult to arrive in Chamonix from outside by rail. There is no direct line from the closest airport in Geneva, so tourists arriving by air normally transfer by car or bus. However, at a cost of 3.3 million euros a year, Chamonix has introduced _a free shuttle service in order to get people out of their cars_ and into buses fitted with particle filters.

H. If the valley's visitors and residents want to know why they need to reduce their environmental impact, they just have to look up; the effects of climate change are there for everyone to see in _the melting glaciers_ that cling to the mountains. The fragility of the Alpine environment has long been a concern among local people. Today, 70 percent of the 805 square kilometres that comprise Chamonix-Mont-Blanc is protected in some way. But now, the impact of tourism has led the authorities to recognise that more must be done if the valley is to remain prosperous: that they must not only protect the natural environment better, but also _manage the numbers of visitors better_, so that its residents can happily remain there.

a system changing the way visitors reach Chamonix
in a valley at 1,035 metres ... in south-eastern France
manage the numbers of visitors better

tourists are warned not to drop rubbish

tasks.title: Questions 19–22: Choose TWO letters, A–E
tasks.instr: Ikkala savol bloki — D va E xatboshilarida.
items: 19–20 Which TWO ways that the authorities aim to educate tourists are mentioned? A) giving instructions about litter B) imposing fines on people who drop litter C) handing out leaflets in the town D) operating a web-based information service E) having a paper-free tourist office

21–22 Which TWO ways that hotels are reducing their carbon emissions are mentioned? A) using natural cleaning materials B) recycling water C) limiting guest numbers D) providing places for rubbish E) harnessing energy from the sun
why: "Tourists are warned not to drop rubbish" (A) va "An internet blog reports environmental news" (D). B tuzoq: ogohlantirish bor, jarima yo'q. E tuzoq: "the 'green' message is delivered with all the tourist office's activities" — qog'ozsiz ofis emas.

"Making recycling bins available for guests" (D) va "installing solar panels" (E). B tuzoq: "restricting water use" — suvni cheklash, qayta ishlash emas. A tuzoq: "cleaning up their act" — ibora, tozalash vositalari emas.

tasks.title: Questions 23–26: Complete the sentences
tasks.type: NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS from the passage
items: The first people to discover the Chamonix valley were ___.
Chamonix's busiest tourist season is the ___.
Public areas, such as the ___ in Chamonix, are using fewer resources.
The ___ on the mountains around Chamonix provide visual evidence of global warming.
why: "Ever since it was discovered by explorers in 1741". Tuzoq: "a French doctor" — cho'qqini zabt etgan, vodiyni kashf etmagan.

Qishda "up to 60,000 visitors at a time during the ski season", yozda esa "in the summer in even greater numbers, swelling the town's population to 100,000". Eng gavjum — yoz. Tuzoq: "ski season" — birinchi ko'rinadi, lekin raqam kichikroq.
"The local ice rink has reduced its annual water consumption". Public areas = public-sector buildings.
"The effects of climate change are there for everyone to see in the melting glaciers that cling to the mountains". "Glaciers" yoki "melting glaciers".
tasks.note: 24-savol testning eng yaxshi tuzog'i: matnda avval "ski season" keladi, lekin "even greater numbers" — yozda. Taqqoslovchi so'zlarni (greater, more, busiest) diqqat bilan o'qing.

readings.title: Passage 3. Reading in a whole new way
readings.source: Jony Academy materiali — Full Practice Reading
text: As technology improves, how does the act of reading change?

Reading and writing, like all technologies, are constantly changing. In ancient times, authors often dictated their books. Dictation sounded like an uninterrupted series of words, so _scribes wrote these down in one long continuous string_, justastheyoccurinspeech. For this reason, text was written without spaces between words until the 11th century. This continuous script made books hard to read, so only a few people were accomplished at reading them aloud to others. Being able to read silently to yourself was considered an amazing talent; writing was an even rarer skill. In fact, in 15th-century Europe, only one in 20 adult males could write.

After Gutenberg's invention of the printing press in about 1440, mass-produced books changed the way people read and wrote. The technology of printing increased the number of words available, and more types of media, such as newspapers and magazines, _broadened what was written about_. Authors no longer had to produce scholarly works, as was common until then, but could write, for example, inexpensive, heart-rending love stories or publish autobiographies, even if they were unknown.

In time, _the power of the written word gave birth to the idea of authority and expertise_. Laws were compiled into official documents, contracts were written down and nothing was valid unless it was in this form. Painting, music, architecture, dance were all important, but the heartbeat of many cultures was the turning pages of a book. By the early 19th century, public libraries had been built in many cities.

Today, words are migrating from paper to computers, phones, laptops and game consoles. Some 4.5 billion digital screens illuminate our lives. Letters are no longer fixed in black ink on paper, but flitter on a glass surface in a rainbow of colors as fast as our eyes can blink. _Screens fill our pockets, briefcases, cars, living-room walls and the sides of buildings._ They sit in front of us when we work – regardless of what we do. And of course, these newly ubiquitous screens have changed how we read and write.

The first screens that overtook culture, several decades ago – the big, fat, warm tubes of television – reduced the time we spent reading to such an extent that it seemed as if reading and writing were over. Educators and parents worried deeply that the TV generation would be unable to write. But _the interconnected, cool, thin displays of computer screens launched an epidemic of writing_ that continues to swell. As a consequence, _the amount of time people spend reading has almost tripled since 1980_. By 2008, the World Wide Web contained more than a trillion pages, and that total grows rapidly every day.

But it is not book reading or newspaper reading, it is screen reading. Screens are always on, and, unlike books, we never stop staring at them. This new platform is very visual, and it is gradually merging words with moving images. You might think of this new medium as books we watch, or television we read. We also use screens to present data, and this encourages numeracy: _visualising data and reading charts, looking at pictures and symbols are all part of this new literacy_.

_Screens engage our bodies, too._ The most we may do while reading a book is to flip the pages or turn over a corner, but when we use a screen, we interact with what we see. In the futuristic movie Minority Report, _the main character stands in front of a screen and hunts through huge amounts of information as if conducting an orchestra_. Just as it seemed strange five centuries ago to see someone read silently, in the future it will seem strange to read without moving your body.

In addition, screens encourage more utilitarian (practical) thinking. A new idea or unfamiliar fact will cause a reflex to do something: to research a word, to question your screen 'friends' for their opinions or to find alternative views. _Book reading strengthened our analytical skills_, encouraging us to think carefully about how we feel. _Screen reading, on the other hand, encourages quick responses_, associating this idea with another, equipping us to deal with the thousands of new thoughts expressed every day. For example, _we review a movie for our friends while we watch it_; we read the owner's manual of a device we see in a shop before we purchase it, rather than after we get home and discover that it can't do what we need it to do.

Screens provoke action instead of persuasion. _Propaganda is less effective, and false information is hard to deliver in a world of screens_ because while misinformation travels fast, corrections do, too. On a screen, it is often easier to correct a falsehood than to tell one in the first place. _Wikipedia works so well because it removes an error in a single click._ In books, we find a revealed truth; on the screen, we assemble our own truth from pieces. What is more, a screen can reveal the inner nature of things. Waving the camera eye of a smartphone over the bar code of a manufactured product reveals its price, origins and even relevant comments by other owners. _It is as if the screen displays the object's intangible essence._ A popular children's toy (Webkinz) instills stuffed animals with a virtual character that is 'hidden' inside; a screen enables children to play with this inner character online in a virtual world.
In the near future, screens will be the first place we'll look for answers, for friends, for news, for meaning, for our sense of who we are and who we can be.

growing status of the written word
the power of the written word gave birth to the idea of authority
screens fill our pockets, briefcases, cars ... / ubiquitous
launched an epidemic of writing ... time spent reading has almost tripled
a wider range of visual skills
visualising data, reading charts, pictures and symbols

tasks.title: Questions 27–31: Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D
tasks.instr: Javoblar matn tartibida. "In the third paragraph" — faqat shu xatboshini o'qing.
items: 27 What does the writer say about dictation? A) It helped people learn to read. B) It affected the way people wrote. C) It was not used until the 11th century. D) It was used mainly for correspondence.

28 According to the writer, what changed after the invention of the printing press? A) Romance became more popular than serious fiction. B) Newspapers became more popular than books. C) Readers asked for more autobiographies. D) Authors had a wider choice of topics.

29 In the third paragraph, the writer focuses on the A) legal concerns of authors. B) rapid changes in public libraries. C) growing status of the written word. D) recognition of the book as an art form.
30 What does the writer say about screens in the fourth paragraph? A) They are hard to read. B) They are bad for our health. C) They can improve our work. D) They can be found everywhere.

31 According to the writer, computers differ from television because they A) encourage more reading. B) attract more criticism. C) take up more of our leisure time. D) include more educational content.
why: "Dictation sounded like an uninterrupted series of words, so scribes wrote these down in one long continuous string". C tuzoq: 11-asr — bo'sh joylar paydo bo'lgan vaqt, diktovka boshlanishi emas. A teskari: kitoblarni o'qish qiyinlashgan.
"Broadened what was written about. Authors no longer had to produce scholarly works". A, B, C — solishtirish va o'quvchi talabi aytilmagan; love stories va autobiographies faqat misol.
"The power of the written word gave birth to the idea of authority and expertise ... nothing was valid unless it was in this form". A tuzoq: qonunlar misol, mualliflarning muammosi emas.
"Screens fill our pockets, briefcases, cars, living-room walls and the sides of buildings" + "ubiquitous". C tuzoq: ish paytida oldimizda turadi, lekin ishni yaxshilashi aytilmagan.
Televizor o'qish vaqtini kamaytirgan, kompyuter esa "launched an epidemic of writing ... the amount of time people spend reading has almost tripled".

tasks.title: Questions 32–36: YES, NO or NOT GIVEN
items: Screen reading has reduced the number of books and newspapers people read.
Screen literacy requires a wider range of visual skills than book-based literacy.
Screen reading is more active than book reading.
Screens and books produce similar thought patterns in their readers.
People are easily persuaded to believe lies on the screen.
why: Muallif "it is not book reading or newspaper reading, it is screen reading" deydi — bu farq, lekin kitob/gazeta o'qish kamaygani haqida fikr yo'q.
"Visualising data and reading charts, looking at pictures and symbols are all part of this new literacy". Kitobda esa faqat so'z.
"The most we may do while reading a book is to flip the pages ... when we use a screen, we interact with what we see".
"Book reading strengthened our analytical skills ... Screen reading, on the other hand, encourages quick responses".
"Propaganda is less effective, and false information is hard to deliver in a world of screens".
tasks.note: 32-savol — eng qiyin NOT GIVEN: muallif ekran va kitob o'qishini FARQLAYDI, lekin kitob o'qish KAMAYDI demaydi. Farq ≠ kamayish.

homework_intro: Bugun birinchi marta to'liq Reading testini imtihon sharoitida ishladik — uyga vazifa ham shundan kelib chiqadi: endi bizga ball emas, har bir xatoning sababi kerak.

Birinchi vazifa — "Xato tahlili jadvali": darsda boshlagan jadvalni uyda oxirigacha to'ldiring, har xato uchun savol raqami, savol turi, o'z javobingiz, to'g'ri javob va sabab yozilsin (paraphrase'ni ko'rmadim, so'z chegarasi, tuzoq yoki vaqt yetmadi) — 15–20 daqiqa oladi.

Ikkinchi vazifa — "Zaif tur takrori": jadvalda eng ko'p xato chiqqan turni oling va o'sha turni o'rgangan darsning uyga vazifa matnini qaytadan bajaring (T/F/NG bo'lsa 6-dars, Y/N/NG bo'lsa 19-dars, matching information bo'lsa 25-dars, sentence endings bo'lsa 31-dars); uchinchisi — "Passage 3 qayta o'qish": "Reading in a whole new way" matnini bu safar vaqtsiz, tinch o'qib chiqib, 10 ta paraphrase juftini yozasiz — chapda savoldagi so'z, o'ngda matndagi ibora (masalan, "can be found everywhere — screens fill our pockets"). Ikkalasi birga 30 daqiqacha oladi.

Eng ko'p qilinadigan xato — jadvalga faqat "noto'g'ri" deb yozib qo'yish: sabab ustuni bo'sh qolsa, vazifa bajarilmagan hisoblanadi, chunki bizga necha xato qilganingiz emas, QAYSI turda xato qilganingiz kerak.

Uchala vazifani ham keyingi dars boshida daftar ochiq holda stolga qo'yasiz; men jadvalingizga qarab har biringizga ikkita zaif savol turini belgilab beraman — 34 va 35-darsdagi mock testlarda aynan shularni kuzataman.

homework.title: Xato tahlili jadvali
homework.instr: Testdagi har xatoingizni jadvalga yozing: savol raqami — savol turi — mening javobim — to'g'ri javob — xato sababi (paraphrase / so'z chegarasi / tuzoq / vaqt).
homework.answers: Ustoz jadval asosida har o'quvchiga 2 ta zaif savol turini belgilaydi.

homework.title: Zaif tur takrori
homework.instr: Eng ko'p xato qilgan savol turingiz bo'yicha oldingi darsdan (masalan, 6, 19, 25 yoki 31-dars) uyga vazifa matnini qayta bajaring.
homework.answers: Javoblar o'sha darsning Reading bo'limida.

homework.title: Passage 3 qayta o'qish
homework.instr: "Reading in a whole new way" matnini vaqtsiz qayta o'qing va 10 ta paraphrase juftini yozing (savoldagi so'z — matndagi ibora).
homework.answers: Reading bo'limidagi paraphrase jadvali bilan solishtiriladi.

lessons.title: Mock oldidan: imtihon kuni strategiyasi va vaqt boshqaruvi
lessons.grammar_topic: Mock testga tayyorgarlik — Listening Part 1–4 va Reading 3 passage uchun daqiqama-daqiqa reja, xom balldan band ballga o'tish
lessons.book_ref: Jony Academy materiali — CRM dagi IELTS mock test bazasi (2026-09-26) va rasmiy xom ball → band jadvallari (Listening va Academic Reading, 40 savoldan).
objectives: Mock kunida nima, qaysi tartibda bo'lishini aniq bilish: Listening, Reading, Writing, Speaking — har biri qanday o'tadi.
Kompyuterdagi ekranni oldindan tanish qilish: 40 savol, taymer, javob katagi va sahifadan chiqish hisoblanishi.
Listening uchun reja: skript BIR MARTA o'qiladi, javob eshitilayotgan paytda yoziladi.
Reading uchun reja: har passage'ga 20 daqiqa, qaysi savol turidan boshlash, qaysi savolni tashlab ketib keyin qaytish.
Bilmagan savolda nima qilishni qoida darajasida o'zlashtirish: bo'sh katak — aniq nol.
40 savoldan olingan xom ballni o'zi band ballga o'gira olish va "30/40 nima degani" degan savolga javob bera olish.
materials: Har o'quvchiga bitta bo'sh "Reading 60 daqiqa rejasi" varaqasi: uch ustun (Passage 1, Passage 2, Passage 3), har ustunda "boshlanadi" va "tugaydi" qatorlari bo'sh — 4-mashqda soat raqamlari bilan to'ldiriladi va mock kuniga olib boriladi.

Doskada qo'ng'iroqqacha yozib qo'yilgan xom ball → band jadvali: chap ustun Listening, o'ng ustun Academic Reading, o'rtada band. 1-mashqgacha yopiq tursin (varaq bilan berkitiladi), chunki 2-mashqda o'quvchilar jadvalni yoddan emas, o'qib ishlatishi kerak.

Ustozda: proyektor yoki bitta kompyuter — guruh test ekranidan mock havolasi ochilib, o'quvchilarga ekranning o'zi ko'rsatiladi (taymer qayerda, savollar ro'yxati qayerda, javob katagi qanday). Havola faqat ko'rsatish uchun ochiladi, test boshlanmaydi.
Sekundomer yoki telefon taymeri — 3-mashqda Part oralig'idagi 30–40 soniyani va 4-mashqda 20 daqiqalik bo'lakni real vaqtda sanash uchun.
Har o'quvchida 33-darsdagi to'ldirilgan xato tahlili jadvali — 7-bosqichda har kim o'zining ikkita zaif savol turini shu jadvaldan topadi.
Bo'sh qog'oz va qalam har o'quvchida: Listening paytida ism va raqamlarni qoralama qilish odati bugun mashq qilinadi.
timeline: Yangi mavzu yo'q; maqsad — mock kunida o'zini qanday tutish
Listening, Reading, Writing, Speaking — nima qachon va qancha davom etadi
